2023-06-1C:1-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: fractional distillation.** Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons whose boiling points increase as their molecules get bigger. The oil is heated so most of it vaporises, and the vapours rise up a fractionating column that is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top. Each fraction, including gasoline, condenses at the height where the column temperature matches its boiling range, so the mixture is separated.
2023-06-1C:1-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:1-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: chromatography.** A spot of black ink is put near the bottom of some absorbent paper and the paper is dipped in solvent. Each dye in the ink dissolves to a different extent and is attracted differently to the paper, so the dyes travel up the paper at different speeds and separate into distinct spots. This is exactly what chromatography is designed to do — separate the substances in a mixture so they can be identified.
2023-06-1C:1-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:1-a-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: simple distillation.** The seawater is heated in a flask until pure water boils off and evaporates. The vapour travels into a water-cooled condenser, where it turns back into liquid and is collected — that distillate is pure water, because the dissolved salt has a very high boiling point and stays behind in the flask. Distillation is the best choice whenever you need to obtain the solvent itself from a solution.
2023-06-1C:1-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:1-b.solutionMd: **Answer: first dissolving, then filtering, then evaporating, then crystallisation.** Copper(II) sulfate is soluble while copper(II) oxide is insoluble, and that difference is what the separation exploits. Start by dissolving the mixture in distilled water: the copper(II) sulfate goes into solution but the copper(II) oxide stays as a solid. Filter the mixture — the copper(II) oxide is trapped on the filter paper as the residue, while the copper(II) sulfate solution passes through as the filtrate. Warm the filtrate to drive off some of the water by evaporating, which concentrates the solution. Finally let the hot, concentrated solution cool slowly so that crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulfate form — crystallisation gives a pure solid sample.
2023-06-1C:1-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:2-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃.** Iron rusts when it is exposed to both water and oxygen from the air, and the reddish-brown product that forms is hydrated iron(III) oxide. The name matters: the iron is present as Fe³⁺ ions (iron(III)), not Fe²⁺, and the solid is hydrated because water is incorporated into it. Simply writing iron oxide is too vague — the oxidation state must be given.
2023-06-1C:2-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:2-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: D — oxidation.** Rusting is iron combining with oxygen from the air, and gaining oxygen is the definition of oxidation. The other options do not fit: combustion (A) is rapid burning in oxygen with a flame and lots of heat, whereas rusting is a slow reaction at room temperature; decomposition (B) would need one substance splitting into simpler ones, but here two substances join together; and neutralisation (C) is an acid reacting with a base to form a salt and water, which plays no part in rusting.
2023-06-1C:2-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:2-a-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: zinc.** Galvanising means coating the iron with a thin layer of zinc. The zinc acts as a physical barrier keeping water and oxygen away from the iron, and because zinc is more reactive than iron it also corrodes sacrificially — it oxidises in preference to the iron, so the iron underneath stays protected even when the coating is scratched.
2023-06-1C:2-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:2-b-i.solutionMd: **Answer: Fe + H₂SO₄ → FeSO₄ + H₂.** Iron is above hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it displaces hydrogen from dilute sulfuric acid: each iron atom gives up electrons to the hydrogen ions, forming iron(II) sulfate solution and hydrogen gas. Check the balancing — one Fe, two H, one S and four O on each side — so the equation is correct with no extra numbers needed.
2023-06-1C:2-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:2-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: put a lighted splint at the mouth of the tube — hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop.** Collect the gas given off and hold a lighted splint (a lit Bunsen flame works too) at the mouth of the tube. The hydrogen mixes with oxygen in the air and ignites rapidly, producing the characteristic squeaky pop sound. Do not use a glowing splint here — that is the test for oxygen, not for hydrogen — and note that just saying the gas burns is not the full test; the pop is the identifying observation.
2023-06-1C:2-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:2-c-i.solutionMd: **Answer: displacement.** Iron is more reactive than copper, so the iron atoms push the copper out of its salt solution — a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound. It is also fine to call this a redox reaction: iron atoms are oxidised (they lose electrons to become Fe²⁺ ions) while the copper ions are reduced as they gain electrons and come out of solution as the metal.
2023-06-1C:2-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:2-c-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: a pink-brown solid forms.** The iron displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate solution, so copper metal is deposited as a pink-brown (orange-brown) coating on the iron surface while the blue colour of the solution fades as the blue copper ions are used up. Just writing copper is not enough — the question wants the appearance, so the colour of the solid must be stated.
2023-06-1C:2-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:2-d.solutionMd: **Answer: iron is less reactive than magnesium — it is lower in the reactivity series — so it cannot displace magnesium from its compound.** A displacement reaction only works when the metal added is the more reactive of the two. Magnesium sits above iron in the reactivity series, so iron is not reactive enough to push magnesium out of magnesium sulfate solution, and no reaction occurs.
2023-06-1C:2-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:3-a.solutionMd: **Answer: Y has covalent bonding with a giant (covalent) structure, and Z has ionic bonding with a giant ionic lattice.** (X is already given as covalent bonding with a simple molecular structure.) The reasoning comes from the conductivity and melting-point columns. Y has a high melting point, so strong bonds must be broken throughout the whole structure, ruling out simple molecular; and since it never conducts, solid or molten, it has no charged particles free to move — the signature of a giant covalent substance such as diamond. Z conducts when molten but not when solid, and only ionic compounds behave this way: in the solid the ions are locked in fixed positions in the giant lattice, but melting frees the ions to move and carry the charge.
2023-06-1C:3-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:3-b.solutionMd: **Answer: X has weak intermolecular forces between its molecules, so only a little energy is needed to overcome them.** In a simple molecular substance the covalent bonds inside each molecule are very strong, but the attractions between one molecule and the next are weak. Melting does not break those covalent bonds — they stay intact — it only separates the molecules from each other. Overcoming the weak intermolecular forces needs little energy, so very little heat is required and the melting point is low. A common error is to claim the covalent bonds break on melting; that is wrong for a simple molecular substance.
2023-06-1C:3-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:4-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: any two of these characteristics of a homologous series: the members share the same general formula; each member differs from the next by CH₂; the members have similar chemical properties because they share the same functional group; the physical properties show a gradual trend, changing as the molecules get bigger.** An example of the pattern is the alkenes: ethene is C₂H₄ and propene is C₃H₆ — one CH₂ added at each step — and both react in the same way because both carry the same C=C functional group, while their boiling points rise steadily along the series. Take care with the last point: physical properties show a trend, they are not the same for every member.
2023-06-1C:4-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:4-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: two shared pairs of electrons between the two carbon atoms, and one shared pair between each hydrogen atom and the carbon it is bonded to.** Ethene, C₂H₄, contains a C=C double bond, so in the dot-and-cross diagram the two carbon atoms share two pairs of outer electrons — four electrons in total, drawn as two overlapping pairs. Each carbon is also bonded to two hydrogen atoms, and every C–H bond is a single shared pair: one electron comes from the carbon and one from the hydrogen. Draw outer shells only, and leave no spare (non-bonding) electrons sitting on either the carbon or the hydrogen atoms.
2023-06-1C:4-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:4-b-i.solutionMd: **Answer: because there are twice as many hydrogen atoms as carbon atoms in every alkene.** The alkenes have the general formula CnH2n: whatever the value of n, the number of hydrogen atoms is double the number of carbon atoms. Dividing any alkene's formula through therefore gives the lowest whole-number ratio of one carbon to two hydrogens — CH₂ — and that simplest ratio is the empirical formula. Ethene (C₂H₄) and propene (C₃H₆) both reduce to exactly that ratio.
2023-06-1C:4-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:4-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: propene is drawn CH₂=CH–CH₃ with every atom and every bond shown, and the repeat unit of poly(propene) is the two-carbon backbone −[CH₂−CH(CH₃)]− with extension bonds sticking out through the brackets.** In the displayed formula of propene the C=C double bond is drawn as two parallel lines, the middle carbon carries a hydrogen, and the end carbon carries the CH₃ (methyl) group. When the monomers polymerise the double bonds open up: the repeat unit keeps the C−C backbone, with 2 H atoms on the first carbon and 1 H plus the CH₃ group on the second. The bonds at each end of the unit must be drawn continuing out of the square brackets, and the letter n outside the brackets stands for the huge number of repeating units.
2023-06-1C:4-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:4-c-i.solutionMd: **Answer: molecular formula C₄H₆; empirical formula C₂H₃.** The structural formula CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂ shows the compound is built from 4 carbon atoms and 6 hydrogen atoms, so its molecular formula is C₄H₆. The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of those atoms: both the 4 and the 6 divide by 2, giving C₂H₃, which has no common factor left so it cannot be simplified further.
2023-06-1C:4-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:4-c-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: add bromine water — it is decolourised.** Shake the hydrocarbon with bromine water in a test tube: an unsaturated compound reacts rapidly with the bromine, so the reagent is decolourised, turning from orange/yellow to colourless. The C=C double bonds are what make this work, because they are reactive enough to open up and add bromine atoms across themselves. A saturated hydrocarbon would not do this in the dark without ultraviolet light, and the orange/yellow colour would simply stay.
2023-06-1C:4-c-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:4-c-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: it is a hydrocarbon because it is made up of just carbon and hydrogen atoms, and it is unsaturated because it contains two C=C (carbon–carbon) double bonds.** Take care to mention atoms, not molecules: the molecule is built only from carbon atoms and hydrogen atoms, with no other element present — that is exactly what the word hydrocarbon means. It is unsaturated because the structural formula CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂ shows two C=C double bonds; a saturated chain would have only single C–C bonds and could hold no more atoms, whereas the double bonds can still open up and add more.
2023-06-1C:4-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:5-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: any two of: effervescence (fizzing, bubbles of gas); the lithium gets smaller and eventually disappears; the lithium moves around on the surface of the water.** Lithium reacts vigorously with water, producing hydrogen gas, so you see effervescence — fizzing and bubbles streaming off the metal. The piece of lithium is gradually used up by the reaction, so it becomes smaller and finally disappears, and because it is less dense than water it skims along, moving across the surface as it reacts.
2023-06-1C:5-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:5-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: the solution turns yellow, because the solution is alkaline.** Lithium reacts with water to make lithium hydroxide, an alkali, so hydroxide ions (OH⁻) build up in the trough as the reaction proceeds. Methyl orange is an indicator that is red in acidic conditions but yellow in alkaline ones, so the final yellow colour is direct evidence that an alkaline solution — lithium hydroxide — has formed from the metal and the water.
2023-06-1C:5-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:5-b.solutionMd: **Answer: do a flame test for the lithium ion, then add dilute acid and test the gas given off with limewater for the carbonate ion.** For the cation: dip a clean wire loop into a sample of the white powder and hold it in the edge of a non-luminous Bunsen flame — a flame test on lithium gives a red (crimson) flame. For the anion: add dilute hydrochloric acid to another sample of the powder. A carbonate fizzes, releasing carbon dioxide gas; pass (bubble) that gas into limewater, and it turns cloudy/milky because a white precipitate of insoluble calcium carbonate forms. The red flame proves Li⁺ is present, and the limewater test proves the carbonate ion is present — so together the two tests show the powder is lithium carbonate.
2023-06-1C:5-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:5-c.solutionMd: **Answer: ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.** In lithium carbonate the lithium atoms lose their outer electron to become positive Li⁺ ions, while the carbonate group carries the negative charge as CO₃²⁻ ions. The strong electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions — pulling them together and holding them in a giant lattice, acting in every direction — is what the term ionic bonding describes.
2023-06-1C:5-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:6-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KCl(aq) → PbCl₂(s) + 2KNO₃(aq).** Both starting materials are dissolved in water, so lead(II) nitrate and potassium chloride are labelled (aq). The lead(II) chloride is the precipitate — the insoluble solid that forms when the two solutions are mixed — so it carries the (s) state symbol, while the potassium nitrate product stays dissolved in the water as (aq).
2023-06-1C:6-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:6-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: the lead ion is Pb²⁺ and the nitrate ion is NO₃⁻.** Ionic compounds contain a positive ion and a negative ion. Here the metal part gives the lead ion, whose 2+ charge is signalled by the (II) in the name, and the non-metal part is the nitrate ion — one nitrogen bonded to three oxygens, carrying a single negative charge overall. Two nitrate ions are needed to balance every Pb²⁺, which is why the formula is written Pb(NO₃)₂.
2023-06-1C:6-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:6-a-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: Mr of Pb(NO₃)₂ = 331.** *Step 1 — one nitrate group:* N = 14 and O = 16, so NO₃ is worth 14 + 16 × 3 = 62. *Step 2 — double the group:* the formula has two nitrate groups inside the bracket, so 62 × 2 = 124. *Step 3 — add the lead:* Pb = 207, giving Mr = 207 + 124 = 331. The bracket is the trap: the × 2 multiplies everything inside it, not just the last oxygen.
2023-06-1C:6-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:6-b-i.solutionMd: **Answer: plot each pair of readings as a small, careful cross — volume of lead(II) nitrate along the x-axis, height of precipitate up the y-axis.** The first reading, for instance, sits at 2.0 cm³ on the volume axis and 0.8 cm up the height axis, and the rest follow the same way. Count carefully and place every cross exactly to the nearest grid line, using a sharp pencil, so that the pattern of the results is easy to read off the finished grid.
2023-06-1C:6-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:6-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: circle the point at 6.0 cm³, where the height reads 2.9 cm.** The rest of the results follow a clean pattern — the height climbs steadily (0.8, then 1.6, then 3.2 cm as the volume increases 2.0 cm³ at a time) and then flattens off at 3.6 cm. The reading of 2.9 cm at 6.0 cm³ jumps clearly above the trend its neighbours set, so it does not belong with the pattern and is the anomalous result.
2023-06-1C:6-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:6-b-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: draw a rising straight line of best fit through the first four points (ignoring the anomalous point) and a horizontal straight line through the last three points, so that the two lines cross.** The first line runs up from the origin through the trend of the early points, placed so the points are balanced evenly either side of it. The final three readings all sit at the same height of 3.6 cm — once every bit of potassium chloride has reacted, adding still more lead(II) nitrate cannot build any more precipitate — so their best-fit line is horizontal. The rising line meets the flat line at the point where the reaction just goes to completion.
2023-06-1C:6-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:6-b-iv.solutionMd: **Answer: any two of: the precipitate was not given time to settle before the height was read; the height was measured incorrectly, for example a parallax error when reading the scale at the side of the tube; or more than 2.0 cm³ of lead(II) nitrate was added in that step, so the total volume added had gone beyond 6.0 cm³.** Each of these slips makes that single reading unreliable — either the solid layer is not the true settled height or the volume axis value is wrong — which is exactly how an anomalous point arises on an otherwise smooth graph.
2023-06-1C:6-b-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:6-b-v.solutionMd: **Answer: because with no lead(II) nitrate added there is no reaction and therefore no precipitate, so the height must be zero.** The solid column is lead(II) chloride, formed only when lead(II) nitrate meets potassium chloride. At a volume of zero on the volume axis nothing has been added to react with the potassium chloride, so no solid can be present, the height of precipitate is zero, and the first line of best fit has to start at the origin.
2023-06-1C:6-b-v.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:6-b-vi.solutionMd: **Answer: about 9.0 cm³ — read from your graph where the two lines cross.** The rising line shows the height of precipitate growing as more lead(II) nitrate is added, while the horizontal line shows the height fixed at 3.6 cm once all the potassium chloride has reacted. The crossing point marks where the mixture just becomes complete: read straight down from it to the volume axis and the volume of lead(II) nitrate solution needed for the 15.0 cm³ of potassium chloride comes out at roughly 9 cm³.

2023-06-1C:7-a.solutionMd: **Answer: 53 protons and 74 neutrons.** The atomic number of iodine is 53, and the atomic number tells you the number of protons in the nucleus (it equals the number of electrons too, since a neutral atom carries no overall charge). The mass number of iodine–127 counts protons plus neutrons, so the neutron count is the difference: 127 − 53 = 74 neutrons.

2023-06-1C:7-b.solutionMd: **Answer: Ar = 79.9 (to three significant figures).** *Step 1 — weighted sum:* multiply each isotope's mass number by its percentage abundance and add them: 79 × 52.8 + 81 × 47.2 = 7994.4. *Step 2 — divide by the total percentage:* the two abundances sum to 100, so 7994.4 ÷ 100 = 79.944. *Step 3 — round:* to three significant figures this gives 79.9. The value sits nearer 79 than 81 because Br–79 is the slightly more abundant isotope (52.8% against 47.2%).

2023-06-1C:7-c.solutionMd: **Answer: minimum mass of chlorine = 21.3 g.** *Step 1 — moles of aluminium chloride:* n(AlCl₃) = 26.7 ÷ 133.5 = 0.2 mol. *Step 2 — moles of chlorine:* the equation 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃ shows that every 2 mol of AlCl₃ formed needs 3 mol of Cl₂, so n(Cl₂) = 0.2 × 3 ÷ 2 = 0.3 mol. *Step 3 — mass of chlorine:* mass = moles × Mr = 0.3 × 71 = 21.3 g. That is the minimum because it assumes all the chlorine reacts and none escapes.

2023-06-1C:7-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: Pair 1 shows chlorine is more reactive than bromine, and Pair 2 shows bromine is more reactive than iodine — so the overall order of reactivity is chlorine > bromine > iodine.**

Pair 1: bromine solution mixed with potassium chloride solution. Nothing happens — there is no reaction and no change in colour; the mixture stays yellow/orange. A halogen can only displace the halogen beneath it in the reactivity order, and here the bromine does not react with the chloride ions to produce chlorine — which can only be because bromine is the less reactive of the two. So chlorine is more reactive than bromine.

Pair 2: bromine solution mixed with potassium iodide solution. This time the mixture turns brown (an orange-brown tinge counts too): the bromine has displaced iodine from its iodide ions, and the brown colour is the iodine released — Br₂ + 2KI → I₂ + 2KBr. Displacement only works when the halogen added is the more reactive one, so bromine is more reactive than iodine.

Combining the experiments: chlorine > bromine from Pair 1 and bromine > iodine from Pair 2, which fixes the order of reactivity as chlorine > bromine > iodine.
2023-06-1C:7-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-1C:8-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: so that the heat is distributed evenly throughout the water.** Stirring keeps the warmed water circulating around the copper can, so the whole body of water settles at the same temperature instead of a hot layer forming next to the metal. The thermometer reading then represents the true average temperature of all the water — and that temperature change is exactly what the energy calculation in the later parts depends on.

2023-06-1C:8-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: so that as little pentanol as possible evaporates before the burner is weighed.** At the end of the experiment the spirit burner is warm and the liquid fuel is volatile, so pentanol keeps evaporating from the wick and the liquid surface every second you delay. **Answer: methyl orange is yellow in potassium hydroxide solution and red (pink) in dilute sulfuric acid.**
Methyl orange is yellow while the mixture is alkaline, so it sits yellow in the potassium hydroxide at the start. As the acid runs in and neutralises the alkali, the indicator changes to red — many people describe the acid colour as pink — and the first permanent red marks the end point.
2023-06-2C:4-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:4-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: so the colour change can be seen clearly.**
The white tile gives a plain white background behind the solution. Against white, the first hint of the yellow-to-red change at the end point stands out sharply, so the student stops the titration at exactly the right moment instead of overshooting it.
2023-06-2C:4-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:4-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: swirling keeps the reaction mixture well mixed.**
Each drop of acid is spread through the alkali as it enters, so the two solutions mix thoroughly and react at once; the colour changes uniformly through the flask rather than in one local patch, and the reaction between the acid and the alkali is speeded up. Without swirling, the end point would be blurry and easy to overshoot.
2023-06-2C:4-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:4-e.solutionMd:
**Answer: titres (results) that are within 0.2 cm³ of each other.**
Concordant titres agree closely: each reading lies within ±0.2 cm³ of the others (0.1 cm³ is sometimes quoted as an even tighter standard). Agreement that close shows the technique was consistent, so the titres can be averaged to give a reliable volume for the concentration calculation.
2023-06-2C:4-e.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:4-f.solutionMd:
**Answer: 0.216 mol / dm³.**
*Step 1 — moles of sulfuric acid:* 15.00 cm³ = 0.0150 dm³, so n(H₂SO₄) = 0.0150 × 0.180 = 0.0027 mol.
*Step 2 — moles of potassium hydroxide:* the equation 2KOH + H₂SO₄ → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O shows 2 mol of KOH reacting with every 1 mol of acid, so n(KOH) = 0.0027 × 2 = 0.0054 mol.
*Step 3 — concentration:* 25.0 cm³ = 0.0250 dm³, so concentration = 0.0054 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.216 mol / dm³.
The doubling in Step 2 is the part students most often miss: forgetting the 2 : 1 ratio gives 0.108, half the true concentration.
2023-06-2C:4-f.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:4-g.solutionMd:
**Answer: the OH⁻ ion bonds with the H⁺ ion — and an H⁺ ion is nothing more than a proton — so the hydroxide ion is the species that takes the proton in, which is exactly what a proton acceptor means.**
A hydrogen atom that has lost its only electron leaves behind a bare nucleus: the H⁺ ion is a proton. In the neutralisation H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), the hydroxide ion reacts with that proton, forming a bond to it and turning the two ions into a water molecule. Because the OH⁻ ion is the particle that receives the proton and bonds with it, it is called a proton acceptor (and the H⁺ ion is the proton donor).
2023-06-2C:4-g.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:5-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: add a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution to a sample of the copper(II) sulfate solution — a blue precipitate forms, showing Cu²⁺ ions are present.**
The hydroxide ions in the alkali react with the copper(II) ions to give insoluble copper(II) hydroxide, which appears as a blue solid falling out of the solution (pale or dark shades both count). Potassium hydroxide or aqueous ammonia work as the alkali too, but the reagent must be an alkali. The alternative route is a flame test: copper(II) ions colour the flame blue-green.
2023-06-2C:5-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:5-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: the Cu²⁺ ions are positively charged, so they are attracted to the negative electrode, where they gain electrons and become copper atoms.**
The copper ions in the solution are cations — they carry a positive charge — so they migrate through the liquid towards the negative electrode (the cathode). When each Cu²⁺ ion reaches the electrode it picks up the electrons it needs and turns into a neutral copper atom: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Atom by atom this builds a coating of copper metal on the negative electrode, and the blue colour of the solution fades as the ions are used up.
2023-06-2C:5-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:5-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: a pink solid coating the electrode.**
The copper forms as a pink (pink-brown or orange-brown) metallic deposit building up on the surface of the negative electrode — a solid coating of metal, not a precipitate suspended in the solution, and not bright red.
2023-06-2C:5-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:5-d-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: hold a glowing splint in the gas — it relights in oxygen.**
A splint that is still glowing (but no longer flaming) bursts back into flame in a tube of oxygen. This is the standard laboratory test: a gas that relights a glowing splint is oxygen.
2023-06-2C:5-d-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:5-d-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻.**
Water is oxidised at the positive electrode. Balance it step by step: the oxygen goes to O₂; the two water molecules supply 4 hydrogen atoms, so 4H⁺ sits on the right; then balance the charge — the 4 positive charges on the right are cancelled by 4 electrons released, written 4e⁻. The fully correct equation is therefore 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻ (the hydroxide-ion form, 4OH⁻ → 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻, describes the same chemistry but is treated as only a partial answer, so learn the water version).
2023-06-2C:5-d-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:5-d-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: because the water (or hydroxide ions) loses electrons — and loss of electrons is oxidation.**
In 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻ the electrons appear on the right-hand side: the water molecules at the positive electrode have given up electrons. Oxidation is defined as the loss of electrons (reduction is the gain), so the formation of oxygen at the positive electrode is an oxidation reaction.
2023-06-2C:5-d-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:6-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄).**
A few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid act as the catalyst: they speed up the reaction between the ethanoic acid and the methanol without being consumed. The other strong acids do the same job — hydrochloric acid (HCl), nitric acid (HNO₃) and phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) all work as the catalyst for making this ester.
2023-06-2C:6-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:6-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: by its distinctive sweet, fruity smell.**
Esters have the characteristic fruity odour of fruits such as pear or banana — a strong, pleasant, sweet smell that neither the acid nor the alcohol has. An oily layer forming on the surface of the mixture is a second sign that the ester product has separated out.
2023-06-2C:6-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:6-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: methyl ethanoate.**
The alcohol part gives the first word of the name and the acid part the second: the CH₃O– fragment from methanol makes it a methyl ester, and the CH₃CO– fragment from ethanoic acid makes it an ethanoate. So methanol + ethanoic acid → methyl ethanoate + water. Spelling matters: in the ester's name it is ethanoate, not ethanoic.
2023-06-2C:6-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:6-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: the C–O bond and the O–H bond.**
Following the displayed formulae, the reactants must each give something up: one C–O bond and one O–H bond break, so that the CH₃CO– fragment can join to the oxygen of the methanol and the freed –OH and H can leave as water. The ester therefore ends up with a fresh C–O link and the water carries a fresh O–H.
2023-06-2C:6-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:6-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: because the same two bonds — C–O and O–H — are broken in the reactants and re-formed in the products, the energy needed to break bonds exactly equals the energy released when the new bonds form, so the overall enthalpy change is approximately 0 kJ / mol.**
Breaking bonds takes energy in; making bonds gives energy out. Here the bonds broken are one C–O and one O–H, and the products contain exactly the same two bond types as new links — the ester's C–O and the water's O–H. Energy in equals energy out, the two cancel, and ΔH comes out as approximately 0 kJ / mol, which is why the displayed equation shows identical bond counts for reactants and products.
2023-06-2C:6-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:7-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: carbon monoxide reduces the capacity of the blood to transport oxygen round the body.**

Haemoglobin in red blood cells normally picks up oxygen in the lungs and releases it to the tissues. Carbon monoxide binds with haemoglobin in place of oxygen, and it grips so strongly that less haemoglobin is left free to carry oxygen. The blood still flows, but every litre of it delivers less oxygen, so the body's cells are starved — which is why the gas is poisonous.
2023-06-2C:7-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:7-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: a nickel catalyst has no effect on the yield of hydrogen at equilibrium.**

A catalyst speeds up the forward and the backward reaction equally, by lowering the activation energy for both directions. The forward and reverse rates rise by the same amount, so the balance point between them never moves: equilibrium is simply reached sooner. The yield of hydrogen therefore stays exactly the same as it was without the catalyst — only the time taken to get there changes.
2023-06-2C:7-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:7-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: the yield of hydrogen decreases when the temperature is reduced to 600 °C.**

The forward reaction is endothermic (ΔH = +206 kJ/mol), so it takes heat in. Lowering the temperature removes heat from the equilibrium mixture, and by Le Chatelier's principle the system opposes that change: the equilibrium shifts to the left-hand side, the exothermic direction, which releases heat. Moving to the reactant side breaks down hydrogen, so less hydrogen is present at equilibrium — the yield decreases.
2023-06-2C:7-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:7-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the yield of hydrogen increases when the pressure is reduced to 4 atmospheres.**

Count the gas moles on each side of CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g): there are 2 mol of gas molecules on the left-hand side and 4 mol on the right-hand side. Lowering the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with more gas molecules, because the system opposes the change by producing more particles. That side is the right-hand side, so more hydrogen forms — the yield increases, even though the pressure drop would slow the reaction rate.
2023-06-2C:7-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2C:7-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2.6 × 10⁷ dm³ of methane.**

*Step 1 — moles of hydrogen:* 6.6 tonnes is 6.6 × 10⁶ g, and the Mr of H₂ is 2, so n(H₂) = 6.6 × 10⁶ ÷ 2 = 3.3 × 10⁶ mol.

*Step 2 — moles of methane:* from CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g), every 1 mol of methane gives 3 mol of hydrogen, so n(CH₄) = 3.3 × 10⁶ ÷ 3 = 1.1 × 10⁶ mol.

*Step 3 — volume at rtp:* one mole occupies 24 dm³ at rtp, so volume = 1.1 × 10⁶ × 24 = 26 400 000 dm³ = 2.64 × 10⁷ dm³, which is 2.6 × 10⁷ dm³ to two significant figures.
2023-06-2C:7-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:1-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: proton — relative mass 1, relative charge +1; neutron — relative mass 1, relative charge 0; electron — relative mass 0.0005, relative charge −1.**

Protons and neutrons have essentially the same mass, so both take a relative mass of 1 on this scale; the electron is tiny by comparison, at just 0.0005. For the charges: a proton is +1, a neutron is neutral (charge 0), and an electron is −1 — the same size of charge as the proton but opposite in sign, which is why atoms are neutral overall.
2023-06-2CR:1-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:1-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — in order of increasing atomic number.**

Moving left to right across the Periodic Table, each element has one more proton in its nucleus than the one before, so the table is arranged by increasing atomic number. Option B is wrong: melting points rise and fall in complicated patterns across a period, so the elements are not arranged by increasing melting point. Option C is wrong: reactivity climbs to a peak in the middle of a period and then falls away, so it cannot be the organising order. Option D is wrong: relative atomic masses happen to increase broadly across the table, but the strict order is atomic number — sorting by relative atomic mass would place a few pairs of elements in the wrong slots.
2023-06-2CR:1-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:1-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: D — phosphorus is in Group 5 and Period 3.**

Count the electrons in phosphorus's outer shell (5 of them) to get the group, and count its occupied shells (3) to get the period. Option A is wrong: Group 2 and Period 5 would put phosphorus among the alkaline-earth metals far down the table. Option B is wrong: Group 3 with Period 5 mixes the two coordinates. Option C is wrong: Group 5 and Period 2 swaps the true position, because Period 2 belongs to nitrogen and its horizontal neighbours, not to phosphorus.
2023-06-2CR:1-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:1-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: xenon (Xe) is the least reactive of the four elements shown.**

Xenon is a noble gas: its atoms have a full outer shell, with 8 electrons in the outermost shell. A full outer shell is uniquely stable, so xenon atoms neither need to lose electrons nor gain them, and xenon takes part in hardly any reactions. Beryllium, fluorine and phosphorus all have incomplete outer shells, so they react readily to reach a full one — fluorine in particular is extremely reactive.
2023-06-2CR:1-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:2-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: fluorine is a pale yellow gas; chlorine is a green gas; bromine is a red-brown liquid; iodine is a grey solid.**

Going down Group 7 the halogen molecules get bigger, so the physical state at room temperature changes from gas (fluorine, chlorine) to liquid (bromine) to solid (iodine), and the colour deepens from pale yellow through green and red-brown to grey. In dilute aqueous solution the halogens give colourless solutions for fluorine and chlorine, orange for bromine and brown for iodine — those solution colours matter when you meet displacement reactions.
2023-06-2CR:2-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:2-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: shake the colourless liquid with bromine water — with an alkene, the orange bromine water is decolourised (it turns colourless).**

Alkenes contain a C=C double bond, which lets them add bromine atoms straight across the double bond in an addition reaction. As the bromine is used up, the bromine water loses its orange colour and goes colourless, and this happens whatever colour the alkene itself started as. A saturated alkane cannot do this, so seeing no colour change means the liquid is not an alkene.
2023-06-2CR:2-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:2-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: the mixture turns from colourless to brown, because iodine is displaced.**

Chlorine is the more reactive halogen, so it takes iodine's place: the chlorine reacts with the iodide ions, iodine (I₂) is displaced and shows itself as the brown colour. In symbols: Cl₂ + 2NaI → 2NaCl + I₂. Displacement only works in one direction — the more reactive halogen always wins — so if you added iodine solution to sodium chloride instead, nothing would happen, because iodine is less reactive than chlorine.
2023-06-2CR:2-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:3-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: magnesium.**

Magnesium burns in air with a dazzling bright white flame — bright enough that powdered magnesium was once used in camera flash powder. The other metals in the box cannot match it: calcium burns with a red flame, aluminium and zinc only burn with difficulty, and gold and silver are too unreactive to burn at all.
2023-06-2CR:3-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:3-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: gold.**

Gold is the least reactive of the metals in the box, so over the history of the Earth it has stayed as the element itself instead of joining with oxygen or other substances to form compounds. That is why gold is found native — as uncombined metal in rocks and nuggets — while every other metal listed is reactive enough to exist mainly as an ore that must be chemically extracted.
2023-06-2CR:3-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:3-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: an alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other metals (or with carbon).**

The ingredients are combined physically, not chemically — no new substance forms, which is exactly why an alloy counts as a mixture rather than a compound. Steel is the everyday example: iron mixed with a small amount of carbon atoms.
2023-06-2CR:3-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:3-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: in an alloy the different-sized atoms distort the regular layers, so the layers can no longer slide over one another easily — the alloy is less malleable.**

In a pure metal every atom is the same size and the atoms sit in neat, regular rows. When a force is applied, whole layers of atoms can slide past one another, so the metal bends without shattering — that is malleability. In steel the carbon atoms are much smaller than the iron atoms, so they wedge into the gaps and the regular arrangement of the atoms becomes irregular and distorted. That misfit makes it more difficult for the layers to slide, so the alloy holds its shape instead of denting.
2023-06-2CR:3-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:4-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: refinery gases — bottled gas for heating and cooking; bitumen — road surfacing (roads) and roofing.**

Refinery gases come off the top of the fractionating column: these small hydrocarbon molecules burn cleanly, so they are bottled under pressure and sold as a bottled fuel for cooking and heating. Bitumen runs off the bottom as the thick, black, sticky residue: it is spread onto road surfaces when hot, and it also waterproofs flat roofs.
2023-06-2CR:4-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:4-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: because refinery gases have the lowest boiling points of all the fractions.**

Their small molecules are the most volatile, so they leave the liquid most easily and stay as vapour all the way up the column — they do not condense until a temperature far colder than anywhere in the column. Heavier fractions have higher boiling points, condense much lower down, and so are tapped off near the base.
2023-06-2CR:4-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:4-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: it is heated, so that it is vaporised (evaporated) before it enters the column.**

Vaporising the crude oil turns most of its hydrocarbons into vapour; inside the hot column each fraction can then rise and condense at the height where the temperature matches its own boiling point, which is what separates the fractions from one another.
2023-06-2CR:4-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:4-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: a high temperature of about 600 – 700 °C, plus a catalyst.**

The heat supplies the energy needed to snap the long hydrocarbon chains into smaller pieces, and the catalyst — alumina (aluminium oxide), silica (silicon dioxide) or a synthetic zeolite — lets the reaction happen fast enough to be economical. Pressure is not an important condition here.
2023-06-2CR:4-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:4-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: propene is in demand for making polymers, and octane is in demand as a fuel (petrol).**

In the cracking equation C₁₄H₃₀ → 2C₃H₆ + C₈H₁₈, the alkene product propene (C₃H₆) is valuable because its molecules carry a C=C double bond — they are unsaturated, so very many of them can join end to end in addition polymerisation to make polymers such as poly(propene), a useful plastic (alkenes can also be reacted to make alcohols). The shorter alkane octane (C₈H₁₈) is wanted because short-chain alkanes make the best fuels: their lower boiling points mean they vaporise and ignite easily — they are more flammable — and octane is precisely the fraction burned in petrol in car engines.
2023-06-2CR:4-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:5-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: mix the two solutions, filter off the precipitate, wash it, then dry it.**

*Step 1 — mix:* add the lead nitrate solution to the potassium bromide solution and stir; they react and insoluble lead(II) bromide forms as a precipitate: Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → PbBr₂(s) + 2KNO₃(aq).

*Step 2 — filter:* pour the mixture through filter paper. The solid lead bromide is caught on the paper and the soluble potassium nitrate stays in the solution that runs through.

*Step 3 — wash:* rinse the solid on the paper with a little deionised water to wash away any potassium nitrate solution clinging to the crystals.

*Step 4 — dry:* leave the washed solid to dry in a warm place (a low oven works, or dab it dry with filter paper). That leaves a pure, dry sample of lead(II) bromide.

Do not try to evaporate the mixture instead — evaporating to dryness would trap soluble potassium nitrate among the crystals, so the sample would not be pure.
2023-06-2CR:5-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:5-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: 90.1%.**

*Step 1 — maximum moles of lead(II) bromide:* the equation Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → PbBr₂(s) + 2KNO₃(aq) links lead(II) nitrate to lead(II) bromide in a 1 : 1 ratio, so 0.150 mol of lead nitrate could make at most 0.150 mol of PbBr₂.

*Step 2 — theoretical mass:* mass = moles × Mr: 0.150 × 367 = 55.05 g.

*Step 3 — percentage yield:* actual mass ÷ theoretical mass, expressed as a percentage:

49.6 ÷ 55.05 × 100 = 90.1%

The student harvested 49.6 g of lead(II) bromide, which is 90.1% of the 55.05 g the equation predicts — the rest was lost on the filter paper and in the filtrate.
2023-06-2CR:5-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:5-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: plot all 6 points from the table, each one landing within half a square of its true position.**

Put the total volume of lead(II) nitrate added on the x-axis (0 to 50 cm³) and the electrical conductivity on the y-axis (9.00 to 10.00 in arbitrary units), then plot the points (0, 10.00), (10, 9.80), (20, 9.77), (30, 9.40), (40, 9.20) and (50, 9.00). Use a sharp pencil and small, neat crosses so each point is easy to read back off the grid.
2023-06-2CR:5-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:5-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: draw a single straight line of best fit that ignores the anomalous result.**

The line slopes gently downward, passing as close as possible to the points at 0, 10, 30, 40 and 50 cm³ while leaving the point at 20 cm³ (9.77) sitting clearly above it — that is the anomaly to leave out. Keep the line straight (do not join dot to dot) and balance it so the reliable points are spread evenly above and below.
2023-06-2CR:5-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:5-c-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the conductivity decreases as more lead(II) nitrate is added, because there are fewer ions in the mixture.**

Each 10 cm³ portion of lead(II) nitrate adds Pb²⁺ ions that pair up with Br⁻ ions from the potassium bromide solution; the two react to form solid lead(II) bromide, PbBr₂, which is insoluble and precipitates out. Ions are the charge carriers in solution, so every ion removed as solid lowers the number of charge carriers in the beaker — and the reading falls steadily from 10.00 towards 9.00.
2023-06-2CR:5-c-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:5-c-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: the student could have forgotten to stir the mixture in Step 4 before measuring the conductivity.**

Without thorough stirring, the lead(II) nitrate would sit unevenly in the potassium bromide solution, the precipitation would be incomplete, and the mixture would still hold more dissolved ions than it should — giving a conductivity reading that is too high, like the anomalous value at 20 cm³. Taking the reading too soon, before the reaction had finished, would have the same effect.
2023-06-2CR:5-c-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:5-c-v.solutionMd:
**Answer: the conductivity would increase.**

Once every Br⁻ ion has been used up, adding still more lead(II) nitrate cannot remove any more ions as precipitate. Instead, each extra 10 cm³ portion simply dissolves and adds its own Pb²⁺ and NO₃⁻ ions to the beaker, so the number of charge carriers rises again and the conductivity climbs back up.
2023-06-2CR:5-c-v.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:5-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: because electrons are lost — the bromide ions lose electrons.**

In the half-equation 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ the two bromide ions each give away their extra electron: the electrons appear on the right-hand side as a product. Loss of electrons is exactly what oxidation means (OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons), so the bromide ions are oxidised to bromine molecules at electrode A.
2023-06-2CR:5-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:6-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.**

In a metal, each atom releases its outer electrons into a shared 'sea' — these electrons are delocalised, free to move through the whole lattice, and they leave behind positive metal ions. The electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the surrounding delocalised electrons acts in every direction and holds the giant structure together: that attraction is the metallic bond.
2023-06-2CR:6-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:6-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: hold a lighted splint at the gas — hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop.**

Put a lighted splint (or the flame of a Bunsen burner) at the mouth of the tube of gas: the hydrogen ignites with the oxygen in the air and you hear the characteristic squeaky pop. A glowing splint is the wrong tool here — that is the test for oxygen, which relights a glowing splint.
2023-06-2CR:6-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:6-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the potassium burns with a lilac flame, and the piece melts into a small shiny ball.**

Potassium reacts so exothermically that the heat released melts the soft metal straight away, and the molten ball moves quickly around on the water surface while the flame is coloured lilac. As the reaction goes on the ball gets smaller and smaller until it disappears completely.
2023-06-2CR:6-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:6-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: lithium is less reactive because its outer electron is more strongly attracted to the nucleus, so it is less easily lost.**

Lithium has fewer occupied shells than potassium — its outer electron sits in the second shell, while potassium's sits in the fourth. Being closer to the nucleus, and shielded from it by fewer inner shells of electrons, the lithium outer electron feels a stronger attraction to the positive nucleus. A more strongly held electron needs more energy to be pulled away, so lithium's outer electron is less easily lost to water than potassium's — and losing that outer electron is what the reaction with water depends on, which is why potassium reacts much more violently.
2023-06-2CR:6-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:6-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: 391 cm³ (to three significant figures).**

*Step 1 — moles of sodium:* n(Na) = mass ÷ Ar = 0.750 ÷ 23 = 0.0326 mol.

*Step 2 — moles of hydrogen:* the equation 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g) shows 2 mol of sodium producing 1 mol of hydrogen, so n(H₂) = 0.0326 ÷ 2 = 0.0163 mol.

*Step 3 — volume of hydrogen:* volume = moles × molar volume: 0.0163 × 24 000 = 391.304, which is 391 cm³ to three significant figures.

The water is in excess, so the sodium is the limiting reactant and fixes how much hydrogen can be made.
2023-06-2CR:6-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:6-e.solutionMd:
**Answer: 0.0652 mol/dm³.**

*Step 1 — volume of sulfuric acid in dm³:* 16.3 ÷ 1000 = 0.0163 dm³.

*Step 2 — moles of sulfuric acid:* moles = concentration × volume = 0.0163 × 0.0500 = 0.000815 mol.

*Step 3 — moles of sodium hydroxide:* the equation 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O needs 2 mol of NaOH for every 1 mol of H₂SO₄, so n(NaOH) = 0.000815 × 2 = 0.00163 mol.

*Step 4 — concentration:* 25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.025 dm³ of alkali, and concentration = moles ÷ volume: 0.00163 ÷ 0.025 = 0.0652 mol/dm³.

The classic slip is to divide by 2 instead of multiplying — the 2 : 1 ratio runs from acid to alkali, so the alkali moles are double the acid moles.
2023-06-2CR:6-e.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:7-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: the forward and reverse reactions continue at the same rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.**

Dynamic equilibrium is dynamic: methanol is still forming from H₂ and CO, and still decomposing back, but the two changes happen at exactly the same rate. With no net change either way, the concentrations of hydrogen, carbon monoxide and methanol settle at steady, constant values — constant, note, but not equal to one another, which is a common misconception.
2023-06-2CR:7-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:7-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: because a catalyst increases the rate of the forward and the reverse reaction equally.**

A catalyst offers both directions a lower-energy route, so each rate rises by the same factor. The balance between them is untouched: the position of equilibrium does not shift, so the yield of methanol at equilibrium is exactly what it would have been without the catalyst — the mixture just gets there sooner.
2023-06-2CR:7-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:7-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the yield of methanol increases.**

The forward reaction (2H₂ + CO ⇌ CH₃OH) is the exothermic direction — ΔH is negative, −119 kJ/mol, meaning heat is released going forwards. When the temperature is lowered, the equilibrium responds by producing extra heat: it favours the exothermic forward direction over the endothermic reverse direction, so more methanol forms and the yield rises.
2023-06-2CR:7-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:7-a-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: the yield of methanol increases.**

On the left of the equation the reactants hold 3 mol of gas — 2 mol of H₂ plus 1 mol of CO — while the products on the right hold just 1 mol of gas (the CH₃OH). Raising the pressure squeezes the same molecules into less space, and the equilibrium responds by shifting towards the side with fewer gas moles, the right-hand side; that means more methanol is made, so the yield increases.
2023-06-2CR:7-a-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:7-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: ΔH = −119 kJ/mol, and the bond energies show exactly where that number comes from.**

*Step 1 — bonds broken in the reactants:* 2 mol of H–H bonds plus 1 mol of C≡O bond: 436 + 436 + 1072 = 1944 kJ/mol absorbed.

*Step 2 — bonds made in the product:* methanol, CH₃OH, contains 3 C–H bonds, 1 C–O bond and 1 O–H bond: 414 + 414 + 414 + 358 + 463 = 2063 kJ/mol released.

*Step 3 — the difference:* 2063 − 1944 = 119 kJ/mol more energy is released making bonds than is absorbed breaking them, so the overall change is ΔH = −119 kJ/mol.
2023-06-2CR:7-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:7-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: because more energy is given out when the new bonds are made than is taken in when the original bonds are broken.**

Breaking bonds always takes in energy (it is endothermic): here the 2 H–H bonds and the C≡O bond absorb 1944 kJ/mol. Making bonds always releases energy (it is exothermic): the 3 C–H, 1 C–O and 1 O–H bonds of methanol release 2063 kJ/mol. Since 2063 is the larger figure, the energy released making bonds beats the energy absorbed breaking them, so there is a net transfer of energy to the surroundings — the reaction is exothermic and ΔH comes out negative.
2023-06-2CR:7-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:7-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: circle the ester functional group, the –C(=O)–O– linkage.**

The functional group of an ester is the carbon of the C=O double bond together with the single-bonded O next to it — 1 carbon and 2 oxygen atoms in total, sitting between the two carbon chains. Circle just that linkage; the H atoms and the rest of the C atoms of the chains stay outside the circle.
2023-06-2CR:7-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-06-2CR:7-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH.**

Methanol provides the –OCH₃ half of the ester, so the carboxylic acid must provide the CH₃CH₂C(=O)– half: joining propanoic acid to methanol, with water eliminated, gives the methyl propanoate shown in the diagram. Its fully displayed formula draws every bond:

H–C(H)(H)–C(H)(H)–C(=O)–O–H

That is a three-carbon acid chain ending in the carboxyl group, with the O–H bond actually displayed rather than squashed into a condensed COOH.
2023-06-2CR:7-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:1-a.solutionMd: **Answer: Draw four extra circles, spaced far apart and scattered randomly through the empty space of the box.** In a gas the particles are widely separated with no regular pattern, so the four added particles should sit randomly in the gaps, each one far from the others and from the particles already drawn — none touching. Lines or arrows between particles are not needed; the key features are random spacing and large gaps.
2023-11-1C:1-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:1-b.solutionMd: **Answer: Heating gives the particles more kinetic energy, so more of them can escape from the liquid.** When a liquid is heated, the mean kinetic energy of its particles increases and they move faster. A greater proportion of particles then have enough energy to overcome the intermolecular forces of attraction holding them in the liquid, so more particles escape from the surface every second and the liquid evaporates more quickly.
2023-11-1C:1-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:1-c-i.solutionMd: **Answer: condensation.** When the temperature decreases, the water particles in the gas state lose energy, slow down and move closer together, so the gas turns into liquid water. A gas changing into a liquid on cooling is called condensation (condensing).
2023-11-1C:1-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:1-c-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: H₂O(g) → H₂O(l).** The substance stays water in both states, so the formula does not change — only the state symbols do: (g) for the gas and (l) for the liquid. Writing the change in words as water(g) → water(l), or starting from steam(g) → water(l), carries exactly the same chemistry; the formula H₂O must be correct.
2023-11-1C:1-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:1-d.solutionMd: **Answer: In a solid the particles are packed closely together in a regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions.** The particles sit in a regular lattice — a neat, repeating pattern in which each particle touches its neighbours — which is why a solid keeps its own shape and volume. The particles do not swap places; they only vibrate backwards and forwards around the fixed positions they occupy.
2023-11-1C:1-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:2-a.solutionMd: **Answer: electron — relative charge −1; proton — relative mass 1 and relative charge +1; neutron — relative mass 1.** The electron is tiny compared with the other two (relative mass 0.0005) and carries a relative charge of −1. A proton has a relative mass of 1 and a relative charge of +1, equal in size and opposite in sign to the electron's charge. A neutron also has a relative mass of 1 but is electrically neutral, so its relative charge is 0.
2023-11-1C:2-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:2-b-i.solutionMd: **Answer: B — 3, because the atomic number of P is its proton count.** The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus, and the table gives P as having 3 protons, so B is correct. Option A (2) is the number of electrons P has, not its proton count. Option C (4) is the number of neutrons in P. Option D (7) is the mass number of P, found by adding the protons and neutrons together: 3 + 4 = 7 — a bigger number, but not the atomic number.
2023-11-1C:2-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:2-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: B — 16, the sum of the protons and neutrons in U.** The mass number counts protons plus neutrons. U has 8 protons and 8 neutrons, and 8 + 8 = 16, so B is correct. Option A (8) is only the proton count — the atomic number of U. Option C (18) comes from adding the electrons as well, since U has 10 electrons: 8 + 10 = 18, but electrons have negligible mass and are never counted in the mass number. Option D (26) counts every subatomic particle in U: 8 + 8 + 10 = 26, which is not the mass number either.
2023-11-1C:2-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:2-b-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: S — the atom with 7 protons.** Group 5 elements have five electrons in their outer shell. S has 7 protons, so a neutral atom of S has 7 electrons, arranged 2 in the first shell and the remaining 5 (7 − 2 = 5) in the second shell — five outer electrons, which is exactly Group 5. The element with proton number 7 is nitrogen, and the letters in the table are deliberately not the real chemical symbols.
2023-11-1C:2-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:2-c-i.solutionMd: **Answer: Q and R are isotopes because they have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.** Both Q and R have 5 protons (and, being uncharged atoms, both also have 5 electrons), so they belong to the same element. But Q has 5 neutrons while R has 6 neutrons — R carries one extra neutron. Same protons but different numbers of neutrons is precisely the definition of isotopes.
2023-11-1C:2-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:2-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: Ar = 10.8 (to one decimal place).**
*Step 1 — mass numbers:* Q has 5 protons and 5 neutrons, so its mass number is 5 + 5 = 10; R has 5 protons and 6 neutrons, so its mass number is 5 + 6 = 11.
*Step 2 — weighted total:* multiply each mass number by its percentage: 20.6 × 10 = 206 and 79.4 × 11 = 873.4, giving a combined total of 206 + 873.4 = 1079.4.
*Step 3 — divide by the combined percentage:* the mass numbers 10 and 11 blend in the ratio of the two percentages, so the weighted total divided by one hundred is 1079.4 ÷ 100 = 10.794; 10.794 rounds to 10.8 to one decimal place.
2023-11-1C:2-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:3-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: fractional distillation.** Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons with different boiling points, and separating it into useful fractions by boiling range in a fractionating column is fractional distillation.
2023-11-1C:3-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:3-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: The crude oil is heated so that it vaporises (boils).** In X, the hot base of the column, the crude oil is heated until it boils; most of it turns from liquid into a mixture of hydrocarbon vapours, which then rise up the column and condense at their own boiling points.
2023-11-1C:3-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:3-a-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: E.** A hydrocarbon with six carbon atoms is a fairly short-chain molecule, so it has a relatively low boiling point and condenses high up the column where the temperature is cooler. Mixture E is the gasoline (petrol) fraction, which contains exactly these short-chain hydrocarbons; the fractions collected near the bottom of the column, such as B, hold much longer chains.
2023-11-1C:3-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:3-a-iv.solutionMd: **Answer: kerosene.** Mixture D is the kerosene (paraffin) fraction — middle-weight hydrocarbons collected part-way up the fractionating column, used for example as jet fuel.
2023-11-1C:3-a-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:3-a-v.solutionMd: **Answer: fuel for ships.** Mixture B is the heavy fuel-oil fraction, and a standard use is as the fuel burned in ships' engines; it can also serve for home or industrial heating, electricity generation in power stations, or as a feedstock for plastics and fertilisers.
2023-11-1C:3-a-v.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:3-b.solutionMd: **Answer: A hydrocarbon in B has a higher boiling point because its molecules have longer chains, giving stronger intermolecular forces that need more energy to overcome.** Mixture B sits lower in the fractionating column than D, so its hydrocarbons are bigger molecules with longer chains (and a greater molecular mass). Longer chains mean more contact between neighbouring molecules, so the intermolecular forces between the molecules are stronger. When the liquid boils, it is those intermolecular forces that must be overcome to separate the molecules into a gas — not the covalent bonds inside each molecule. Because the forces in B are stronger, more energy is needed to overcome them and pull the molecules apart, so a higher temperature is needed: B has the higher boiling point.
2023-11-1C:3-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:3-c-i.solutionMd: **Answer: silica (silicon dioxide, SiO₂) or alumina (aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃).** Hot hydrocarbon vapour is passed over a heated solid catalyst such as silica or alumina — aluminosilicate (zeolite) catalysts are also used — and the long chains split apart over its surface into shorter alkane and alkene molecules.
2023-11-1C:3-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:3-c-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: C₁₅H₃₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄ + C₅H₁₀ (equally good: C₁₅H₃₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₃H₆ + C₄H₈).** Check the first pair by counting atoms: carbon gives 8 + 2 + 5 = 15 and hydrogen gives 18 + 4 + 10 = 32, so the equation balances. The second pair works the same way: 8 + 3 + 4 = 15 carbons and 18 + 6 + 8 = 32 hydrogens. Both mystery products must be alkenes, so each needs a C=C double bond — C₂H₄, C₃H₆, C₄H₈ and C₅H₁₀ all fit the alkene general formula; a pair such as C₃H₈ would be an alkane and would not balance.
2023-11-1C:3-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:3-c-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: making polymers — short-chain alkenes are the monomers for addition polymerisation, producing plastics such as polyethene and polypropene.** The C=C double bond makes alkenes reactive, so industry uses them as chemical feedstock: joined end-to-end in polymerisation reactions they build addition polymers, and they can also be converted into alcohols. They are far too useful (and too scarce) to burn as fuels.
2023-11-1C:3-c-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:4-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: nitrogen.** Air is about 79 % nitrogen (N₂, Mr 28) by volume, with almost all of the rest being oxygen — so the gas making up roughly four-fifths of the atmosphere is nitrogen.
2023-11-1C:4-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:4-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: carbon dioxide (CO₂).** It is the only gas in the table built from two different elements — carbon joined to oxygen — and elements chemically combined make a compound. Argon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen are all elements, each made of one kind of atom only.
2023-11-1C:4-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:4-a-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: argon.** Argon is a noble gas: its outer electron shell is already complete, so it has no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons and it takes part in almost no reactions — making it the least reactive gas in the table.
2023-11-1C:4-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:4-a-iv.solutionMd: **Answer: hydrogen.** Hydrogen (H₂, Mr 2) is not one of the normal atmospheric gases — nitrogen, oxygen, argon and carbon dioxide dominate the air, but hydrogen is only ever present in tiny traces because it is too light and too reactive to accumulate in the atmosphere.
2023-11-1C:4-a-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:4-a-v.solutionMd: **Answer: carbon dioxide (CO₂).** Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas: it absorbs infrared radiation given off by the Earth's surface and re-radiates it, so the more CO₂ there is in the atmosphere the more energy is trapped, enhancing global warming.
2023-11-1C:4-a-v.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:4-a-vi.solutionMd: **Answer: Mr of CO₂ = 44.** Carbon has Ar 12 and oxygen has Ar 16, and a molecule of carbon dioxide contains one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms, so Mr = 12 + 2 × 16 = 44.
2023-11-1C:4-a-vi.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:4-a-vii.solutionMd: **Answer: Air is a mixture of gases, so it has no single formula or fixed Mr.** A mixture contains several different substances that are not chemically joined and have no fixed composition; only a pure substance with one definite formula can be given an Mr, so no single Mr value can be quoted for air.
2023-11-1C:4-a-vii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:4-b-i.solutionMd: **Answer: thermal decomposition.** Heating copper(II) carbonate with a Bunsen flame breaks a single compound down into simpler substances — copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide — and using heat to split a compound up like this is thermal decomposition.
2023-11-1C:4-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:4-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: green to black.** Copper(II) carbonate is a green solid, and as it thermally decomposes it changes into copper(II) oxide, which is black. So the colour change seen during the reaction is from green to black — quote the starting colour first, then the final colour, since the order matters.
2023-11-1C:4-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:4-b-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂.** One formula unit of copper(II) carbonate decomposes into one formula unit of copper(II) oxide plus one molecule of carbon dioxide; counting atoms of copper, carbon and oxygen on each side shows the equation is already balanced.
2023-11-1C:4-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:5-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: Isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural (displayed) formulae.** They contain exactly the same numbers of each kind of atom, but those atoms are arranged differently within the molecule — same formula, different structure.
2023-11-1C:5-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:5-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: Isomer 1 is butane, a straight chain; isomer 2 is methylpropane, a branched chain.** Drawn out with every bond shown, butane is CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃: four carbon atoms in one unbroken row, each carbon carrying enough hydrogen atoms to complete its four bonds. Methylpropane is CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₃: three end carbons all bonded to a central carbon, so the fourth carbon sticks out as a branch from the middle of the chain. Both have the molecular formula C₄H₁₀, but their displayed formulae — with every C–C and C–H bond drawn — are different, which is what makes them isomers.
2023-11-1C:5-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:5-b-i.solutionMd: **Answer: ultraviolet (UV) light.** Ethane, like any alkane, only reacts with bromine when the mixture is exposed to ultraviolet radiation (bright sunlight); the UV light supplies the energy needed to start the substitution reaction.
2023-11-1C:5-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:5-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: C₂H₆ + Br₂ → C₂H₅Br + HBr.** One hydrogen atom of the ethane is swapped for one bromine atom, so the organic product is bromoethane (C₂H₅Br) and the displaced hydrogen leaves combined with the second bromine as hydrogen bromide (HBr). Counting carbon, hydrogen and bromine atoms on each side shows the equation balances.
2023-11-1C:5-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:5-b-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: substitution.** A bromine atom replaces — substitutes for — a hydrogen atom in the ethane molecule. Nothing is added across a double bond (alkanes have none), so alkane reactions with halogens are substitution reactions.
2023-11-1C:5-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:5-c.solutionMd: **Answer: Ethane is saturated because its carbon atoms are joined by single bonds only, so no more atoms can be added to the molecule.** Every C–C bond in ethane is a single bond — there is no double or multiple bond anywhere in the molecule. Each carbon is already bonded to the maximum number of hydrogen atoms it can hold, so ethane cannot take part in addition reactions; the only reaction open to it is substitution, where one atom swaps places with another.
2023-11-1C:5-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2023-11-1C:5-d.solutionMd: **Answer: with ethane the bromine water stays orange/yellow; with ethene it is decolourised (turns from orange/yellow to colourless).** Ethane is an alkane, so nothing happens — the bromine water remains orange/yellow because alkanes do not react with bromine water. Ethene is an alkene: its C=C double bond opens up and bromine adds across it, so the bromine water quickly changes from orange/yellow to colourless.
