Both halves of the definition matter. A fuel is burned — it undergoes combustion (it catches fire and reacts with oxygen) — and that burning releases thermal energy that can be put to use. The liquid fuel in the burner does exactly this: as it combusts it gives out heat, which warms the water in the metal can above it.

2024-06-1CR:6-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:6-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: temperature at the start = 20.4 °C; highest temperature reached = 77.6 °C (both to the nearest 0.1 °C).**

The thermometer diagram (scale 18–23 °C) shows the starting temperature of the water as 20.4 °C. The table gives the temperature rise as 57.2 °C, so the highest temperature reached = 20.4 + 57.2 = 77.6 °C. Quote both temperatures to 1 decimal place so they match the precision of the thermometer reading.

2024-06-1CR:6-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:6-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: Q = 150 × 4.2 × 57.2 = 36 036 J, which is approximately 36 000 J.**

*Step 1 — collect the data:* the metal can contains water of mass m = 150 g; for water, c = 4.2 J/g/°C; and the temperature rise from the completed table is ΔT = 57.2 °C.

*Step 2 — calculate:* Q = m × c × ΔT = 150 × 4.2 × 57.2 = 36 036 J. To the accuracy the question asks for, that is approximately 36 000 J — the value the next part uses.

2024-06-1CR:6-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:6-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: ΔH = −720 kJ/mol (to 2 significant figures, negative because combustion releases heat).**

*Step 1 — energy in kJ:* from the previous part, Q = 36 036 J, which is 36.036 kJ.

*Step 2 — amount of ethanol burned:* n(C₂H₅OH) = 2.3 ÷ 46 = 0.05 mol, using the Mr of ethanol, 46.

*Step 3 — energy per mole:* 36.036 ÷ 0.05 = 720.72 kJ/mol.

*Step 4 — sign and rounding:* burning ethanol is exothermic, so the molar enthalpy change carries a negative sign: ΔH = −720.72 kJ/mol, which rounds to −720 kJ/mol to 2 significant figures.

2024-06-1CR:6-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:6-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: heat is lost to the surroundings — for example, some is absorbed by the metal can and some escapes into the air — so less energy reaches the water than the data-book value assumes.**

Other possible reasons: the ethanol may burn incompletely, forming carbon monoxide and soot instead of carbon dioxide, which releases less energy per gram; and heat radiates away from the can to the surroundings instead of heating the water. Each of these makes the measured temperature rise smaller, so the calculated ΔH comes out less exothermic than the data book value.

2024-06-1CR:7-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:7-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: a measuring cylinder.**

A measuring cylinder measures the volume of a liquid — here the 50 cm³ of dilute sulfuric acid — to the accuracy the experiment needs. A burette or a pipette would also be suitable for a liquid volume. A gas syringe is not: it is built to measure the volume of gases, not of liquids.

2024-06-1CR:7-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:7-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: because the zinc is in excess.**

The zinc is added in more than enough amount to react with all of the dilute sulfuric acid, so the acid is the limiting reactant. Since the volume of acid (not the Zn) fixes how much hydrogen can be produced, the exact mass of zinc pieces does not affect the final gas volume — an approximate 5 g of small pieces is enough.

2024-06-1CR:7-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:7-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: so that as little gas as possible is lost before the syringe is connected.**

The zinc and the dilute sulfuric acid begin reacting the moment they meet, producing hydrogen straight away. Connecting the gas syringe quickly in Step 3 keeps as much of that hydrogen as possible inside the apparatus, so the volume readings start near zero and the rate calculated from them is accurate.

2024-06-1CR:7-a-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:7-a-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: no more bubbles (effervescence) form, and no more gas collects in the syringe.**

When the reaction has finished, fizzing stops in the flask and the gas syringe reading stays constant — the plunger no longer moves, so the syringe does not move between one 30-second reading and the next. Either observation tells the student that all of the acid has reacted and the volume of hydrogen has reached its maximum.

2024-06-1CR:7-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:7-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: rate = 50 ÷ 150 = approximately 0.33 cm³/s.**

*Step 1 — draw a gradient triangle on the tangent:* on the tangent drawn at 80 s, read off a change in volume of 50 cm³ for a change in time of 150 s (a large triangle makes the gradient more reliable).

*Step 2 — calculate the gradient:* rate = change in volume ÷ change in time = 50 ÷ 150 = approximately 0.33.

*Step 3 — the units:* the units are cm³/s (cubic centimetres of gas per second), because volume is divided by time.

2024-06-1CR:7-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:7-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the curve is steepest from 0 s to 60 s, becomes less steep from 60 s to 150 s, and levels off from 150 s to 240 s — because the acid particles are gradually used up.**

From 0 s to 60 s the gradient is at its steepest. The concentration of the dilute sulfuric acid is highest at the start, so there are the most acid particles per unit volume and the most frequent collisions with the surface of the excess zinc every second — hydrogen is produced fastest.

From 60 s to 150 s the curve becomes less steep. As the reaction proceeds, acid particles are used up, so the concentration falls: fewer acid particles per unit volume means fewer frequent collisions each second, and the rate slows.

From 150 s to 240 s the curve levels off and becomes flat (the volume of gas becomes constant): the reaction has stopped because all of the sulfuric acid has been used up, so no further hydrogen is made however long the student waits.

2024-06-1CR:8-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:8-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: crude oil is heated and vaporised; the vapour enters the bottom of the fractionating column, which is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top; the vapours rise, cool and condense at different heights; each fraction is collected where the column temperature falls below its boiling point.**

First, the crude oil is heated (boiled) so that most of its hydrocarbons turn to vapour, and this vapour enters the lower part — the bottom — of the fractionating column. The column has a temperature gradient: it is hottest at the bottom and cooler towards the top. As the vapours rise up the column they cool, and each hydrocarbon condenses to a liquid at the height where the temperature in the column has fallen below its own boiling point. The condensed fractions are then separated according to their boiling points: short-chain fractions with low boiling points condense near the cool top, while long-chain fractions with high boiling points condense near the hot bottom.

2024-06-1CR:8-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:8-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: cracking turns surplus long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful alkanes and into alkenes for making polymers.**

Fractional distillation of crude oil produces more long-chain hydrocarbons than can be used directly — demand for these thick, less flammable fractions is lower than the supply. Cracking splits them, as in C₁₅H₃₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₃H₆ + 2C₂H₄, producing shorter-chain alkanes such as those in petrol, which are more flammable and much more useful as fuels. Cracking also produces alkenes (such as C₃H₆ and C₂H₄), which are used to make polymers (plastics). So cracking matches the supply of fractions to the demand, delivering both better fuels and valuable starting materials.

2024-06-1CR:8-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:8-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: fuels contain sulfur impurities; when the fuel burns, the sulfur produces sulfur dioxide, which dissolves in clouds and causes acid rain.**

The impurity in the fuel is sulfur. On burning, the sulfur reacts with oxygen in the air, producing sulfur dioxide (SO₂), which leaves the engine or furnace in the exhaust gases. The sulfur dioxide dissolves in moisture in the atmosphere and reacts further, causing acid rain — this damages buildings and statues, harms forests, and acidifies lakes and rivers.

2024-06-1CR:9-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:9-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: NaCl, ZnO and (NH₄)₂SO₄.**

Balance the charges of each pair of ions so the compound is neutral. Na⁺ paired with Cl− needs one of each: NaCl. Zn²⁺ paired with O²− cancels 2+ against 2− in a one-to-one ratio: ZnO. NH₄⁺ paired with SO₄²− needs two ammonium ions for each sulfate ion, so the formula is (NH₄)₂SO₄ — the brackets go round the NH₄ group because two of them are needed. Write the charges outside the formula only as ion labels; the compound formula itself carries no charges.

2024-06-1CR:9-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:9-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: zinc sulfate.**

Zn²⁺ is the zinc ion and SO₄²− is the sulfate ion, so the compound ZnSO₄ is named zinc sulfate — the metal first, then the negative ion, with no prefixes needed because the charges already fix the one-to-one ratio.

2024-06-1CR:9-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:9-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: draw the 2 bonding electrons shared between H and Cl as a single covalent bond, and give chlorine three lone pairs for the rest of the molecule.**

In the dot-and-cross diagram hydrogen contributes its single electron and chlorine contributes one electron to the shared pair, making 2 bonding electrons drawn in the overlap between the two atoms (use dots for one atom and crosses for the other, or any combination — the origin just needs to be clear). The rest of the molecule is chlorine's remaining outer-shell electrons, drawn as three lone pairs around the Cl only. Hydrogen's outer shell is complete with just the bonding pair, so it gets no lone pairs.

2024-06-1CR:9-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:9-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the magnesium ion is Mg2+ (the magnesium atom with its outer-shell electrons removed) and the chloride ion is Cl− (the chlorine atom with one extra electron); show the charge on each ion.**

Magnesium loses the two electrons from its outermost shell to become Mg2+: draw the same complete electronic configuration as the magnesium atom but with no electrons in the outer shell, and label the ion Mg2+ (a 2+ charge). Chlorine gains one electron to fill its outer shell and becomes Cl−: draw the chlorine configuration with one additional electron in the outer shell, and label the ion Cl−. Dots, crosses or any combination are all acceptable ways to show the electron origins, but the full configurations and the charge labels are what the question asks for.

2024-06-1CR:9-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:9-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: magnesium chloride is a giant ionic lattice held together by strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, while hydrogen chloride is simple molecular with only weak intermolecular forces between its molecules — so far more energy is required to separate the particles in MgCl₂ than in HCl.**

Hydrogen chloride exists as simple molecules (simple molecular, with covalent bonding within each H–Cl molecule). Between one HCl molecule and the next there are only weak intermolecular forces, and it is these weak forces that are overcome when HCl melts — the strong covalent bonds inside the molecules are not broken at all.

Magnesium chloride, in contrast, is a giant ionic lattice (an ionic structure) made of Mg2+ and Cl− ions. Throughout the lattice there is strong electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions, acting in every direction. Much more energy is therefore required to break the many strong ionic bonds in MgCl₂ than to overcome the weak intermolecular forces in HCl, which is why magnesium chloride has a much higher melting point than hydrogen chloride.

2024-06-1CR:10-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:10-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: a catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway (route) with a lower activation energy.**

The manganese(IV) oxide gives the decomposition of the hydrogen peroxide a different route to follow — one that needs less energy from each collision for the particles to react. Because this alternative pathway has a lower activation energy, a greater proportion of collisions are successful, so more oxygen is released each second and the rate of reaction increases. The catalyst itself is unchanged by the reaction.

2024-06-1CR:10-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:10-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: a conical flask.**

The glass container drawn — flat bottom, conical body, narrow neck — is a conical flask, the standard vessel for a gas-evolution reaction like this decomposition, because its shape lets the gas escape steadily through the neck while the contents can be swirled safely.

2024-06-1CR:10-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)
2024-06-1CR:10-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: filter off the manganese(IV) oxide, leave it to dry, then reweigh it — the mass should still be 1.0 g, showing it was not used up.**

*Step 1:* filter the reaction mixture. The manganese(IV) oxide is insoluble, so it is caught as the residue on the filter paper while the liquid passes through.

*Step 2:* leave the residue to dry completely, so only the solid black powder is weighed.

*Step 3:* reweigh the dried solid. A catalyst is not consumed by the reaction it speeds up, so the same mass should be left — still the 1.0 g that was added at the start. A reactant would have been used up and its mass would have fallen, so an unchanged mass of 1.0 g shows the manganese(IV) oxide acted as a catalyst and not as a reactant.

2024-06-1CR:11-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: diamond contains only one type of atom — carbon.**
An element is a substance built from a single kind of atom, and every atom in diamond is a carbon atom. Diamond and graphite are both forms of the element carbon: they are different giant covalent structures of the same element, not compounds, because no second type of atom is present anywhere in the structure.
2024-06-1CR:11-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-1CR:11-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: the attraction is between the shared pair of electrons and the nuclei (plural) of the two bonded atoms.**
In a covalent bond the two atoms share a pair of electrons. That shared pair sits between the atoms and is attracted electrostatically to the positive nucleus of one atom and to the positive nucleus of the other at the same time. Both attractions acting together are what hold the bond: a shared pair of electrons strongly attracted to two nuclei. The word must be nuclei, plural — a bond always involves two positive centres pulling on the same shared electrons.
2024-06-1CR:11-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-1CR:11-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: graphite contains delocalised electrons that can move and flow throughout the structure.**
Each carbon atom in graphite is bonded to only three others, so one outer electron per atom is not tied up in a bond. These electrons become delocalised — free to travel through the whole giant lattice. A current is exactly a flow of charged particles, so the mobile delocalised electrons let graphite conduct electricity. Ions and molecules are irrelevant here: it is the electrons that carry the charge through the solid.
2024-06-1CR:11-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-1CR:11-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: diamond is hard because every carbon atom is bonded to four others in a rigid 3D tetrahedral lattice, so the strong covalent bonds need a lot of energy to break; graphite is soft because it is built of layers that can slide over one another.**
In diamond each carbon atom is joined to four other carbon atoms in a giant tetrahedral network with no weak direction. To cut or scratch diamond you would have to break strong covalent bonds, and those bonds need a lot of energy to break — that is why diamond is so hard. There are no separate molecules in diamond at all, so speaking of weak intermolecular forces between molecules in diamond would be wrong chemistry.
Graphite is the opposite: within each layer the covalent bonds are strong, but the layers are held to each other only weakly. Because the bonding between layers is so feeble, the layers can slide over one another easily, so graphite flakes and feels soft — which is why it works as a lubricant and as the 'lead' in pencils.
2024-06-1CR:11-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-1CR:11-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: the Mr of Cx is 842.8, and x is 70.**
*Step 1 — mass of one mole:* one mole of Cx contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules and each single molecule has a mass of 1.40 × 10⁻²¹ g, so the mass of one mole is 1.40 × 10⁻²¹ × 6.02 × 10²³ = 842.8. That value is the relative formula mass, the Mr of Cx (a relative formula mass carries no units).
*Step 2 — the value of x:* each carbon atom contributes Ar = 12 to the total, so x = 842.8 ÷ 12 = 70.23, and because a molecule must contain a whole number of atoms (an integer), x = 70. Cx is therefore C₇₀.
2024-06-1CR:11-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-1CR:12-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2TaCl₅(s) + 5H₂(g) → 2Ta(s) + 10HCl(g).**
Balance by counting atoms. Two TaCl₅ supply 2 tantalum atoms and 10 chlorine atoms, so 10 HCl must appear on the right to carry the 10 chlorine atoms. Those 10 HCl need 10 hydrogen atoms, which come from 5 H₂. Check: 2 Ta, 10 Cl and 10 H on each side — balanced (any whole-number multiple or fraction of these coefficients is equally balanced).
2024-06-1CR:12-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-1CR:12-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: the mass of solid stops changing — the last three readings, at 5, 6 and 7 hours, are all 1267 kg.**
While the reaction is running, tantalum chloride is being used up, so the solid mass falls. Once the reading holds constant at 1267 kg for hour after hour, no further change is happening: the reaction is complete and the only solid left is the tantalum product.
2024-06-1CR:12-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-1CR:12-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the mole ratio works out at 1 Ta : 5 Cl, so the formula is TaCl₅.**
*Step 1 — mass of chlorine that has been lost:* the solid falls from 2510 kg to 1267 kg, and the 1267 kg left behind is tantalum, so mass of chlorine = 2510 − 1267 = 1243 kg.
*Step 2 — moles of each element:* moles of tantalum = 1 267 000 ÷ 181 = 7000 mol; moles of chlorine = 1 243 000 ÷ 35.5 = 35 014 mol.
*Step 3 — the ratio:* 7000 : 35 014 is the same ratio as 7 : 35, which simplifies to 1 : 5. One tantalum atom to five chlorine atoms gives the formula TaCl₅.
2024-06-1CR:12-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-1CR:12-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: carbon is oxidised and tantalum(V) oxide is reduced — oxygen is transferred from the oxide to the carbon.**
In Ta₂O₅ + 5C → 2Ta + 5CO the carbon gains oxygen, ending up in carbon monoxide, and gaining oxygen is oxidation — so the carbon is oxidised. At the same time the tantalum oxide loses oxygen (its oxygen goes to the carbon), and losing oxygen is reduction — so the tantalum oxide is reduced. One substance losing oxygen while another gains it is exactly what makes this a redox reaction. Keep the direction straight: the tantalum itself never loses oxygen — its oxide does, which is why the oxide is the substance that is reduced.
2024-06-1CR:12-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-1CR:12-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the 2000 mol of Ta₂O₅ would need only 120 000 g of carbon, far less than the 500 000 g supplied, so the carbon is in excess.**
*Step 1 — carbon required:* from Ta₂O₅ + 5C → 2Ta + 5CO, each mole of tantalum(V) oxide needs 5 moles of carbon, so 5 × 2000 = 10 000 mol of carbon.
*Step 2 — convert to grams:* 10 000 × 12 = 120 000 g of carbon needed.
*Step 3 — compare with what is available:* 120 000 g needed is much less than the 500 000 g actually heated with the oxide, so there is more than enough carbon to react with all of the tantalum(V) oxide — the carbon is in excess.
2024-06-1CR:12-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-1CR:12-c-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 724 000 g of tantalum.**
*Step 1 — moles of tantalum:* from Ta₂O₅ + 5C → 2Ta + 5CO, each mole of Ta₂O₅ produces 2 moles of Ta, so 2 × 2000 = 4000 mol of tantalum.
*Step 2 — mass:* mass = moles × Ar = 4000 × 181 = 724 000 g.
2024-06-1CR:12-c-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:1-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: sulfur.**
The element with atomic number 16 is sulfur (symbol S): count sixteen boxes along the Periodic Table and you land on S, in Group 6. Check the small number at the top of the box — it reads 16, which is the proton number.
2024-06-2C:1-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:1-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: beryllium.**
Scan the Periodic Table for the box whose bigger number (the relative atomic mass) is 9: that box is beryllium, Be, the top element of Group 2. Its proton number is smaller than its mass number, and the 9 is the value to match here.
2024-06-2C:1-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:1-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: boron.**
Find where Group 3 meets Period 2: run a finger along the second period until you reach the third column — the element in that position is boron, B. It sits just to the left of carbon at the top of the group.
2024-06-2C:1-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:1-a-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2,8,4.**
Silicon sits in Group 4 and Period 3, so its atoms have three occupied shells: 2 electrons in the first shell, 8 in the second and 4 in the outer shell. Written out that is the electronic configuration 2,8,4 (equally fine as 2.8.4, or as a labelled shell diagram showing the same arrangement).
2024-06-2C:1-a-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:1-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: sodium is more reactive than lithium because its outer electron is further from the nucleus and so is more easily lost.**
A sodium atom has one more occupied shell than a lithium atom — the arrangements are 2,8,1 against 2,1 — so in sodium the outer shell is further from the nucleus and sodium has the larger atomic radius. Because that outer electron sits further out, with more inner shells shielding it, there is less attraction between the outer electron and the positive nucleus in sodium than in lithium. Weaker attraction means the outer electron is lost more easily in a reaction, so sodium reacts more readily than lithium.
2024-06-2C:1-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:2-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: 1 oxygen (O₂ from the air); 2 water (H₂O, moisture).**
Iron rusts only where it is in contact with both oxygen and water at the same time — dry air on its own, or air-free water on its own, will not rust it. Rusting is therefore an oxidation of iron that needs air and moisture together, which is why keeping either one away from the metal stops the rust.
2024-06-2C:2-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:2-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: paint the iron (or oil/grease it, coat it with plastic, wax it, electroplate it, or galvanise it).**
A barrier method simply keeps the two rusting agents, air and moisture, away from the iron surface by covering it with a layer of something the water and oxygen cannot get through. Galvanising counts as a barrier coating too — it is not the same idea as sacrificial protection, which works chemically instead.
2024-06-2C:2-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:2-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: a more reactive metal, such as zinc or magnesium, is connected to (or coated on) the iron and reacts in its place.**
In sacrificial protection the iron is joined to a more reactive metal — zinc and magnesium are the usual choices. That metal takes part in the reactions with oxygen and water more readily than iron does, so it oxidises/corrodes instead of the iron: it is 'sacrificed'. Even if the coating is scratched, the more reactive metal keeps corroding first, so the iron underneath stays intact and does not rust.
2024-06-2C:2-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:3-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: fraction A is refinery gases; fraction F is bitumen.**
In the fractionating column the crude oil separates from top to bottom in order of boiling point. A is the topmost fraction — the very short-chain refinery gases that boil off first — and F is the thick, dark residue drawn from the bottom of the column, bitumen, used for road surfacing and roofing.
2024-06-2C:3-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:3-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: kerosene is used as aircraft fuel.**
Kerosene is the fraction collected between gasoline and diesel in the column, and its biggest use is burning as jet fuel in aircraft engines.
2024-06-2C:3-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:3-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: heat the crude oil until it vaporises, let the vapours rise up a fractionating column, and tap off the kerosene where it condenses.**
*First,* the crude oil is heated so that most of it evaporates/vaporises. *Next,* the vapour passes into the fractionating column and rises up it, with the temperature falling towards the top. *Finally,* each hydrocarbon condenses at the height where the column's temperature matches its boiling point range: the kerosene fraction condenses part-way up the column and is tapped off/removed there. Heavier fractions such as diesel and fuel oil condense much lower down because their boiling points are higher.
2024-06-2C:3-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:3-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: catalyst — silica (silicon dioxide, SiO₂) or alumina (aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃); temperature — between 600 and 700 °C.**
Catalytic cracking passes vaporised long-chain fractions over a hot powdered silicon dioxide/aluminium oxide (zeolite-type) catalyst at roughly 600–700 °C. The hot catalyst plus the high temperature together give the conditions needed to split the carbon–carbon bonds in the long-chain molecules.
2024-06-2C:3-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:3-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: cracking is useful because long-chain fractions are in surplus while smaller ones are in demand, and it makes alkenes for polymers.**
There is a surplus supply of (less demand for) the larger fractions — the thick, viscous long-chain hydrocarbons such as fuel oil and bitumen — but a far greater demand than supply for the smaller fractions. Cracking balances this mismatch: it splits the surplus long-chain molecules into shorter alkanes, and smaller fractions/alkanes like gasoline are needed as petrol/fuel for cars. It also produces alkenes, which are needed to make polymers (plastics) and ethanol. So low-value heavy fractions are converted into high-demand products instead of being wasted.
2024-06-2C:3-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:4-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: plot temperature on the x-axis and mass dissolved on the y-axis, marking a neat cross for each solute at every temperature in the table.**
For potassium nitrate plot (10, 5), (25, 10), (40, 16), (60, 28) and (75, 39); for sodium nitrate plot (10, 21), (25, 23), (40, 26), (60, 31) and (75, 35). Every point must sit within half a small square of its true position — that is the plotting accuracy the grid work demands — and a consistent, clearly visible symbol for each solute keeps the two data sets distinguishable.
2024-06-2C:4-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:4-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: draw one smooth curve of best fit through the potassium nitrate (KNO₃) points, a second smooth curve through the sodium nitrate (NaNO₃) points, and label each curve.**
A curve of best fit is a single smooth line that follows the trend of the points, with roughly as many points sitting just above it as just below it — never join the crosses dot-to-dot with a jagged line. The KNO₃ curve climbs steeply, because its solubility rises quickly with temperature, while the NaNO₃ curve rises only gently and begins to level off. Labelling matters: with two unlabelled (or wrongly swapped) curves the reader cannot tell which solute is which.
2024-06-2C:4-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:4-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: approximately 68 °C.**
Find the point where the two plotted lines cross and read straight down to the temperature axis: the curves meet at about 68 °C. That is the temperature at which the maximum mass dissolved is the same for both solutes — below it sodium nitrate is the more soluble, above it potassium nitrate is.
2024-06-2C:4-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:4-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: 96 g per 100 g of water.**
*Step 1 — read the graph:* at 30 °C the sodium nitrate curve gives a mass of approximately 24 g dissolved in 25 cm³ of water.
*Step 2 — scale up to 100 g of water:* 1.0 cm³ of water has a mass of 1.0 g, so 25 cm³ of water has a mass of 25 g, and 100 g of water is 4 times that amount. solubility = 24 × 4 = 96 g per 100 g of water.
2024-06-2C:4-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:4-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: approximately 13 g of potassium nitrate crystallises out.**
*Step 1 — read the graph at the start:* at 50 °C the saturated solution holds approximately 21 g of KNO₃ in the 25 cm³ of water (mark this reading on the graph with a dashed line).
*Step 2 — read the graph at the end:* on cooling to 20 °C the curve gives approximately 8 g.
*Step 3 — take the difference:* the solid that can no longer stay dissolved crystallises out, so mass = 21 − 8 = 13 g. Show both readings as dashed lines on the graph so that the working behind the subtraction is visible.
2024-06-2C:4-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:5-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: 1 the members share the same general formula; 2 they have the same functional group (and therefore similar chemical properties).**
Any two of these count as characteristics of a homologous series: the same general formula; the same functional group; similar chemical properties; a gradation (trend) in physical properties, such as boiling point rising as the chains lengthen; and consecutive members differing by a CH₂ unit. The alcohols show all of them — methanol, the first member, carries the −OH functional group, and the next member, ethanol, differs from it by exactly one CH₂.
2024-06-2C:5-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:5-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: H₂SO₄ (sulfuric acid).**
Methanol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI): the dichromate is the oxidising agent, and the other reagent that acidifies the mixture is dilute sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄. Without the acid the dichromate oxidation does not work properly.
2024-06-2C:5-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:5-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the colour change is from orange to green.**
Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) starts orange. As it oxidises the methanol to methanoic acid, the orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ ions are reduced to green Cr³⁺ ions, so by the end the mixture looks green. Keep the order right: orange first, green last.
2024-06-2C:5-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:5-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: methanol is drawn as H−C−O−H with an H above and an H below the carbon; methanoic acid is drawn as H−C−O−H with a second oxygen joined to the carbon by a double bond.**
For methanol, display every single bond: the central C carries three H atoms (one to its left, one above, one below) and a fourth single bond to O, with the last H on the right of the O. For methanoic acid, the C is bonded to one H, to an −O−H, and to a second O by a double bond — draw that O above the C with two parallel bond lines (the C=O of the O=C(O)H arrangement). Both structures must show every bond individually; a condensed formula such as CH₃OH is not a displayed formula.
2024-06-2C:5-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:5-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: CH₃OH + HCOOH → HCOOCH₃ + H₂O.**
This is esterification: the alcohol and the carboxylic acid join, splitting off water. Methanol plus methanoic acid gives the ester methyl methanoate, HCOOCH₃, plus H₂O. Count the atoms to confirm the balance — the left side holds C₂H₆O₃ and the right side holds C₂H₆O₃, so the equation is balanced.
2024-06-2C:5-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:5-d-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — butyl ethanoate.**
Split the structural formula CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ at the ester link −COO−: the CH₃COO− half comes from ethanoic acid, so the acid-derived part of the name is ethanoate, while the alkyl group on the other side, −CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃, carries four carbon atoms — butyl. Name the alkyl part first and the acid part second: butyl ethanoate. Why the others fail: B, butyl methanoate, is wrong because a methanoate must come from methanoic acid (HCOO−), not from CH₃COO−; C, ethyl butanoate, is wrong because ethyl is the two-carbon group −CH₂CH₃ and the acid half would not match either; D, methyl butanoate, is wrong because methyl is the one-carbon group −CH₃. None of B, C or D fits the printed formula CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃.
2024-06-2C:5-d-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:5-d-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: C₆H₁₂O₂.**
Count the atoms in CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃: carbon — two in the CH₃COO− part plus four in the butyl chain, six in total; hydrogen — 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 12; oxygen — two. Written as a molecular formula that is C₆H₁₂O₂.
2024-06-2C:5-d-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:6-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: filter off the solid, wash it with distilled water, then dry it.**
Lead(II) bromide is insoluble, so it forms as a precipitate. *First,* filter the reaction mixture: the lead(II) bromide collects on the filter paper as the residue while the sodium nitrate solution runs through as the filtrate. *Second,* wash the solid on the paper with distilled water to rinse off any sodium nitrate solution clinging to the crystals. *Third,* drying: press the washed solid between filter papers, or leave it to dry in air, in a warm oven or in a desiccator. Nothing needs crystallising or evaporating — the product is already the solid on the paper.
2024-06-2C:6-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:6-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: amount = concentration × volume = 2.0 × 0.025 = 0.05 mol.**
Convert the volume first: 25 cm³ = 25 ÷ 1000 = 0.025 dm³. Then multiply by the concentration: 2.0 mol/dm³ × 0.025 dm³ = 0.05 mol — written to two decimal places, 0.050 mol, the amount of sodium bromide used.
2024-06-2C:6-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:6-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: approximately 9 g of lead(II) bromide.**
*Step 1 — moles of PbBr₂:* the equation Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2NaBr → PbBr₂ + 2NaNO₃ uses 2 mol of NaBr for every 1 mol of PbBr₂ (a 2 : 1 ratio), so n(PbBr₂) = 0.05 ÷ 2 = 0.025 mol.
*Step 2 — mass:* mass = moles × Mr = 0.025 × 367 = 9.175 g, which rounds to approximately 9 g.
2024-06-2C:6-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:6-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: in the solid the ions are locked in fixed positions in the lattice; only when molten are the ions free to move and carry the current.**
Solid lead(II) bromide is a giant ionic lattice: the Pb²⁺ and Br⁻ ions vibrate about fixed positions and cannot wander, so there are no charged particles free to move — the solid cannot conduct, and electrolysis cannot happen. Melting collapses the lattice: the ions become free to move throughout the liquid, so they travel to the electrodes and carry charge through the electrolyte, and electrolysis occurs. It is the movement of the ions that matters — not electrons.
2024-06-2C:6-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:6-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: graphite electrodes — they are inert and able to withstand the high temperature.**
The electrolyte is held at 400 °C, so the electrodes must survive it: graphite has a very high melting point, far above 400 °C, and it is chemically inert, so it does not react with the molten lead(II) bromide or with the products at either electrode. Graphite also conducts electricity, which the electrodes must do to feed current into the electrolyte. Platinum would serve equally well for the same two reasons: it conducts and it is unreactive at this temperature.
2024-06-2C:6-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:6-c-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb.**
At the negative electrode reduction happens: each lead ion, Pb²⁺, gains 2 electrons to become a neutral lead atom, Pb. The half-equation balances both ways — one Pb on each side, and the 2 electrons on the left exactly cancel the 2+ charge of the ion, so atoms and charge both balance.
2024-06-2C:6-c-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:6-d-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: a brown vapour (red-brown fumes) of bromine forms at the positive electrode.**
The Br⁻ ions are discharged at the positive electrode, and the bromine produced escapes above the molten electrolyte as a brown vapour/gas. Describe the colour as brown or red-brown — on its own, orange or plain red is not the accepted description of bromine vapour.
2024-06-2C:6-d-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:6-d-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: because the bromide ions lose electrons.**
In 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ each Br⁻ ion gives up its extra electron to form a neutral bromine atom, and loss of electrons is the definition of oxidation. Be precise that it is the bromide ion, Br⁻, that loses the electrons — the bromine atoms made are the product of that loss.
2024-06-2C:6-d-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:7-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: a covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of the two atoms and the shared pair of electrons.**
When two non-metal atoms share a pair of electrons, that negatively charged shared pair sits between the two atoms and is attracted simultaneously to the positive nucleus of one atom and to the positive nucleus of the other. This mutual attraction between the shared pair of electrons and the nuclei (plural — both nuclei) is what holds the covalent bond together.
2024-06-2C:7-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:7-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: in the organic solvent the litmus paper stays blue; in the aqueous solution it turns red.**
In the organic solvent the hydrogen chloride stays as covalent HCl molecules — it does not dissociate — so there are no H⁺ ions in the solution and the solution is not acidic: dry blue litmus paper dipped into it stays blue, with no change. In water the HCl molecules ionise instead: H⁺ ions are formed and hydrochloric acid forms, and it is those H⁺ ions that make the solution acidic, so the dry blue litmus paper turns red. Same compound, two different behaviours — the acidity only appears when H⁺ ions are actually present, which is why hydrogen chloride shows its acidic properties only in aqueous solution.
2024-06-2C:7-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:7-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: ΔH = −184 kJ/mol.**
*Step 1 — bonds broken in the reactants (energy in):* break the one H−H bond (436 kJ/mol) and the one Cl−Cl bond (242 kJ/mol): 436 + 242 = 678 kJ/mol.
*Step 2 — bonds formed in the products (energy out):* make 2 H−Cl bonds: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ/mol released.
*Step 3 — overall:* more energy is released making bonds than is needed to break them: 862 − 678 = 184 kJ/mol given out to the surroundings. The reaction is exothermic, so the enthalpy change carries a negative sign: ΔH = −184 kJ/mol.
2024-06-2C:7-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2C:7-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: an exothermic reaction profile — a horizontal reactants line for H₂ + Cl₂, an activation-energy hump, and a lower horizontal products line for 2HCl.**
Use horizontal lines drawn in the correct positions for the energy levels. *Reactants:* the left-hand level is labelled H₂ + Cl₂. *Products:* the right-hand level is labelled 2HCl and sits lower than the reactants, because ΔH is negative for this exothermic reaction. *Activation energy:* from the reactants' level, draw a vertical line or arrow pointing up to the top of the hump and label it Ea (activation energy) — it must point up. *ΔH:* draw a vertical arrow from the reactants' level down to the products' level and label it ΔH — for this exothermic reaction it points down. The hump above the reactants is the energy barrier that must be climbed before the reaction can proceed; here that energy comes from the ultraviolet radiation.
2024-06-2C:7-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:1-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: B — 3.** The period number of an element equals the number of occupied electron shells in its atoms. A sulfur atom has its electrons arranged in three shells, so sulfur sits in period 3. Option A (2) is wrong because sulfur is not in period 2; option C (4) is wrong because sulfur is not in period 4; option D (6) is wrong because sulfur is not in period 6 — six is the number of electrons in sulfur's outer shell, not the period number.
2024-06-2CR:1-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:1-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: D — 2−.** A sulfur atom is in Group 6 and has six electrons in its outer shell, so it gains two electrons to complete that shell; gaining two negative electrons leaves the sulfide ion with a charge of 2−. Option A (1+) is wrong because the sulfide ion is negative, not positive; option B (2+) is also a positive charge and so cannot describe a sulfide ion; option C (1−) has the right sign but the wrong size — sulfur gains two electrons, not one.
2024-06-2CR:1-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:1-b-i.solutionMd: **Answer: heating gives the zinc and the sulfur enough energy to react — the reaction has a high activation energy.** At room temperature the mixture barely reacts, so the zinc and sulfur particles must be given extra kinetic energy to overcome the activation energy barrier before zinc sulfide can form. Heating therefore starts the reaction and increases the rate of reaction once it is going.
2024-06-2CR:1-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:1-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: Mr of ZnS = 97.** The formula unit contains one zinc and one sulfur, so add the two relative atomic masses printed in the question: 65 + 32 = 97. Relative formula mass has no units, so any unit written after the number is unnecessary.
2024-06-2CR:1-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:2-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: C — neutron.** W sits inside the nucleus alongside the protons but carries no charge at all, and an uncharged particle found in the nucleus is a neutron. Option A (electron) is wrong because electrons orbit the nucleus in shells and are never inside it; option B (ion) is wrong because an ion is a whole atom or group of atoms that has lost or gained electrons, not a particle inside a nucleus; option D (proton) is wrong because protons have a positive charge, and the diagram already uses + symbols for the positively charged particles.
2024-06-2CR:2-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:2-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: C — 9.** Mass number counts protons plus neutrons: the atom shown has 4 protons and 5 neutrons, and 4 + 5 = 9. Option A (4) is just the proton number; option B (5) is just the number of neutrons; option D (13) is wrong because it adds the electrons as well — 13 is the total of protons + neutrons + electrons, and electrons are so light that they are never counted in the mass number.
2024-06-2CR:2-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:2-b-i.solutionMd: **Answer: similarity — both isotopes have the same number of protons; difference — they contain different numbers of neutrons.** Isotopes of lithium share a proton number (3), and neutral atoms of each isotope therefore have the same number of electrons too, which is why both behave chemically as lithium. What changes is the neutron count: mass number − proton number gives the neutrons, so lithium-6 has 6 − 3 = 3 neutrons while lithium-7 has 7 − 3 = 4 neutrons.
2024-06-2CR:2-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:2-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: Ar = 6.925, which is 6.9 to 2 significant figures.** *Step 1 — weighted contributions:* relative atomic mass is a weighted mean of the isotope masses, so multiply each mass number by its percentage abundance: 7.5 × 6 = 45 and 92.5 × 7 = 647.5. *Step 2 — add them:* 45 + 647.5 = 692.5. *Step 3 — divide by the total percentage:* 692.5 ÷ 100 = 6.925. Because lithium-7 is by far the more abundant isotope, the answer sits much closer to 7 than to 6 — a simple average of the two mass numbers would be wrong.
2024-06-2CR:2-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:3-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: label the circles as positive ions (cations) and the free particles between them as delocalised electrons.** In solid magnesium each atom has lost its outer electron, so the structure is a regular lattice of Mg²⁺ positive ions packed in layers, surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons that can move freely through the whole metal. That combination of fixed positive ions and mobile delocalised electrons is the metallic bonding model the diagram is testing.
2024-06-2CR:3-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:3-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: magnesium is malleable because its layers of atoms (ions) can slide over one another.** The positive ions in the lattice sit in neat rows held together by the sea of delocalised electrons. When a force is applied, whole layers shift and settle into new positions while the metallic bonding still holds — the metal bends and flattens instead of shattering, which is exactly what malleable means.
2024-06-2CR:3-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:3-b-i.solutionMd: **Answer: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s).** *Balancing:* oxygen exists as diatomic O₂ molecules, so the two oxygen atoms must end up in two separate MgO units — putting a 2 in front of both Mg and MgO gives two magnesium atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side of the equation. *State symbols:* magnesium is a solid metal (s), oxygen is a gas (g), and the magnesium oxide formed when magnesium burns in oxygen is a solid (s).
2024-06-2CR:3-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:3-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: because magnesium gains oxygen.** Oxidation means gain of oxygen: in the reaction 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO each magnesium atom takes oxygen from the oxygen molecules and ends up inside magnesium oxide, so magnesium is the substance that is oxidised. The same idea in electron terms: each Mg atom loses electrons to form Mg²⁺, and loss of electrons is also oxidation.
2024-06-2CR:3-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:3-c-i.solutionMd: **Answer: powdered magnesium has a far larger surface area than ribbon.** With more of the metal exposed to the acid at once, magnesium particles collide with acid particles more frequently, so the rate of reaction increases and the magnesium is used up faster — the reaction finishes sooner without changing the products at all.
2024-06-2CR:3-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:3-c-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: to be certain that every trace of acid has reacted.** Adding magnesium in excess means there is more metal than the acid needs, so all of the hydrochloric acid is used up (neutralised) and the solution left contains only magnesium chloride in water; the leftover solid magnesium is then removed by filtration in Step 4.
2024-06-2CR:3-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:3-c-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: 0.60 g of magnesium.** *Step 1 — amount of acid:* 25.0 × 2.00 = 50, and 50 ÷ 1000 = 0.05 mol of hydrochloric acid. *Step 2 — amount of magnesium:* the equation Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g) shows that 1 mole of magnesium reacts with 2 moles of hydrochloric acid, so n(Mg) = 0.05 ÷ 2 = 0.025 mol. *Step 3 — mass:* mass = moles × Ar = 0.025 × 24 = 0.6 g. This is the minimum mass, because the method deliberately adds extra magnesium in excess so that no acid is left over.
2024-06-2CR:3-c-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:4-a.solutionMd: **Answer: a temperature of about 30°C, and yeast to supply the enzymes.** Fermentation is carried out at a warm 30°C — anything in the 30–40°C range keeps the enzymes working without denaturing them. The yeast provides enzymes such as zymase, which catalyse the conversion of glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide; without the yeast the reaction is far too slow to be useful.
2024-06-2CR:4-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:4-b.solutionMd: **Answer: because oxygen in the air would react with the ethanol, oxidising it to ethanoic acid.** The yeast must work anaerobically: if air is present, the ethanol product is oxidised by the oxygen into ethanoic acid — the acid in vinegar — destroying the product you want. With plenty of oxygen the ethanol would not be formed at all, because the yeast respires aerobically and produces carbon dioxide (CO₂) and water (H₂O) instead.
2024-06-2CR:4-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:4-c-i.solutionMd: **Answer: 2CO₂.** The fermentation equation is C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂: glucose carries 6 C, 12 H and 6 O atoms; the 2C₂H₅OH on the right accounts for 4 C, 12 H and 2 O, so the missing 2 C and 4 O must come from 2 molecules of CO₂.
2024-06-2CR:4-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:4-c-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: 12.5%.** *Step 1 — theoretical moles:* from C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, each mole of glucose would give 2 moles of ethanol, so 500 mol of glucose could produce 500 × 2 = 1000 mol of ethanol (at 100% yield that would be 1000 × 46 = 46 000 g). *Step 2 — actual moles:* the fermentation actually produced 5750 g of ethanol, and 5750 ÷ 46 = 125 mol. *Step 3 — percentage yield:* 125 ÷ 1000 × 100 = 12.5%, so the fermentation delivered an eighth of the ethanol that was possible.

2024-06-2CR:5-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: a volumetric pipette.** A volumetric pipette is designed to deliver one exact volume — the 25.0 cm³ needed here — with the accuracy a titration demands; a burette could measure the volume out precisely too. A measuring cylinder is the apparatus to avoid, because its graduations are not accurate enough for this quantitative work.
2024-06-2CR:5-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:5-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: titrate the sodium hydrogensulfate against the alkali.** Fill a burette with the sodium hydrogensulfate solution and record the initial reading. Add a few drops of indicator to the 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide in the conical flask. Run in the sodium hydrogensulfate while swirling the flask continuously so the two solutions mix thoroughly. As the indicator's colour starts to flicker, add the sodium hydrogensulfate dropwise near to the endpoint until a single extra drop makes the indicator change colour permanently, then record the final reading — the difference between the two readings is the accurate volume needed. Repeat the titration until at least two results are concordant, and use the mean of the concordant volumes.

2024-06-2CR:5-b.solutionMd: **Answer: evaporate gently, crystallise, separate, then dry — never heat to complete dryness.** Warm the sodium sulfate solution so that water evaporates until crystals first start to form and the solution is saturated (roughly when the volume is about half the original volume), then stop heating at the crystallisation point. Leave the hot, concentrated solution to cool slowly so that more crystals crystallise out as the temperature falls. Pour off the excess liquid that the crystals sit in (or filter the crystals off), because that liquid carries the soluble impurities away. Finally leave the crystals in a warm place to dry — a warm oven, a desiccator, or pressing them between sheets of filter paper all work. Heating until everything is dry would drive off the water of crystallisation and spoil the hydrated crystals, so the drying stage must be gentle.
2024-06-2CR:5-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:5-c.solutionMd: **Answer: x = 10.** *Step 1 — masses from the table:* the anhydrous sodium sulfate left behind weighs 27.96 − 25.12 = 2.84 g, and the water driven off weighs 31.56 − 27.96 = 3.60 g. *Step 2 — moles:* moles of Na₂SO₄ = 2.84 ÷ 142 = 0.02 mol, and moles of H₂O = 3.60 ÷ 18 = 0.20 mol. *Step 3 — simplest whole-number ratio:* 0.20 ÷ 0.02 = 10, so x = 10 — each formula unit of the hydrated salt Na₂SO₄.xH₂O carries ten molecules of water of crystallisation. (Check: Mr of the hydrated salt = 142 + (10 × 18) = 322.)

2024-06-2CR:6-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: platinum.** The electrodes must be inert — they must not react with the dilute sulfuric acid or with the products collecting on their surfaces — and platinum is a dense, unreactive metal that fills the role perfectly. Graphite is another suitable material, being both unreactive and a good conductor of electricity.

2024-06-2CR:6-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: hold a glowing splint in the gas collected at the positive electrode — if the splint relights, the gas is oxygen.** Oxygen relights a glowing (no longer flaming) splint because it supports combustion, so a relight is the positive result of this standard gas test.

2024-06-2CR:6-a-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: hold a lit splint at the mouth of the tube of gas — hydrogen gives a squeaky pop.** The hydrogen made at the negative electrode burns in air with the characteristic squeaky pop as the small amount of gas explodes gently; hearing that sound is the positive result of the hydrogen test.

2024-06-2CR:6-a-iv.solutionMd: **Answer: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.** The H⁺ ions from the dilute sulfuric acid are attracted to the negative electrode, where each ion gains an electron — this gain of electrons is reduction. Two hydrogen ions between them take up the two electrons shown and form one hydrogen molecule, H₂.

2024-06-2CR:6-a-v.solutionMd: **Answer: 0.0237 g of oxygen, to 3 significant figures.** *Step 1 — moles of gas:* moles = volume ÷ molar volume = 17.8 ÷ 24 000 = 0.000742 mol, using the room-temperature molar volume of 24 000 cm³ printed in the question. *Step 2 — Mr of oxygen:* oxygen gas is O₂, so Mr = 32. *Step 3 — mass:* mass = moles × Mr = 0.000742 × 32 = 0.0237 g.

2024-06-2CR:6-b-i.solutionMd: **Answer: because it contains ions that are free to move.** In sodium chloride solution the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are surrounded by water and drift freely; when the power supply pushes them, the positive ions migrate to the negative electrode and the negative ions to the positive electrode, carrying electric charge through the liquid. In the solid the ions would be locked in the lattice and unable to move, so a solid would not conduct.
2024-06-2CR:6-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:6-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: hydrogen is less reactive than sodium.** When both H⁺ and Na⁺ ions reach the negative electrode, only the ion of the less reactive element is discharged: hydrogen lies below sodium in the reactivity series, so the H⁺ ions gain electrons more easily than Na⁺ ions do and bubble off as hydrogen gas instead of forming metallic sodium.
2024-06-2CR:6-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:6-b-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: the universal indicator turns blue or purple.** At the negative electrode the H⁺ ions are discharged as hydrogen gas, which leaves OH⁻ hydroxide ions behind in the sample of solution; the liquid there has effectively become sodium hydroxide, an alkaline solution. Universal indicator shows alkaline solutions as blue, going purple as the alkalinity strengthens — so the final colour is blue/purple because hydroxide ions are present in that solution.
