2024-06-2CR:7-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: the yield of ethanol decreases.** The equilibrium C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ C₂H₅OH(g) has two gas molecules on the left but only one on the right. Decreasing the pressure shifts the position of equilibrium towards the side with more moles of gas, because that choice raises the pressure again — so the equilibrium moves to the left, the backward direction, and less ethanol is present at equilibrium.
2024-06-2CR:7-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:7-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: the yield of ethanol at equilibrium does not change.** A catalyst works by lowering the activation energy, and that speeds up the forward reaction and the backward reaction equally. The forward and backward rates rise by the same amount, so the balance between them is untouched: equilibrium is simply reached sooner, but the position of equilibrium — and with it the yield of ethanol — stays exactly where it was without the catalyst.
2024-06-2CR:7-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:7-b-i.solutionMd: **Answer: ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed ≈ −40 kJ/mol.** *Step 1 — bonds broken:* the reactants C₂H₄ + H₂O contain 4 C–H bonds and 1 C=C bond in the ethene plus 2 O–H bonds in the steam: 4 × 414 = 1656 and 2 × 463 = 926, and the C=C adds 614, so the total is 1656 + 926 + 614 = 3196 kJ/mol. *Step 2 — bonds formed:* the product C₂H₅OH holds 5 C–H, 1 C–C, 1 C–O and 1 O–H bond: 5 × 414 = 2070, then 2070 + 346 + 358 + 463 = 3237 kJ/mol. *Step 3 — enthalpy change:* the sum of bonds broken minus the sum of bonds formed gives 3237 − 3196 = 41 kJ/mol more energy released than absorbed, so ΔH ≈ −41 kJ/mol — approximately −40 kJ/mol, exactly what the question asks you to show.
2024-06-2CR:7-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:7-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: more energy is released when bonds are made than is taken in when bonds are broken.** Breaking bonds takes in energy — it is endothermic — while making bonds gives out energy, which is exothermic. For this reaction the energy required to break the bonds in the ethene and the steam is smaller than the energy released when the bonds of the ethanol form, so there is a net release of energy to the surroundings and the enthalpy change ΔH is negative.
2024-06-2CR:7-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:7-b-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: two energy levels, with the products line below the reactants line.** Draw a vertical energy axis. Place the left hand line higher and label it with the reactants, C₂H₄ + H₂O (ethene + steam); place the right hand line lower and label it with the product, C₂H₅OH (ethanol), because the exothermic reaction releases energy and the products end up with less of it. Then mark the enthalpy change: a downwards arrow from the reactant level to the product level, labelled ΔH (about −40 kJ/mol).
2024-06-2CR:7-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:7-c-i.solutionMd: **Answer: draw ester A as ethyl ethanoate, CH₃–COO–CH₂CH₃, with every bond shown.** The displayed formula keeps the CH₃ and C=O part of the ethanoic acid, then joins the acid's single-bonded oxygen to the CH₂ of the ethanol fragment: that –COO– arrangement is the displayed ester linkage, the feature that defines an ester. Show each atom by its symbol and each bond as a line, including the C=O double bond; the rest of the molecule is simply the two-carbon acid chain and the two-carbon alcohol chain unchanged, and the H₂O released is built from the acid's –OH and an H from the alcohol.
2024-06-2CR:7-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-06-2CR:7-c-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: ethyl ethanoate.** Ester names put the alcohol part first and the acid part second: the ethanol supplies the ethyl group (C₂H₅), and the ethanoic acid supplies the ethanoate part (CH₃COO). So the ester made from ethanol reacting with ethanoic acid is named ethyl ethanoate.
2024-06-2CR:7-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:1-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: liquid → solid is freezing; gas → liquid is condensing; solid → gas is sublimation.**
Freezing is what happens when a liquid cools: its particles lose energy and lock into fixed positions in a regular lattice, so the liquid becomes a solid. Condensing (the noun is condensation) is the reverse of evaporation — a gas loses energy and its particles pull close together to form a liquid. Sublimation is the change straight from solid to gas with no liquid formed in between. The other words in the box do not fit these rows: melting is solid to liquid, evaporation is liquid to gas, and heating and cooling describe energy changes rather than naming a change of state.
2024-11-1C:1-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:1-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: draw six circles of a similar size, randomly arranged through the box, with none of them touching.**
In the gas state the atoms are free to move and are widely separated, so the six circles should be spread out in a random arrangement across the whole box — make sure at least one circle sits near the top of the box and at least one near the bottom, and keep them the same size as the circles already drawn. No two circles may touch: touching circles would show the close packing of a solid or liquid, not the wide spacing of a gas.
2024-11-1C:1-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:1-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — the atoms move randomly in the gas state.**
Gas atoms fly around freely in every direction, colliding and spreading out, so their motion is completely random. B is wrong because atoms in a solid do not move randomly — they can only vibrate about fixed positions in the lattice. C is wrong because it is the solid state, not the gas state, that holds atoms in fixed positions; gas atoms travel wherever they like. D is wrong because atoms in the liquid state are not in fixed positions either — they can slide past one another, which is why a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.
2024-11-1C:1-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:1-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: H₂O(l) → H₂O(s).**
Water turning into ice is the liquid state changing to the solid state, so the first state symbol is (l) for liquid and the second is (s) for solid. It is still the same substance, H₂O, on both sides of the arrow — only the arrangement and energy of the molecules changes. State symbols are written in brackets straight after the formula, and upper case or lower case letters are both fine here as long as you are consistent.
2024-11-1C:1-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:2-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: oxygen (O₂).**
Combustion is burning, and a fuel can only burn if oxygen is present — oxygen is the gas that supports combustion, combining with the fuel in an exothermic reaction. None of the other gases in the table supports burning: nitrogen is very unreactive, chlorine will not make a fuel burn, and hydrogen chloride is not involved in combustion at all.
2024-11-1C:2-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:2-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: nitrogen (N₂).**
Air is a mixture of gases, and nitrogen is by far the most abundant one — roughly four-fifths of the air by volume. Oxygen comes second at about a fifth, and gases such as chlorine, hydrogen chloride and hydrogen are only ever present in tiny traces in the atmosphere.
2024-11-1C:2-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:2-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: chlorine (Cl₂).**
Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper: moist blue or purple litmus turns white in this gas. The bleaching happens because chlorine reacts with the water on the damp paper to make acidic, bleaching products. No other gas in the table does this, so a damp litmus test is a quick way to identify chlorine.
2024-11-1C:2-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:2-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: hydrogen chloride is a compound because it contains atoms of two different elements, hydrogen and chlorine, chemically bonded together.**
Two things make a substance a compound. First, its atoms must be atoms of different elements — hydrogen chloride contains two different elements, hydrogen and chlorine, so it qualifies. Second, those atoms must be chemically joined, not just physically mixed: in hydrogen chloride each hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to a chlorine atom, so the two elements are combined together in one substance with a fixed formula. A jar holding hydrogen gas and chlorine gas separately would be a mixture; once the atoms are bonded, it is the compound hydrogen chloride.
2024-11-1C:2-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:2-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: D — chlorine has the strongest forces of attraction between its molecules.**
When a simple molecular substance like chlorine boils, the covalent bonds inside its molecules are never broken — what is overcome is the attraction between one molecule and the next. Chlorine has the highest boiling point in the table (−35 °C), so more energy is needed to separate its molecules than for any other gas listed, which means the forces of attraction between chlorine molecules are the strongest. A is wrong because the covalent bonds between the atoms are not broken when chlorine boils. B is wrong because covalent bonds do not occur between molecules — they act only within a molecule. C is wrong because chlorine is a molecular substance and has no ionic bonds at all.
2024-11-1C:2-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:3-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: 1 oxygen (or air); 2 water.**
Iron needs both oxygen and water at the same time to rust. A nail kept in dry air stays bright, and a nail standing in water that has been boiled to remove dissolved oxygen (and sealed with oil) stays bright too — only a nail exposed to both air and moisture rusts. Rusting is an oxidation reaction of iron, so the two substances it must take from the air and surroundings are oxygen and water.
2024-11-1C:3-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:3-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: hydrated iron(III) oxide.**
Rust is a compound, not just dirty iron: it is iron(III) oxide with water built into its structure, which is why the full name is hydrated iron(III) oxide (the oxide part is Fe₂O₃, with the iron present as Fe³⁺ ions). The word hydrated records the water of crystallisation held in the solid. An older name for the same compound is ferric oxide.
2024-11-1C:3-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:3-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: the paint acts as a barrier — a protective layer that keeps water and oxygen away from the iron.**
Rusting cannot happen unless both oxygen and water reach the iron surface. A layer of paint forms a physical barrier that prevents air and moisture getting to the iron, so the reactants never meet the metal and no rust can form. That is also its weakness: the protection lasts only while the layer is unbroken, which is why method A stops working the moment the paint is scratched.
2024-11-1C:3-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:3-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: galvanising.**
Coating iron or steel with zinc is called galvanising. It is also an example of sacrificial protection, because the zinc coating sacrifices itself — it reacts in preference to the iron underneath, so the iron stays protected even where the zinc layer is damaged.
2024-11-1C:3-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:3-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: zinc is more reactive than iron, so the zinc reacts instead of the iron — it oxidises, forming zinc oxide, before the iron can react.**
Zinc is above iron in the reactivity series: it has a greater tendency to lose electrons than iron does. When the coating is scratched, both metals are exposed to oxygen and water, but the more reactive zinc atoms lose their electrons first — the zinc oxidises, forming zinc oxide, and reacts before any iron is attacked. The iron is therefore protected by sacrificial action: the zinc corrodes in its place. Note that zinc does not rust (rusting is what iron does), and the zinc does not react with the iron — it reacts with the oxygen and water instead of the iron.
2024-11-1C:3-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:4-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: draw a pencil start line just above the bottom of the paper, put a spot of each ink on it, stand the paper in a beaker of solvent with the spots above the solvent, and let the solvent rise.**
*Step 1* — use a ruler to draw a line in pencil just above the bottom of the chromatography paper. Pencil is used because graphite is insoluble, so the line stays put and does not dissolve into the solvent. *Step 2* — put a small spot of each ink (A, B, C, D and E) along the pencil line, spaced apart, before the paper has any contact with the solvent. *Step 3* — pour some solvent into the beaker. *Step 4* — place the paper upright in the beaker so that the ink spots sit above the level of the solvent; spots below the surface would simply dissolve off the paper into the solvent instead of travelling up it. *Step 5* — leave the apparatus until the solvent has risen up the paper, nearly to the top, then take the paper out. As the solvent climbs, each dye dissolves to a different extent and is carried a different distance, separating the dyes in each ink.
2024-11-1C:4-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:4-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: ink E — its dye stayed on the start line and did not travel up the paper.**
A dye can only move up a chromatogram if it dissolves in the solvent, because the moving solvent is what carries the dissolved dye particles along. On this chromatogram the spot of ink E has not moved at all: it is still sitting on the pencil start line while every other ink has produced spots further up the paper. The dye in ink E therefore has an Rf value of 0 — it stayed on the start line because it is insoluble in the solvent.
2024-11-1C:4-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:4-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: inks A and C — their dye spots have travelled to the same height on the chromatogram.**
Dyes with the same solubility in the solvent are carried the same distance in the same time, so two spots that finish level with each other belong to the same dye. Here the spot from ink A and the spot from ink C both sit at the same height — they have travelled the same distance from the start line, giving them the same Rf value — which shows the two inks contain that same dye.
2024-11-1C:4-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:4-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: measure two distances from the pencil start line and divide one by the other: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent.**
*Step 1* — measure the distance from the start line to the centre of the dye spot from ink C: this is the distance moved by the spot. *Step 2* — measure the distance from the start line to the solvent front, the furthest point the solvent has climbed: this is the distance moved by the solvent. *Step 3* — the Rf value is the first distance ÷ the second distance. Both measurements must start from the same reference line, and the answer always comes out between 0 and 1, because the dissolved dye can never outrun the solvent that carries it.
2024-11-1C:4-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:5-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: a glowing splint relights in oxygen.**
Put a splint that is glowing (no longer flaming) into a sample of the gas: oxygen supports burning so strongly that it relights the glowing splint. This is the standard laboratory test, and it confirms that the gas being collected during the decomposition of the hydrogen peroxide is oxygen.
2024-11-1C:5-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:5-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: a catalyst provides an alternative pathway (an alternative route) for the reaction, with a lower activation energy.**
The catalyst gives the reacting particles a different route from reactants to products — an alternative pathway whose activation energy is lower than that of the uncatalysed reaction. Because less energy is needed for a collision to lead to reaction, many more collisions are successful every second, so the hydrogen peroxide decomposes faster. The catalyst itself is unchanged at the end and is not used up, which is why only a small amount is needed.
2024-11-1C:5-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:5-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: A is the conical flask; B is the gas syringe.**
The hydrogen peroxide and the catalyst are mixed in apparatus A, the conical flask. The oxygen produced then passes into B, the gas syringe, whose printed scale (0 to 100 cm³) lets the student read off the volume of gas collected each minute.
2024-11-1C:5-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:5-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 38 cm³.**
*Step 1* — find 4 minutes on the time axis and draw a vertical line up from it until it meets the curved line of the graph. *Step 2* — from that point, read horizontally across to the volume axis. *Step 3* — the reading is 38 cm³ (a reading anywhere between 37 and 39 cm³ fits the graph). That is the volume of oxygen gas collected during the first 4 minutes of the decomposition.
2024-11-1C:5-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:5-c-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: approximately 7.5 cm³/minute.**
*Step 1* — at 8 minutes on the graph, draw a tangent to the curve: a straight line drawn so that it touches the curve once only at that point and matches its steepness there. *Step 2* — take two measurements from widely separated points on your tangent: the volume change between them and the time change between them. A rise of 58 to 60 cm³ over a run of 8 minutes fits this tangent. *Step 3* — use the measurements to calculate the rate: rate = 60 ÷ 8 = 7.5. *Step 4* — the units are volume ÷ time, so the rate of reaction at 8 minutes is 7.5 cm³/minute. The tangent is steepest early in the reaction and shallower here, showing the rate has fallen as the hydrogen peroxide is used up.
2024-11-1C:5-c-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:6-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: AlCl₃, ZnSO₄ and (NH₄)₃N.**
*Step 1* — aluminium ions are Al³⁺ and chloride ions are Cl⁻; charges must cancel, so three 1− chloride ions balance one 3+ aluminium ion: AlCl₃. *Step 2* — zinc ions are Zn²⁺ and sulfate ions are SO₄²⁻; the 2+ and 2− charges cancel one-to-one: ZnSO₄. *Step 3* — ammonium ions are NH₄⁺ and nitride ions are N³⁻, so three 1+ ammonium ions are needed per nitride ion: (NH₄)₃N. Always check that the total positive charge equals the total negative charge, and put brackets round NH₄ so the subscript 3 applies to the whole ammonium ion.
2024-11-1C:6-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:6-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: aluminium sulfate.**
Al₂(SO₄)₃ is an ionic compound built from aluminium ions and sulfate ions, so its name simply joins the two ion names: aluminium sulfate (the older spelling aluminium sulphate means the same compound). Ionic names never use prefixes to count the ions — the sizes of the charges fix the formula.
2024-11-1C:6-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:6-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: each magnesium atom loses its two outer electrons, and each of two chlorine atoms gains one of them, forming Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.**
Magnesium has two electrons in its outermost shell. It gives away (transfers) those two electrons, leaving a full outer shell and a 2+ charge: the metal becomes Mg²⁺. Chlorine has seven outer electrons and needs just one more to complete its outer shell, so a chlorine atom gains one electron and becomes a Cl⁻ ion — it is the neutral chlorine atom that gains the electron, not a chloride ion. One magnesium atom has two electrons to give, but each chlorine atom can take only one, so two chlorine atoms are needed for every magnesium atom, giving the formula MgCl₂. The oppositely charged ions are then pulled together by strong electrostatic attraction into a giant lattice.
2024-11-1C:6-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:6-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: draw one shared pair of electrons between the nitrogen and each of the three hydrogen atoms, and one lone pair — two non-bonding electrons — on the nitrogen.**
Nitrogen has five outer-shell electrons and each hydrogen has one. Three single N–H bonds form, and in a dot-and-cross diagram each bond is drawn as two electrons shared between the nitrogen and a hydrogen atom — one dot from nitrogen and one cross from hydrogen per bond. That uses three of nitrogen's five electrons, and the remaining two stay on the nitrogen as two non-bonding electrons (a lone pair). Every hydrogen is then surrounded by two electrons, and the nitrogen by eight.
2024-11-1C:6-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:6-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the covalent bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between the shared pair of electrons and the nuclei of the two bonded atoms.**
The shared pair of electrons sits between the two atoms and is attracted at the same time to the positive charge of both nuclei — this double pull on the shared electrons is what holds the two nuclei together and forms the strong covalent bond. Note that the attraction acts between the shared electrons and the nuclei, inside the molecule: these are intramolecular forces, not intermolecular forces between separate molecules. It must also be both nuclei (plural) — a shared pair between two atoms is held by two positive centres, not one.
2024-11-1C:6-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:7-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: the ice condenses the water vapour, so all the water driven off is collected as a liquid in tube B.**
The water of crystallisation leaves the hot crystals as water vapour (steam). Surrounding tube B with ice keeps its surface very cold, so the vapour condenses back into liquid as soon as it reaches the tube instead of passing straight out of the top. That way every drop of water given off ends up collected in tube B as a liquid, which is what makes the mass readings a fair measure of the water lost.
2024-11-1C:7-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:7-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the mass of tube B stops increasing — it stays constant at 22.1 g for the last two readings (5 and 6 minutes give the same value).**
While water vapour is still arriving and condensing, the balance reading for tube B keeps going up. Once all the water of crystallisation has been given off, no more vapour reaches the tube and its mass no longer changes: the readings at 5 minutes and 6 minutes are both 22.1 g, so the decomposition is complete.
2024-11-1C:7-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:7-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: add white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate to the liquid — it turns from white to blue if water is present.**
*Step 1* — add a little anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, a white powder, to a sample of the liquid from tube B (anhydrous cobalt chloride, which is blue, is an alternative). *Step 2* — if the liquid contains water, the white copper(II) sulfate takes the water up and turns from white to blue (the cobalt chloride turns from blue to pink). The colour change happens because the anhydrous salt becomes hydrated, so this colour change is the chemical test for water.
2024-11-1C:7-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:7-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: x = 7.**
*Step 1* — mass of water collected: tube B rises from 15.8 g at the start to 22.1 g at the end, so mass of water = 22.1 − 15.8 = 6.3 g. *Step 2* — moles of MgSO₄ left in the tube: moles = mass ÷ Mr = 6.0 ÷ 120 = 0.05 mol (for MgSO₄, Mr = 120). *Step 3* — moles of H₂O collected: moles = 6.3 ÷ 18 = 0.35 mol (for H₂O, Mr = 18). *Step 4* — in MgSO₄.xH₂O → MgSO₄ + xH₂O the mole ratio of water to MgSO₄ gives x: x = 0.35 ÷ 0.05 = 7, so the crystals are MgSO₄.7H₂O, with seven waters of crystallisation per formula unit.
2024-11-1C:7-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:8-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: the carbon dioxide formed escapes from the flask, so that mass is lost from the balance reading.**
The reaction between the marble chips and the hydrochloric acid produces carbon dioxide gas. The cotton wool plug lets this gas escape out of the flask (while keeping acid spray in), so as the CO₂ leaves the apparatus the total mass sitting on the balance falls.
2024-11-1C:8-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:8-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: the rate is greatest at the start because the concentration of the hydrochloric acid is at its highest, so collisions happen most frequently.**
At the start there are more acid particles in each cm³ of solution than at any later time — the concentration of the acid is highest before any of it has been used up. With more acid particles crowded around the marble chip surfaces, there are more collisions per unit time between acid particles and the surface of the chips. As the reaction proceeds the acid is used up, its concentration drops, the collisions become less frequent and the rate falls — which is why the mass-loss curve is steepest at the beginning and levels off later.
2024-11-1C:8-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:8-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: the hydrochloric acid has been used up.**
Some solid marble is still left, so the chips are in excess — the acid is the reactant that runs out first. Once the last of the hydrochloric acid has reacted there is nothing left to collide with the chip surfaces, so the reaction stops even though marble remains.
2024-11-1C:8-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:8-d-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: 1 the same mass of marble chips; 2 the same concentration of hydrochloric acid.**
For a fair test only the temperature may change, so every other variable that affects the rate must be kept the same in both experiments: the mass (amount) of marble chips, the surface area of the chips (the same size of chips), and the concentration and volume of the hydrochloric acid. If any of these changed as well, you could not tell whether a difference in rate came from the temperature or from the other changed variable.
2024-11-1C:8-d-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:8-d-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction.**
*Step 1* — the rate of reaction increases as the acid gets hotter. *Step 2* — at the higher temperature the acid particles have more energy (and they move faster), so a greater proportion of them have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy needed for a reaction. *Step 3* — the result is more successful collisions per unit time: collisions happen at least as often as before, and a bigger share of them now lead to reaction, so the warmer acid reacts faster and the mass falls more quickly.
2024-11-1C:8-d-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:9-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: aluminium is a better conductor of heat than glass.**
The water is heated through the wall of its container, so how quickly the water warms depends on how well that wall conducts heat. Aluminium conducts heat far better than glass, so more of the fuel's energy passes quickly into the water instead of being wasted, which makes the measured temperature rise larger.
2024-11-1C:9-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:9-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: carbon (soot).**
The black solid coating the can is carbon, commonly called soot, whose symbol is C.
2024-11-1C:9-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:9-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the fuel is burning by incomplete combustion because the supply of oxygen is limited.**
In plenty of oxygen a hydrocarbon fuel burns completely to carbon dioxide and water. Here the flame cannot draw in enough air, so some of the carbon is only partly oxidised and is released as solid carbon — the soot seen on the cold can above the flame is the visible sign of that incomplete combustion.
2024-11-1C:9-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:9-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: heat energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature rise = 100 × 4.2 × 50 = 21 000 J, which is approximately 20 000 J.**
*Step 1* — quote the printed data: m = 100 g of water, a temperature rise of 50 °C, and for water c = 4.2 J/g/°C. *Step 2* — put them into E = m × c × ΔT: 100 × 4.2 × 50 = 21 000 J. *Step 3* — 21 000 J rounds to approximately 20 000 J (about 20 kJ), which shows that raising 100 g of water by 50 °C needs approximately 20 000 J of heat energy.
2024-11-1C:9-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:9-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: ΔH = −525 kJ/mol.**
*Step 1* — the heat released in the experiment is 21 kJ (that is the 21 000 J from part (c)(i)). *Step 2* — moles of ethanol burned: moles = mass ÷ Mr = 1.84 ÷ 46 = 0.04 mol (for ethanol, Mr = 46). *Step 3* — molar enthalpy change: 21 ÷ 0.04 = 525 kJ/mol. *Step 4* — combustion gives out heat, so the enthalpy change is negative: ΔH = −525 kJ/mol. The negative sign is what shows the combustion of ethanol is exothermic.
2024-11-1C:9-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:9-d-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: 5O₂.**
Count the oxygen atoms on the right-hand side of C₄H₉OH(l) + O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 2CO(g) + 5H₂O(g): the two CO₂ hold 4 oxygen atoms, the two CO hold 2 and the five H₂O hold 5, and 4 + 2 + 5 = 11 oxygen atoms in total. One of those eleven is already inside the butanol molecule (in its OH group), so the oxygen gas has to supply the other 10: 10 ÷ 2 = 5, so the balancing number in front of O₂ is 5. (If the whole equation were doubled, every coefficient would double too, but for the equation as printed the answer is 5.)
2024-11-1C:9-d-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:9-d-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 0.45 mol.**
*Step 1* — for butanol (C₄H₉OH), Mr = 74. *Step 2* — moles of butanol burned: moles = mass ÷ Mr = 3.7 ÷ 74 = 0.05 mol. *Step 3* — moles of gas made per mole of butanol: from 2CO₂ + 2CO + 5H₂O, that is 2 + 2 + 5 = 9 mol of gas molecules. *Step 4* — total amount of gas = 0.05 × 9 = 0.45 mol. The water counts as gas here because it is produced as H₂O(g) in this equation.
2024-11-1C:9-d-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:10-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: ethane is saturated — it contains single bonds only, with no double bond.**
An addition reaction needs a C=C double bond that can open up and take extra atoms on across it. In ethane (C₂H₆) every carbon–carbon bond is a single covalent bond and each carbon already has its full share of hydrogen atoms, so bromine atoms have nowhere to add without first breaking bonds. That is why ethane reacts with bromine only by substitution under special conditions, while ethene, with its double bond, adds bromine readily.
2024-11-1C:10-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:10-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: C₂H₆ + Br₂ → C₂H₅Br + HBr, with ultraviolet light (UV radiation) as the essential condition.**
This is a substitution reaction: in ultraviolet radiation, one bromine atom replaces a hydrogen atom of the ethane. The organic product is bromoethane, C₂H₅Br, and the displaced hydrogen leaves combined with the second bromine atom as hydrogen bromide, HBr. The equation balances (6 H and 2 Br on each side). The condition matters: without UV light the mixture stays unchanged, because an alkane such as ethane simply does not react with bromine in the dark.
2024-11-1C:10-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:10-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the bromine water changes from orange to colourless.**
The C=C double bond in ethene opens up and each carbon atom gains a bromine atom, forming colourless 1,2-dibromoethane, so the orange colour of the bromine water is lost — the water is decolourised. This fast decolourising is the standard test for an unsaturated alkene: a saturated alkane such as ethane leaves bromine water orange.
2024-11-1C:10-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:10-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: 1 they all contain the same functional group; 2 they show similar chemical properties and a gradual trend in their physical properties.**
Members of a homologous series share the same functional group — for the alkenes it is the C=C double bond — so they react in the same sort of ways (similar chemical properties and similar reactions). Their physical properties, such as boiling point, change in a smooth, predictable trend as the molecules get larger, and each successive member differs from the previous one by CH₂ — one more carbon atom and two more hydrogen atoms in the molecular formula.
2024-11-1C:10-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:10-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: they have the same molecular formula but different displayed (structural) formulae.**
Both compounds contain exactly four carbon atoms and eight hydrogen atoms, so both have the molecular formula C₄H₈ — the same atoms in the same numbers. What makes them isomers is that those atoms are connected differently: the C=C double bond sits in a different place in the structure, so the two molecules have different displayed formulae (different structures). Same molecular formula plus a different arrangement of atoms is exactly what defines isomers.
2024-11-1C:10-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:10-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: draw 2-methylpropene — a branched alkene with the same molecular formula, C₄H₈, as the two straight-chain alkenes shown.**
Display it with a central carbon joined by a double bond to a CH₂ group and by single bonds to two CH₃ groups: CH₂=C(CH₃)₂. A drawing of the differently arranged form of a straight-chain isomer (the E/trans structure of but-2-ene) also counts as another isomer. Isomerism only rearranges the same four carbons and eight hydrogens — it never changes the molecular formula. That is quite separate from polymerisation, where opening the C=C bonds of ethene joins thousands of units together, so that the carbon chain length in poly(ethene) is far longer than the chain of the monomer itself.
2024-11-1C:10-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:10-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: three differences: the polymer chain is far longer than the ethene monomer; the polymer has only single covalent bonds where the monomer has a C=C double bond; and ethene is a gas while poly(ethene) is a solid.**
*Chain length* — poly(ethene) is built from thousands of linked ethene units, so the carbon chain length is much longer in poly(ethene) than the two-carbon chain of an ethene molecule. *Type of bond* — ethene is unsaturated because its two carbon atoms are joined by a double bond (C=C); when the monomer molecules add together those double bonds open, so the polymer contains only single (covalent) C–C bonds, with no double bond left — the product is saturated. *State of matter* — ethene is a gas at room temperature, but the long, tangled poly(ethene) chains make a solid plastic.
2024-11-1C:10-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:11-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2PbS + 3O₂ → 2PbO + 2SO₂.**

Stage 1 is lead(II) sulfide heating in air: the reactant formulae are PbS and O₂, and the products named are lead(II) oxide, PbO, and sulfur dioxide, SO₂. Balance the rest of the equation by putting a 2 in front of PbS so the two lead and two sulfur atoms match the 2PbO and 2SO₂, then a 3 in front of O₂ so the oxygen atoms balance as well. Multiples or fractions of this equation are equally valid.
2024-11-1C:11-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:11-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: sulfur dioxide causes acid rain.**

Sulfur dioxide dissolves in moisture in the air and makes the rain acidic; acid rain damages stonework and buildings, kills fish in lakes and harms plants. The gas also causes breathing problems in people, such as asthma, which is why it must be prevented from escaping into the atmosphere rather than vented straight out of the furnace.
2024-11-1C:11-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:11-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 88 tonnes of carbon dioxide.**

*Step 1 — moles of lead(II) oxide:* 892 tonnes is 892 × 10⁶ g (1 tonne = 1 × 10⁶ g), and n = mass ÷ Mr, so n(PbO) = 892000000 ÷ 223 = 4000000 mol.

*Step 2 — moles of carbon dioxide:* the equation 2PbO + C → 2Pb + CO₂ shows that every 2 moles of PbO release 1 mole of CO₂, so n(CO₂) = 4000000 ÷ 2 = 2000000 mol.

*Step 3 — mass of carbon dioxide:* mass = moles × Mr = 2000000 × 44 = 88000000 g, which is 88 tonnes once you divide by the 10⁶ grams in each tonne.
2024-11-1C:11-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:11-a-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: lead(II) sulfide is a solid with a very high melting point because it is a giant ionic lattice with strong bonds to overcome, while sulfur dioxide is a gas because it is simple molecular with only weak intermolecular forces between its molecules.**

Lead(II) sulfide has a giant ionic structure: a huge lattice of oppositely charged ions, Pb²⁺ and S²⁻. The ionic bonds between these ions are strong electrostatic forces of attraction, and because the ions are held so firmly in place, a lot of energy is needed to break the lattice apart — so a very high temperature is needed to melt it.

Sulfur dioxide is a simple molecular (covalent) substance. Inside each SO₂ molecule the covalent bonds are strong, but the forces between one molecule and the next are weak intermolecular forces. Only a little energy is needed to overcome these weak forces, so the molecules pull apart easily and sulfur dioxide boils far below room temperature, existing as a gas at room temperature.

The wording matters: for lead(II) sulfide talk about ions in a lattice, never molecules; for sulfur dioxide talk about molecules and weak intermolecular forces between them, never ions or ionic bonds.
2024-11-1C:11-a-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-1C:11-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: the empirical formula is Pb₃O₄.**

*Step 1 — moles of each element (treating the percentages as masses):* n(Pb) = 90.7 ÷ 207 = 0.438 mol and n(O) = 9.3 ÷ 16 = 0.581 mol, using the relative atomic masses Ar(Pb) = 207 and Ar(O) = 16 — the atomic numbers would give nonsense.

*Step 2 — simplest ratio:* divide each by the smaller: Pb 0.438 ÷ 0.438 = 1 and O 0.581 ÷ 0.438 = 1.33, so the ratio of moles is 1 : 1.33.

*Step 3 — whole numbers:* 1.33 × 3 = 3.99, which rounds to 4, so multiply both parts by 3: Pb 3 and O 4. The empirical formula of the oxide of lead is therefore Pb₃O₄.
2024-11-1C:11-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:1-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: D.**

Species D has 9 protons but 10 electrons — one more electron than protons — so it carries an overall negative charge: it is a negative ion. Every other species in the table has equal numbers of protons and electrons (A has 1 and 1, B 3 and 3, C 3 and 3, E 13 and 13), so those species are all neutral atoms.
2024-11-2C:1-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:1-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: D.**

Species D is the negative ion from (a)(i): it holds 10 electrons in total, which exactly fill its shells, so its outer shell is full — the stable electronic structure of a noble gas. D has 9 protons, so the atom it came from is fluorine, a Group 7 element that gains 1 electron to complete its outer shell. A, B and C all still have outer shells left to fill.
2024-11-2C:1-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:1-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: A.**

The mass number is the number of protons plus the number of neutrons, while the atomic number is just the number of protons. For species A the mass number is 1 + 0 = 1 and the atomic number is 1, so the two are equal — species A is a hydrogen atom with no neutrons. In every other species the neutrons make the mass number bigger than the atomic number.
2024-11-2C:1-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:1-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: B and C are atoms of the same element because they both have 3 protons, and they show identical chemical properties because they both have the same electron configuration, each atom carrying 3 electrons.**

Which element an atom belongs to depends only on its number of protons: B and C each have 3, so both are lithium. C carries one extra neutron (4 instead of 3), which makes it a different isotope with a different mass number, but neutrons carry no charge and do not affect how atoms react. Chemical behaviour is decided by the electron configuration, and with identical proton and electron counts the two atoms react in exactly the same way.
2024-11-2C:1-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:1-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: 1.1714 × 10⁻²³ g.**

The nucleus of species C contains its 3 protons and 4 neutrons — electrons sit outside the nucleus and their mass is negligible.

*Step 1:* 3 × 1.6726 = 5.0178 and 4 × 1.6740 = 6.696, both values in units of 10⁻²⁴ g.

*Step 2:* 5.0178 + 6.696 = 11.7138, so the mass of the nucleus is 1.17138 × 10⁻²³ g.

*Step 3:* quote the answer in standard form: 1.17138 × 10⁻²³ ≈ 1.1714 × 10⁻²³ g.

2024-11-2C:2-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: metals are malleable because the layers of atoms (ions) in their structure can slide over one another.**

In a solid metal the positive ions sit in neat rows, forming layers held together by the attraction of the delocalised electrons moving between them. When a force is applied, whole layers can slide over each other and settle into new positions without breaking the metallic bonding, so the metal bends and flattens instead of shattering — that is what makes it malleable and able to be hammered into new shapes.
2024-11-2C:2-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:2-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: metals are good conductors of electricity because they contain delocalised electrons that can move and flow throughout the whole structure.**

The outer-shell electrons of each metal atom detach into a shared mobile sea and become delocalised, free to drift around the lattice of fixed positive ions. When a potential difference is applied across the metal, these mobile electrons flow in one direction, carrying charge through the structure as an electric current. The ions themselves are held rigidly in place — it is the moving electrons, not any moving ion, that conduct the electricity.
2024-11-2C:2-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:2-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: extraction using carbon is the most suitable method for obtaining iron from iron(III) oxide.**

Iron is less reactive than carbon, so carbon can remove the oxygen from the iron(III) oxide, reducing the ore to iron inside a blast furnace. Electrolysis of the molten oxide would also work, but it needs huge amounts of electricity and is far more expensive; electrolysis earns its cost only for metals more reactive than carbon, such as aluminium. Because iron sits below carbon in the reactivity series, heating with carbon is the cheaper, sensible choice.
2024-11-2C:2-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:2-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: add sodium hydroxide solution to samples of both solutions — the iron(II) sulfate gives a green precipitate.**

*Method:* pour a little of each unknown solution into a separate test tube and add a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution to each. The iron(II) sulfate forms a green precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide, while the iron(III) sulfate forms a brown precipitate instead, so the tube that turns green identifies the iron(II) sulfate solution. Both ions react with hydroxide ions to give coloured insoluble hydroxides, which is why the colour of the precipitate tells the two sulfates apart.
2024-11-2C:2-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:3-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: D — fractional distillation.**

The apparatus separates two liquids with different boiling points by fractional distillation: the ethanol and water mixture is heated in the flask, ethanol vaporises first at its lower boiling point, then condenses on the cold surface of the condenser and runs out to be collected, while the water stays behind. The other options cannot do this job: A, chromatography, separates dissolved substances by how far they travel along paper with a solvent; B, crystallisation, obtains a dissolved solid as the solvent evaporates from a saturated solution; C, filtration, separates an insoluble solid from a liquid — useless here because ethanol and water mix completely.
2024-11-2C:3-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:3-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: X is the thermometer, Y is the (Liebig) condenser and Z is the beaker.**

X sits at the top of the apparatus to measure the temperature of the vapour reaching the condenser, which tells you when ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) is coming over. Y is the condenser: a cold-water jacket around a central tube, with water entering at the bottom and leaving at the top, that turns the ethanol vapour back into liquid. Z is the beaker standing at the outlet, collecting the distilled ethanol as it drips from the condenser.
2024-11-2C:3-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:3-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: measure the boiling point of the liquid — a pure substance boils at a fixed temperature.**

*Test:* boil a sample of the collected liquid and watch the thermometer. Pure ethanol boils at a fixed temperature of 78 °C, so a steady reading of 78 °C throughout the boiling shows the ethanol is pure; an impure sample contaminated with water boils gradually over a range of temperatures instead. (A melting-point test would be no use here because ethanol is a liquid at room temperature.)
2024-11-2C:3-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:4-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: effervescence — bubbles of hydrogen fizzing off the metal — and the piece of lithium getting smaller until it disappears.**

Two further observations would also earn credit: the lithium floats and moves about on the surface of the water, and it leaves a white trail behind it as it reacts. Lithium is only mildly reactive for a Group 1 metal, so the reaction is steady rather than violent — nothing catches fire here, and quoting a flame would spoil the answer.
2024-11-2C:4-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:4-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the universal indicator turns blue (or purple), because lithium hydroxide — an alkali — is produced.**

Lithium reacts with water to make lithium hydroxide solution and hydrogen: 2Li + 2H₂O → 2LiOH + H₂. The lithium hydroxide dissolves, releasing hydroxide ions (OH⁻) into the solution, so the solution becomes alkaline. Universal indicator shows blue and purple colours in alkaline solutions, so the final colour of the indicator in the flask is blue or purple.
2024-11-2C:4-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:4-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: 0.321 g of lithium.**

*Step 1 — moles of hydrogen:* n(H₂) = 550 ÷ 24000 = 0.0229 mol (one mole of gas occupies 24 000 cm³ at rtp).

*Step 2 — moles of lithium:* from 2Li + 2H₂O → 2LiOH + H₂ the Li : H₂ ratio is 2 : 1, so n(Li) = 0.0229 × 2 = 0.0458 mol.

*Step 3 — mass of lithium:* mass = moles × Ar = 0.0458 × 7 = 0.321 g, to three significant figures.
2024-11-2C:4-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:4-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: potassium gives a lilac flame.**

Potassium reacts so vigorously that the hydrogen it produces ignites, burning with a characteristic lilac flame — something lithium never shows in cold water. Other differences you could quote instead: the small piece of potassium melts into a shiny ball, and its effervescence is noticeably faster than lithium's.
2024-11-2C:4-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:4-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: potassium is more reactive because its outer-shell electron is further from the nucleus, less strongly attracted, and therefore more easily lost.**

A potassium atom has four shells of electrons (2,8,8,1) while a lithium atom has only two (2,1), so the potassium atom is the bigger atom, with a larger atomic radius and more shielding of the outer electron from the pull of the nucleus. Because that outer-shell electron sits further from the positive nucleus, it is less strongly attracted to it. The weaker the attraction, the more easily the electron is lost — and losing the outer electron is exactly what Group 1 metals do in their reactions — so potassium reacts more vigorously than lithium.
2024-11-2C:4-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:5-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: a (volumetric) pipette.**

A volumetric pipette delivers one fixed volume — here 25.0 cm³ — with the accuracy a titration demands. A dropping pipette would be the wrong choice: it transfers liquid drop by drop without measuring out a fixed volume.
2024-11-2C:5-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:5-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: yellow to red.**

Methyl orange is yellow in the alkaline sodium hydroxide sitting in the flask. As the nitric acid runs in, the mixture neutralises and the indicator turns red (passing through an orange/pink shade) as soon as the acid is in excess — so the colour change seen in step 4 is yellow → red, quoted in that order.
2024-11-2C:5-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:5-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: universal indicator changes colour gradually over a wide range of pH values, so it never gives one sharp colour change to mark the end point.**

A titration needs an indicator that flips suddenly at a single pH, so the exact end-point volume can be read from the burette. Universal indicator shows a whole spread of colours across the pH scale, so the colour of the mixture drifts rather than flips and the end point is hard to pin down — which is why methyl orange, with its single sharp yellow-to-red change, is the sensible choice here.
2024-11-2C:5-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:5-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: end reading 23.80 cm³, start reading 2.15 cm³, volume added 21.65 cm³.**

Read each burette level at the bottom of the meniscus, taking the reading to the nearest 0.05 cm³ because the meniscus falls between graduations: the rough titration ends at 23.80 cm³ and starts at 2.15 cm³. The volume delivered is the difference: 23.80 − 2.15 = 21.65 cm³, recorded to two decimal places like every other titration in the table.
2024-11-2C:5-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:5-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 21.40 cm³.**

*Step 1 — pick the concordant pair:* results within 0.20 cm³ of each other agree with one another. Titration 1 (21.30 cm³) and titration 3 (21.50 cm³) differ by exactly 21.50 − 21.30 = 0.20 cm³, so they are concordant and only they are used for the mean. Titration 2 (22.70 cm³) and titration 4 (24.00 cm³) lie far outside that band, and the rough titration is always discarded.

*Step 2 — take the mean of the concordant results:* (21.30 + 21.50) ÷ 2 = 21.40 cm³.
2024-11-2C:5-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:5-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: repeat the titration without indicator, heat the neutral solution until crystals first form, cool the saturated solution, filter off the crystals and dry them.**

*Step 1 — make the solution cleanly:* run the titration again using the same volumes of nitric acid and sodium hydroxide solution but without adding methyl orange, so no indicator contaminates the product; the measured volumes tell you when neutralisation is complete.

*Step 2 — concentrate:* heat the solution gently to evaporate some of the water and stop at the crystallisation point, when crystals first start to form — a glass rod dipped in and lifted out shows small crystals forming at its edge. Do not evaporate all the way to dryness over the flame: sodium nitrate decomposes at high temperatures.

*Step 3 — crystallise:* leave the saturated solution to cool slowly so that pure sodium nitrate crystals grow.

*Step 4 — separate:* filter off the crystals (or pour off the excess liquid they sit in).

*Step 5 — dry:* pat the crystals dry with filter paper, or leave them to dry in a warm place such as a warm oven or a desiccator.
2024-11-2C:5-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:6-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: crude oil is heated so its hydrocarbons vaporise, the vapours rise up a fractionating column that is hotter at the bottom than at the top, and each hydrocarbon condenses at its own boiling point, draining off as a fraction.**

*Step 1 — vaporise:* the crude oil is heated strongly and most of it boils, turning into a mixture of hydrocarbon vapours and gases.

*Step 2 — rise:* the vapours rise up the column.

*Step 3 — temperature gradient:* the column is hotter at the bottom and cooler towards the top, so the vapours cool as they rise.

*Step 4 — condense:* as soon as a vaporised hydrocarbon reaches a height where the temperature has fallen below its own boiling point, it condenses to a liquid and is collected. Long-chain hydrocarbons have high boiling points and condense low down; short-chain ones travel further up before condensing.
2024-11-2C:6-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:6-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: a high temperature of 600–700 °C and a catalyst of silica or alumina.**

Cracking passes the long-chain alkane vapour over a hot catalyst: the catalyst is powdered silica (silicon dioxide, SiO₂) or alumina (aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃), and the temperature needed is in the range 600–700 °C. The catalyst speeds the reaction up so the long chains split into shorter ones quickly at that temperature.
2024-11-2C:6-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:6-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: shorter-chain alkanes are more flammable — they ignite and burn more easily — and that makes them more useful as fuels.**

Petrol and other in-demand fuels come from short-chain alkanes because they vaporise readily, light easily and burn well, whereas long-chain alkanes are thick, sticky liquids that are hard to ignite and of little use as fuels. Cracking is worthwhile precisely because it converts the surplus long chains into these more flammable, more useful shorter ones.
2024-11-2C:6-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:6-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: ΔH = −95 kJ/mol, which is about −100 kJ/mol, as the question asks to show.**

*Step 1 — bonds broken (energy taken in):* the C=C double bond in ethene and the Br–Br bond in bromine: 612 + 193 = 805 kJ/mol. The working must be shown for a show-that question, so write this sum out rather than quoting the total.

*Step 2 — bonds formed (energy given out):* in the product one C–C single bond forms and two C–Br bonds form: 2 × 276 = 552, and 348 + 552 = 900 kJ/mol.

*Step 3 — combine:* ΔH is bonds-broken minus bonds-formed: 805 − 900 kJ/mol. The difference is 900 − 805 = 95 kJ/mol given out overall, so ΔH = −95 kJ/mol — between −80 and −120 kJ/mol, i.e. about −100 kJ/mol.
2024-11-2C:6-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:6-b-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: the reaction is exothermic because more energy is released when the new bonds in the products form than is taken in to break the bonds in the reactants.**

Breaking bonds takes energy in: the C=C and Br–Br bonds of the reactants need 805 kJ/mol. Forming bonds gives energy out: the C–C and two C–Br bonds of the product release 900 kJ/mol. Because the 900 kJ/mol given out is greater than the 805 kJ/mol taken in, energy is left over and passes to the surroundings, so the enthalpy change is negative (ΔH = −95 kJ/mol) and the reaction is exothermic.
2024-11-2C:6-b-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:7-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: propan-1-ol.**

Alcohol A is CH₃CH₂CH₂OH: three carbon atoms give the stem propan-, the OH group adds the ending -ol, and the OH sitting on the end carbon fixes the locant 1 — propan-1-ol. Writing just propanol is also fine, but propan-2-ol would be wrong: that name puts the OH on the middle carbon, which is not the structure given here.
2024-11-2C:7-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:7-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: H–C–C–C–O–H with every covalent bond drawn as a line and every atom shown.**

Draw the three carbon atoms in a row; put three H atoms on the first carbon, two H atoms on the middle carbon, and on the end carbon two H atoms plus the O–H group. The essential detail is the hydrogen on the oxygen: show it as the separate bond -O-H, never abbreviated to -OH, because a displayed formula must display each individual bond, including the one between O and H.
2024-11-2C:7-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:7-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: n = 13.**

*Step 1 — mass belonging to the end groups:* the CH₃ group has Mr 15 and the COOH group has Mr 45, so the two ends account for 15 + 45 = 60 of the Mr of 242. That leaves 242 − 60 = 182 for the chain of CH₂ units.

*Step 2 — divide by one CH₂ unit:* each CH₂ group has Mr 14, so n = 182 ÷ 14 = 13. The answer has to come out as a whole number — an integer — and 13 does.
2024-11-2C:7-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:7-a-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: water, H₂O.**

An ester forms when the OH of the alcohol and the COOH of the acid link together, splitting off H₂O in the process — so alongside the ester, the other product of the reaction between alcohol A and carboxylic acid B is water.
2024-11-2C:7-a-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2024-11-2C:7-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: 0.107 mol/dm³ (to three significant figures).**

*Step 1 — moles of NaOH:* 25.0 cm³ is 0.0250 dm³, so n(NaOH) = 0.150 × 0.0250 = 0.00375 mol.

*Step 2 — moles of dicarboxylic acid C:* the equation HOOCCH₂CH₂COOH + 2NaOH → NaOOCH₂CH₂COONa + 2H₂O shows that 1 mol of acid C needs 2 mol of NaOH, so n(C) = 0.00375 ÷ 2 = 0.001875 mol.

*Step 3 — concentration of C:* 17.5 cm³ is 0.0175 dm³, so concentration = 0.001875 ÷ 0.0175 = 0.10714 mol/dm³ ≈ 0.107 mol/dm³.

2024-11-2C:7-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the repeat unit is −O−CH₂−CH₂−O−CO−CH₂−CH₂−CO−, with the ester linkages drawn displayed and continuation bonds at each end.**

Diol D (HOCH₂CH₂OH) and dicarboxylic acid C (HOOCCH₂CH₂COOH) polymerise by condensation: each ester linkage forms between the C of a COOH group and an O of a HO group, releasing water. The repeat unit keeps the −CH₂−CH₂− from the diol and the −CH₂−CH₂− that sat between the two COOH groups of the acid, with each ester linkage drawn as −C(=O)−O−: −O−CH₂−CH₂−O−C(=O)−CH₂−CH₂−C(=O)−. Get the ester linkage right first, then check that the rest of the molecule matches the two monomers exactly, with the open bonds shown at both ends.
