2025-06-1C:1-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: the solid dot (•) labels the proton, the small circle (o) labels the neutron, and the cross (x) labels the electron.**

The diagram uses a different symbol for each subatomic particle, so match each symbol to its particle. The proton and the neutron are the two heavy particles packed into the nucleus at the centre of the atom — the • marks are the protons and the o marks are the neutrons, and those two labels must be the right way round. The x marks sit on the shells outside the nucleus: those are the electrons, the lightest particles, moving around in their energy levels.
2025-06-1C:1-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:1-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons; group number = number of electrons in the outer shell; period number = number of occupied shells; electronic configuration = 2,3.**

Each row is read straight off the atom diagram. The mass number counts the particles in the nucleus, so it is the number of • particles (protons) plus the number of o particles (neutrons). The group number is fixed by the outermost shell — count the electrons in it. The period number counts how many shells are occupied. The electronic configuration lists the electrons shell by shell, working outwards: 2 electrons in the first shell and 3 in the second, written 2,3 — and it is that outer-shell count which fixes the group number.
2025-06-1C:1-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:1-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: boron.**

The electronic configuration 2,3 means the atom has 2 + 3 = 5 electrons in total. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so the proton number is 5, and the element with proton number 5 is boron (symbol B).
2025-06-1C:1-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:2-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: effervescence (fizzing, bubbles of gas) and the lithium floats and moves about on the surface of the water.**

Lithium is less dense than water, so the piece floats while it reacts. The reaction produces hydrogen gas, which escapes as bubbles — steady fizzing, called effervescence — and the bubbling nudges the metal around on the surface. As the lithium is used up the piece gets smaller until it disappears. You only need two observations; fizzing plus floating (or moving along the surface) is the classic pair to quote.
2025-06-1C:2-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:2-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — lithium hydroxide and hydrogen.**

A reactive metal dropped into water makes the metal hydroxide and releases hydrogen gas: 2Li + 2H₂O → 2LiOH + H₂. The trough therefore ends up containing lithium hydroxide solution, with hydrogen bubbling off. B is wrong because the oxygen from the water ends up inside the hydroxide — oxygen gas is not released when a metal simply reacts with water. C and D are wrong because lithium oxide is not made here at all: lithium oxide forms when lithium burns in oxygen, not when it reacts with water, so any option containing lithium oxide cannot be right.
2025-06-1C:2-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:2-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: the solution turns blue/purple, with a pH in the range 10 to 14, because it is alkaline.**

The reaction has produced lithium hydroxide, so the solution left in the trough is alkaline. Universal indicator turns blue or purple in alkaline solutions, and an alkali of this strength reads near the top of the pH scale — between 10 and 14. The three linked ideas are: the solution is alkaline, so the colour is blue/purple, so the pH value falls in the range 10 to 14.
2025-06-1C:2-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:2-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: OH⁻ (the hydroxide ion, also written HO⁻).**

Lithium hydroxide is an alkali because it releases hydroxide ions, OH⁻, into the water — an O and an H joined together into one negatively charged group. It is the OH⁻ ions that the universal indicator is responding to when it turns blue/purple, so the hydroxide ion is what is responsible for the high pH.
2025-06-1C:2-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:2-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: C — red.**

In a flame test, lithium ions colour the bunsen flame red (a crimson red). A is wrong because a lilac flame identifies potassium ions, not lithium. B is wrong because orange is not the flame colour that lithium ions produce. D is wrong because a yellow flame is characteristic of sodium ions. Only the red flame points to Li⁺.
2025-06-1C:2-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:3-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: pencil is used because graphite does not dissolve in the solvent, while ink would dissolve and travel up the paper.**

The start line has to stay exactly where it is drawn, because every Rf measurement is made from it. Pencil marks are insoluble in the solvent, so the line stays put. If the line were drawn in ink, the dyes in the ink would dissolve in the solvent and move up the chromatogram with the samples, producing extra spots that interfere with the results and make the Rf values meaningless.
2025-06-1C:3-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:3-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: X and Z — the two inks whose dye has travelled the furthest up the paper.**

The further a dye travels up the paper in a fixed time, the more soluble that dye is in the moving solvent, because a soluble dye is carried along easily in the solvent as it soaks up the paper. On the chromatogram, X and Z both show spots much higher up than V, W and Y, so those two inks contain the dye that is the most soluble in the solvent.
2025-06-1C:3-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:3-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: W produces only one spot, so it contains only one dye; V may contain more than one dye because its spot has not moved from the start line, so the dyes have not separated.**

Each different dye in a mixture makes its own spot on a chromatogram, so a single spot means a single dye — W shows exactly one spot. V behaves differently: nothing has travelled up the paper at all, which shows that its dye (or dyes) is insoluble in this solvent and so cannot be carried up the paper. Because the spot has neither moved nor separated into several spots, you cannot count how many dyes are in V — it may be one insoluble dye or several insoluble dyes sitting on top of each other — so V may contain more than one dye.
2025-06-1C:3-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:3-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: Rf = 0.32 (to two significant figures).**

*Step 1 — distance from the start line to the spot of W:* 2.2 cm (22 mm; a diagram reading anywhere in the 2.2–2.3 cm range is fine).

*Step 2 — distance from the start line to the solvent front:* 6.9 cm (69 mm).

*Step 3 — divide the two measurements:* Rf = 2.2 ÷ 6.9 = 0.32. Rf values have no units. Reading the spot at 2.3 cm instead gives 2.3 ÷ 6.9 = approximately 0.33 — the small reading uncertainty does not change the conclusion, and the answer is quoted to two significant figures.
2025-06-1C:3-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:4-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: C — 13 atoms.**

Work inside the bracket first: (PO₄)₂ means the bracket contents are doubled, giving 2 × 4 = 8 oxygen atoms and 2 phosphorus atoms. Then add the 3 calcium atoms from Ca₃: 3 + 2 + 8 = 13 atoms in total. A (8) is wrong because it counts only the oxygen atoms. B (11) is wrong because it forgets to double the bracket. D (19) is wrong because the bracket doubles the phosphorus and oxygen once only — the calcium count stays at 3.
2025-06-1C:4-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:4-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻.**

Calcium is in Group 2, so each calcium atom loses 2 electrons to form the Ca²⁺ ion. The phosphate ion is the polyatomic ion PO₄³⁻, carrying a 3− charge. The charges also confirm the formula of calcium phosphate: 3 calcium ions give 3 × 2 = 6 positive charges and 2 phosphate ions give 2 × 3 = 6 negative charges, so Ca₃(PO₄)₂ is neutral overall. A is wrong because the phosphate ion is 3−, not 2−; C is wrong because a calcium ion is 2+, not 3+; D is wrong because both ions carry the wrong charge.
2025-06-1C:4-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:4-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: Mr = 310.**

*Step 1 — count the atoms and their relative atomic masses:* Ca₃(PO₄)₂ contains 3 Ca, 2 P and 8 O atoms, and Mr is found by the addition of the contributions: Ca = 40, P = 31 and O = 16.

*Step 2 — add up:* 40 × 3 = 120 and 31 × 2 = 62 and 16 × 8 = 128, so Mr = 120 + 62 + 128 = 310.
2025-06-1C:4-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:4-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 39% (38.7% to one decimal place).**

*Step 1 — mass of calcium in one formula unit:* 40 × 3 = 120.

*Step 2 — divide by the Mr and scale up to a percentage:* 120 ÷ 310 × 100 = 38.7%, which rounds to 39%. So just over a third of the mass of calcium phosphate is calcium.
2025-06-1C:4-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:4-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: 3Ca(OH)₂ + 2H₃PO₄ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 6H₂O.**

Balance in stages. The 3 calcium atoms on the right need 3 Ca(OH)₂ on the left, and the 2 phosphate groups then need 2 H₃PO₄. The hydrogens decide the water: the hydroxides supply 3 × 2 = 6 hydrogens and the acid supplies 2 × 3 = 6 more, and 6 + 6 = 12 hydrogens in total, which is exactly 6 water molecules. The oxygen balances too — 8 oxygen atoms in the phosphate and 6 in the water on the right, matching the 8 in the two phosphates and the 6 in the three hydroxides on the left. Any whole-number multiple (or a fraction) of this equation is equally balanced.
2025-06-1C:4-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:5-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: butane is a hydrocarbon because it contains only hydrogen and carbon atoms, and it is saturated because its molecules contain only single bonds.**

Hydrocarbon means built from hydrogen and carbon alone — C₄H₁₀ has nothing else in it. Saturated means the carbon atoms are joined to each other by single bonds only: there are no double bonds (and no multiple bonds of any kind) anywhere in the butane molecule, so the chain carries as many hydrogen atoms as single-bonded carbons can hold.
2025-06-1C:5-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:5-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O.**

Write the correct formulae first — butane C₄H₁₀ burning in oxygen O₂ to give carbon dioxide CO₂ and water H₂O — then balance by counting atoms. Two butane molecules contain 8 carbon atoms, so 8 CO₂ are needed, and they contain 10 × 2 = 20 hydrogen atoms, so 10 H₂O are needed. Those products then hold 8 × 2 = 16 oxygen atoms in the carbon dioxide plus 10 in the water, and 16 + 10 = 26 oxygen atoms on the right, which is supplied by 26 ÷ 2 = 13 O₂ molecules. Any whole-number multiple (or a fraction) of this equation balances equally well.
2025-06-1C:5-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:5-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: carbon (soot).**

With a limited oxygen supply the butane cannot burn cleanly, so besides the carbon monoxide the flame can release unburnt carbon as black soot particles. Water (steam) is another product you could name instead — the hydrogen in the fuel still ends up as water even when the oxygen supply is short.
2025-06-1C:5-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:5-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: carbon monoxide binds to the haemoglobin in red blood cells, so the blood can transport less oxygen.**

CO attaches itself to haemoglobin in place of oxygen (it forms carboxyhaemoglobin), which reduces the capacity of the blood to carry oxygen around the body. Body cells are then starved of oxygen, which is what makes the gas poisonous.
2025-06-1C:5-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:5-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural (displayed) formulae.**

The molecular formula is identical — the same numbers of carbon and hydrogen atoms — but the atoms are connected and arranged differently, so the displayed formulae look different. For C₄H₁₀, both isomers contain 4 carbons and 10 hydrogens, yet one is a straight chain and the other is branched.
2025-06-1C:5-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:5-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: one isomer is the straight chain (butane) and the other is the branched molecule (methylpropane); every bond must be shown.**

Straight chain — all four carbons in a row:

H   H   H   H
I   I   I   I
H − C − C − C − C − H
    I   I   I   I
    H   H   H   H

Branched — three carbons in the chain with a CH₃ branch attached to the middle carbon:

H   H   H
I   I   I
H − C − C − C − H
I   I   I
H   H − C − H
        I
        H

Each line (drawn here as − or I) is one covalent bond, so all the H−C and C−C bonds appear explicitly; nothing may be condensed away in a displayed formula.
2025-06-1C:5-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:5-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: hexane has a higher boiling point because its molecules are larger with longer chains, so there are stronger intermolecular forces between the molecules and more energy is needed to overcome them.**

A C₆H₁₄ molecule is a longer chain than C₄H₁₀, giving more contact between neighbouring molecules, so the intermolecular forces of attraction are stronger in hexane than in butane. Boiling separates the molecules from one another — no covalent bonds are broken — so the stronger the intermolecular forces, the more energy is needed to overcome them and the higher the temperature at which the liquid boils. Butane has weaker intermolecular forces between its smaller molecules, so they are overcome at a lower temperature and it boils first.
2025-06-1C:5-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:6-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: oxygen (from the air) and water.**

Both are needed at the same time: iron only rusts when it is exposed to air (which supplies the oxygen) and to moisture. The rust that forms is iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃. Take either one away — dry air, or water with no dissolved oxygen — and no rust forms, which is why both conditions must be stated.
2025-06-1C:6-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:6-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — galvanisation.**

Coating iron with a layer of zinc is called galvanising (galvanisation). B is wrong because oxidation is the name of a type of reaction (gain of oxygen, or loss of electrons), not of a coating process. C is wrong because reduction is also a type of reaction, not a coating process. D is wrong because sacrificial protection is the protection the zinc layer then provides chemically — zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes in place of the iron — but it is not the name of the coating process itself.
2025-06-1C:6-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:6-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: C — aluminium, then zinc, then iron, then copper, going from most reactive to least reactive.**

The reactivity order for these four metals is aluminium > zinc > iron > copper. Option A is wrong because it puts copper above iron and zinc — copper is actually the least reactive of the four. Option B is wrong because it places iron above zinc, when zinc is the more reactive of that pair. Option D is wrong because it starts with zinc above aluminium, when aluminium is the more reactive metal of the two.
2025-06-1C:6-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:6-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: add sodium hydroxide solution; a brown precipitate forms.**

*Test:* add a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution to a sample of the solution being tested.

*Result:* a brown (red-brown to orange-brown) precipitate appears — insoluble iron(III) hydroxide, Fe(OH)₃, made from the Fe³⁺ ions and the OH⁻ ions. The colour of the precipitate is the giveaway: a pale green precipitate would have pointed to Fe²⁺ ions instead, so brown confirms Fe³⁺.
2025-06-1C:6-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:6-e-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: it is a redox reaction because reduction and oxidation happen together — the iron(III) oxide loses oxygen (it is reduced) while the carbon monoxide gains oxygen (it is oxidised).**

In Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, the Fe₂O₃ gives up its oxygen and ends as iron, so iron(III) oxide is reduced. The CO takes that oxygen and becomes CO₂, so carbon monoxide is oxidised. Oxygen is transferred from one species to the other within the same reaction, and that pairing of reduction with oxidation is exactly what makes it redox.
2025-06-1C:6-e-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:6-e-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 40 g of iron(III) oxide.**

*Step 1 — amount of Fe:* n(Fe) = 28 ÷ 56 = 0.5 mol, using Ar(Fe) = 56.

*Step 2 — amount of Fe₂O₃:* the equation Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ shows 1 mol of Fe₂O₃ makes 2 mol of Fe, so n(Fe₂O₃) = 0.5 ÷ 2 = 0.25 mol.

*Step 3 — mass of iron(III) oxide:* mass = 0.25 × 160 = 40 g, using the given Mr of 160. That is the minimum needed to give a theoretical yield of 28 g of iron.

2025-06-1C:6-e-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 75%.**

*Step 1 — the percentage-yield relationship:* percentage yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100.

*Step 2 — substitute the printed yields:* 21 ÷ 28 × 100 = 75%, so three-quarters of the predicted iron was actually collected from the sample.
2025-06-1C:6-e-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:7-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2NaOH(aq) + H₂SO₄(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l).**

Both starting solutions are aqueous, so NaOH and H₂SO₄ carry (aq). The salt sodium sulfate is soluble, so it is also (aq), and the water produced is liquid, so it carries (l). The equation is balanced as written: 2 sodium ions and one sulfate group on each side, with the hydrogen and oxygen ending up as 2H₂O. State symbols matter here because this neutralisation happens between solutions.
2025-06-1C:7-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:7-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: use a polystyrene cup instead of the glass beaker — or put a lid on the beaker — because less heat is lost to the surroundings.**

The temperature rise being measured is small, so heat escaping through the sides of a glass beaker (and from the open top) noticeably lowers the recorded maximum. Polystyrene is a good thermal insulator, and a lid cuts losses from the liquid surface, so more of the energy released by the neutralisation stays in the mixture and the maximum temperature recorded is closer to the true value.
2025-06-1C:7-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:7-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: plot all nine points — temperature of mixture (°C) against total volume of acid (cm³) — with each cross exactly on its value.**

Take each pair from the table: 0 cm³/21.0 °C, 5 cm³/22.3 °C, 10 cm³/23.8 °C, 15 cm³/24.4 °C, 20 cm³/26.5 °C, 25 cm³/28.0 °C, 30 cm³/28.5 °C, 35 cm³/28.2 °C, 40 cm³/27.9 °C. Mark each point precisely in its correct small square of the grid, because everything read off this graph later (the crossing point, the anomaly) depends on the plots being exact.

2025-06-1C:7-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: circle the point at 15 cm³ (24.4 °C).**

Every other point follows the smooth climb (and then the gentle fall) in temperature, but the 15 cm³ reading of 24.4 °C sits clearly below the points on either side of it, breaking the pattern — that is the anomalous result to ring with your circle.
2025-06-1C:7-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:7-c-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: draw the first straight line of best fit through the first six points (0–25 cm³), leaving out the anomalous point at 15 cm³, and a second straight line of best fit through the last three points (30, 35 and 40 cm³), extended until the two lines cross.**

The first line rises steadily as each added portion of acid warms the mixture further; the second line falls gently once the alkali has been neutralised and extra acid simply adds cool liquid. Balance the points evenly above and below each line, and make sure the two lines are extended far enough to actually cross near the top of the curve.

2025-06-1C:7-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: volume of acid ≈ 27.5 cm³ and maximum temperature ≈ 28.6 °C.**

Read from your graph: the two lines of best fit cross at approximately 27.5 cm³ of acid, and the temperature at that crossing point is approximately 28.6 °C. The crossing volume is the amount of acid needed to exactly neutralise the 50 cm³ of sodium hydroxide, and the temperature there is the maximum the mixture reached.
2025-06-1C:7-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:7-e.solutionMd:
**Answer: the temperature was taken too early — before the mixture had reached its highest temperature.**

A sensible explanation is that the student read the thermometer too soon after adding that portion of acid, before the reaction had finished warming the mixture, so the true maximum was missed. The same low point would also appear if the student did not stir the mixture: without stirring, the heat lingers where the acid entered instead of spreading evenly, so the thermometer never registers the highest temperature. Either fault links the single low reading to the effect in the plotted points: the 15 cm³ value is low, while the following points (20 cm³, 25 cm³ and beyond) carry on the steady climb.

2025-06-1C:8-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: diamond has a high melting point because its atoms are held by strong covalent bonds — there are very many of them, and a large amount of energy is needed to break them.**

Diamond is a giant covalent structure: every carbon atom is covalently bonded to several others in a rigid 3D network. Because the structure is giant, melting is not a matter of freeing a molecule — strong covalent bonds throughout the whole lattice have to be broken, and there are enormous numbers of them. Overcoming that many strong bonds needs a large amount of thermal energy, which is why diamond melts only at a very high temperature. (This is about breaking covalent bonds in the giant lattice — diamond has no separate molecules between which weak forces could act.)
2025-06-1C:8-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:8-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: graphite is soft because it is layered — strong covalent bonds hold each carbon atom to three others within flat layers, but the weak forces between the layers let them slide over each other — and it conducts electricity because each carbon atom contributes one delocalised electron that is free to move through the solid.**

Structure: in graphite each carbon atom is joined to three other carbon atoms by covalent bonds, so the atoms form flat hexagonal sheets — a 2D layer structure — rather than the 3D network of diamond.

Why it is soft: within a layer the covalent bonds are strong, but the forces between neighbouring layers are weak. Little energy is needed to slide one layer over another, so the layers flake off easily — which is why a pencil leaves graphite on paper and why graphite feels soft.

Why it conducts: because each carbon is bonded to only three neighbours, one outer-shell electron per atom is left out of the bonding. These electrons become delocalised between the layers, and delocalised electrons are free to move through the whole solid. When a voltage is applied they drift along and carry charge, so graphite conducts electricity — unlike diamond, where every outer electron is locked into a covalent bond and nothing can move.
2025-06-1C:8-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:9-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: draw the two carbon atoms sharing two pairs of electrons (the C=C double bond), with each carbon sharing a pair with each of its hydrogens and one carbon sharing a pair with the chlorine — every outer-shell electron shown, using dots for one atom and crosses for the other.**

Chloroethene, C₂H₃Cl, keeps its C=C double bond: between the two carbon atoms draw two shared pairs — four electrons, two dots contributed by one carbon and two crosses by the other. One carbon is bonded to two hydrogens; the other is bonded to one hydrogen and one chlorine. The rest of the molecule must be fully correct: each of those single bonds is one shared pair (one dot + one cross), and the chlorine's remaining outer electrons sit on it as lone pairs, so every atom ends with a full outer shell drawn in dots and crosses.
2025-06-1C:9-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:9-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: a covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the two nuclei of the bonded atoms.**

The shared pair of electrons sits between the two atoms and is attracted at the same time by the positive charge on both nuclei. This mutual electrostatic attraction between the nuclei and the shared electrons is what holds the two atoms together in the molecule. The precise wording matters: attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the two nuclei — plural, one nucleus from each of the two atoms.
2025-06-1C:9-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:9-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the repeat unit is −(CH₂−CHCl)−, drawn out with every bond shown:**

H   H
I   I
− C − C −
I   I
H   Cl

with a bond continuing out of each end of the unit (extension bonds) to show where the next repeat unit attaches; brackets and the n are optional. In the polymer the C=C double bond of the monomer has opened into a single bond, and the unit keeps the atoms of chloroethene: two hydrogens on one carbon, and one hydrogen plus one chlorine on the other.
2025-06-1C:9-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:9-a-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: landfill — the non-biodegradable polymer takes up space and stays intact for a very long time; burning — the burning produces hydrogen chloride, a toxic gas.**

*Landfill:* poly(chloroethene) does not rot, so its disposal in landfill sites means it simply accumulates, taking up space, because it is inert and takes a very long time to decompose.

*Burning:* burning poly(chloroethene) releases hydrogen chloride (HCl), a toxic, acidic gas, and the combustion can also produce other toxic gases and greenhouse gases.

Each disposal method therefore creates its own problem: permanent waste building up in the ground, or poisonous gases released into the air.
2025-06-1C:9-a-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:9-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: C₂H₅Br.**

*Step 1 — moles of each element:* the division is percentage ÷ relative atomic mass (using Ar: C = 12, H = 1, Br = 80) — never the atomic numbers, and never upside down.

C: 22.0 ÷ 12 = 1.83
H: 4.6 ÷ 1 = 4.6
Br: 73.4 ÷ 80 = 0.92

*Step 2 — divide every result by the smallest (0.92);* this calculation gives the ratio:

C: 1.83 ÷ 0.92 = 2
H: 4.6 ÷ 0.92 = 5
Br: 0.92 ÷ 0.92 = 1

*Step 3 — read off the ratio:* C : H : Br = 2 : 5 : 1, so the empirical formula is C₂H₅Br.
2025-06-1C:9-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:9-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: ethane reacts by substitution only in ultraviolet light, decolourising the bromine very slowly (if at all) and making two products — bromoethane and hydrogen bromide; ethene reacts by addition immediately, even in the dark, decolourising the orange bromine straight away and making one product, dibromoethane.**

*Ethane (saturated):* its C−C single bonds are strong, so a substitution reaction happens only when ultraviolet (UV) radiation supplies the energy — one bromine atom replaces a hydrogen atom, producing bromoethane (C₂H₅Br) and hydrogen bromide (HBr). The orange colour of the bromine fades only very slowly, if at all.

*Ethene (unsaturated):* its reactive C=C double bond opens and bromine atoms add across it — an addition reaction that happens immediately, with no light needed. The orange colour turns colourless at once, and the single product is the addition compound dibromoethane (C₂H₄Br₂).

So the differences to state: substitution vs addition, UV light needed vs not needed, decolourising very slowly vs immediately, and two products vs one.
2025-06-1C:9-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:10-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: use the same volume of water in the copper can every time, and keep the spirit burner the same distance below the can.**

*Variable 1 — same volume (or same mass) of water:* the water is what absorbs the fuel's heat, so if one fuel were tested with more water it would need more heat for the same temperature rise, and the comparison of fuels would be invalid. Fixing the volume makes the temperature rise a fair measure of the energy each fuel delivers.

*Variable 2 — same distance from burner to can:* if one burner sits closer to the copper can, less of its heat escapes into the air on that run, so the fuels would not be compared fairly. Keeping the spirit burner the same distance from the can keeps the heat loss the same.

Also worth controlling: stir the water so its temperature is uniform throughout, and always stop at the same maximum temperature (30°C).
2025-06-1C:10-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:10-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: Q = 5040 J.**

*Step 1 — temperature rise:* ΔT = 30 − 18 = 12 °C.

*Step 2 — heat energy absorbed by the water:* Q = mass × c × ΔT = 100 × 4.2 × 12 = 5040 J. The water's mass is 100 g, because 1.0 cm³ of water has a mass of 1.0 g, and c = 4.2 J/g/°C.
2025-06-1C:10-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1C:10-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: ΔH = −1008 kJ/mol (which rounds to about −1000 kJ/mol).**

*Step 1 — mass of ethanol burned:* 38.52 − 38.29 = 0.23 g.

*Step 2 — amount of ethanol:* 0.23 ÷ 46 = 0.005 mol, using the Mr of ethanol = 46.

*Step 3 — energy per mole:* 5040 ÷ 0.005 = 1008000 J/mol
and then 1008000 ÷ 1000 = 1008 kJ/mol.

*Step 4 — attach the sign:* the 5040 J went into the water, so the burning ethanol released that energy — combustion is exothermic and ΔH must be negative, giving ΔH = −1008 kJ/mol.
2025-06-1C:10-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:1-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: freezing.** When a liquid turns into a solid the particles lose energy, slow down and lock into fixed positions — that change of state is called freezing (the reverse of melting, and different from condensing, which is a gas turning into a liquid).
2025-06-1CR:1-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:1-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: evaporation.** Liquid to gas is evaporation: particles at the liquid surface gain enough energy to escape and move about freely as a gas. It is the reverse of condensing (gas to liquid), and quite different from freezing or melting, which are changes that involve the solid state.
2025-06-1CR:1-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:1-a-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: sublimation.** When a solid changes directly into a gas, with no liquid forming in between, the change is called sublimation. The particles gain enough energy to escape the solid lattice completely and spread out as a gas — this differs from evaporation (liquid to gas) because the liquid state is never reached.
2025-06-1CR:1-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:1-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: In a gas the particles are far apart, randomly and irregularly arranged, and they move freely and quickly with high energy.**
The particles are widely spaced — most of the volume is empty space between them — and there is no regular pattern, so their arrangement is completely random and irregular.
Because the forces between gas particles are negligible, each particle has (almost) total freedom of movement: they move fast and freely in random directions, colliding with each other and with the container walls.
Gas particles also carry the highest kinetic energy of the three states, which is why they travel fastest.
2025-06-1CR:1-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:2-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: water.** The experiment shows that iron needs oxygen to rust; the other substance essential for rusting is water (moisture — liquid water or water vapour). Iron only rusts when oxygen and water are both present together.
2025-06-1CR:2-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:2-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: hydrated iron(III) oxide.** Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide — Fe₂O₃ combined with water of crystallisation — and its old name is ferric oxide. The roman numeral (III) tells you the iron is in its 3+ oxidation state in the compound.
2025-06-1CR:2-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:2-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: The paint acts as a barrier: the iron is coated with a protective layer that keeps oxygen and water away from the metal.**
Rusting needs both oxygen (from the air) and water. Because the painted coating is impermeable, it prevents oxygen and water from getting to the iron surface, so the rusting reaction cannot occur. The layer only works while it stays unbroken — a deep scratch would let air and moisture reach the iron underneath.
2025-06-1CR:2-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:2-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: galvanising (galvanisation).** Coating the iron with a layer of zinc is called galvanising; it is also described as sacrificial protection, because the zinc sacrifices itself to keep the iron rust-free — that idea is the key to part (b)(iii).
2025-06-1CR:2-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:2-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it reacts in preference to the iron even where the coating is damaged.**
Zinc sits higher in the reactivity series than iron. At a scratch, the zinc atoms lose electrons — the zinc oxidises, and zinc oxide forms on the surface instead of rust. So the zinc corrodes and reacts sacrificially: it acts as a reducing agent and gets used up rather than the iron, which stays protected even though it is exposed to the air and moisture.
2025-06-1CR:2-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:3-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: dissolving first, then diffusion.**
Before the two solids can react they must each dissolve: the crystals of copper(II) sulfate and of sodium hydroxide dissolve in the water, releasing copper ions and hydroxide ions into solution (dissolution).
Then diffusion spreads those particles through the water — the ions diffuse from opposite ends of the container towards the middle, and the insoluble copper(II) hydroxide forms where copper ions meet hydroxide ions.
2025-06-1CR:3-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:3-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: The particles move faster, so the ions collide and react sooner.**
At a higher temperature the dissolved ions have more kinetic energy, so they move faster and diffuse faster through the water. Faster-moving particles collide more often, so particles collide and react after a shorter period of time — the insoluble copper(II) hydroxide therefore appears in less time.
2025-06-1CR:3-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:3-c-i.solutionMd: **Answer: three (3).** The formula Cu(OH)₂ contains three different elements: copper, oxygen and hydrogen. The copper comes from the copper(II) sulfate crystals, while the hydroxide part (oxygen plus hydrogen) comes from the sodium hydroxide.
2025-06-1CR:3-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:3-c-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: 2+ (Cu²⁺).** Each hydroxide ion carries a single 1− charge. Two hydroxide ions give 2− in total, and the compound Cu(OH)₂ is electrically neutral, so the one copper ion must carry a charge of 2+ to balance them.
2025-06-1CR:3-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:4-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: neutron — relative mass 1, relative charge 0; proton — relative mass 1, relative charge +1; electron — relative mass 0.0005 to 0.0006 (1/1800 to 1/2000), relative charge −1.**
The neutron is neutral, so its relative charge is 0, but it is heavy: its relative mass is 1, the same as the proton's. The proton carries a single positive charge, +1. The electron is tiny — only about 1/1800 to 1/2000 of a proton's mass, i.e. 0.0005 to 0.0006 — and carries a single negative charge, −1. Remember that a relative mass never takes a sign: writing a mass as +1 would be wrong, even though the charges are signed.
2025-06-1CR:4-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:4-b-i.solutionMd: **Answer: A.** Species A has 13 protons and 13 electrons — a neutral aluminium atom. Its electrons fill the shells so that exactly 3 electrons sit in the outer shell, which is what the question asks for; none of the other species has 3 outer-shell electrons.
2025-06-1CR:4-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:4-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: D.** Species D has 7 protons but 10 electrons — three more electrons than protons — so it carries a 3− charge. It is the nitride ion, N³⁻: a nitrogen atom that has gained three electrons to complete its outer shell.
2025-06-1CR:4-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:4-b-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: C.** Mass number = protons + neutrons. Species C has 9 protons and 10 neutrons, so its mass number is 9 + 10 = 19. The extra electron (10 electrons against 9 protons) makes it a negative ion, but mass number only counts the particles in the nucleus.
2025-06-1CR:4-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:4-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: Similarity — they have the same number of protons (3 protons each) and the same number of electrons, so their electron configurations are identical. Difference — they have different numbers of neutrons: ⁶Li has 3 neutrons while ⁷Li has 4 neutrons, so their mass numbers differ.**
Isotopes of an element always share the proton count (that is what makes both of them lithium) and therefore the same electron arrangement; the extra neutron in ⁷Li is what gives it the bigger mass number.
2025-06-1CR:4-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:4-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: Ar = 24.3.**
*Step 1 — multiply each mass number by its percentage abundance:* 79 × 24 = 1896 and 10 × 25 = 250 and 26 × 11 = 286.
*Step 2 — add the products and divide by 100:* 1896 + 250 + 286 = 2432 and then 2432 ÷ 100 = 24.32.
*Step 3 — round to one decimal place:* Ar = 24.3 for this sample. The mean lands just below the middle because the most abundant isotope, magnesium-24, dominates the sample.

2025-06-1CR:5-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: chlorine — gas; bromine — brown liquid; astatine — black solid.**
Going down Group 7 the halogens become darker in colour and change physical state at room temperature from gas to liquid to solid. Fluorine is a pale yellow gas and chlorine a pale green gas; bromine, the liquid member, is a brown colour (orange-brown or red-brown); iodine is a dark grey solid; and astatine, directly below iodine, must be a black solid.
2025-06-1CR:5-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:5-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: Cl₂ + 2NaBr → Br₂ + 2NaCl.**
Chlorine is the more reactive halogen, so it displaces bromine from sodium bromide solution. Every formula is correct — chlorine molecules are Cl₂, sodium bromide is NaBr, the displaced bromine is Br₂ and the salt is sodium chloride, NaCl — and the equation is balanced, with 2 sodium and 2 bromine atoms on each side. State symbols are not needed.
2025-06-1CR:5-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:5-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: No reaction takes place.**
Displacement only works when the added halogen is the more reactive of the two elements. Bromine is less reactive than chlorine, so bromine water cannot displace chlorine from sodium chloride solution — a less reactive element never pushes a more reactive one out of its compounds. Nothing changes: the bromine stays orange and no reaction is seen.
2025-06-1CR:5-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:5-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: because both oxidation and reduction happen at once — it is a redox reaction.**
In 2At⁻ + Br₂ → At₂ + 2Br⁻ the astatide ions (At⁻) lose electrons: each At⁻ becomes an astatine atom in At₂, so the astatide is oxidised and acts as the reducing agent. At the same time the bromine molecules (Br₂) gain those electrons: each Br atom becomes Br⁻, so the bromine is reduced and acts as the oxidising agent. One species oxidised and the other reduced, with electrons transferred — that is exactly what makes the equation redox.
2025-06-1CR:5-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:6-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: D — as a proton donor.**
An acid donates hydrogen ions, H⁺, to the other reactant, and a hydrogen ion is exactly one proton. Option A (electron acceptor) and option B (electron donor) describe electron transfer, which belongs to oxidation and reduction, not to acid behaviour. Option C (proton acceptor) is the definition of a base — the opposite job to an acid. Hydrochloric acid releases H⁺ ions in its reactions, so it behaves as a proton donor.
2025-06-1CR:6-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:6-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: effervescence — fizzing bubbles of hydrogen gas.**
Magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen, so you see bubbles of gas rising (effervescence, fizzing). Other correct observations: the magnesium powder gradually dissolves and gets smaller, a colourless solution forms, and the mixture gets warm because the reaction is exothermic.
2025-06-1CR:6-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:6-c.solutionMd: **Answer: to ensure that all of the hydrochloric acid has reacted (has been neutralised).** Adding magnesium in excess means every trace of acid is used up, so the only solute left in solution is magnesium chloride — any unreacted acid would contaminate the crystals collected later.
2025-06-1CR:6-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:6-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: filter, heat to crystallisation, cool, filter again, then dry the crystals gently.**
*Filter* the mixture from (c) to remove the excess magnesium — the residue on the filter paper is the unreacted metal, and the filtrate is magnesium chloride solution.
*Heat* the filtrate gently to evaporate some of the water, watching until crystals first start to form (that is, until a saturated solution is reached). Do not heat to dryness, or the hydrated crystals would lose their water of crystallisation.
*Cool* the concentrated solution slowly so the hydrated magnesium chloride crystallises out.
*Filter* again — or pour off / decant the excess liquid — to separate the crystals from the remaining solution.
*Dry* the crystals by leaving them in a warm place (a warm oven or a desiccator also works, or pat them dry with a paper towel).
2025-06-1CR:6-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:7-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: 120.0 g.**
*Step 1 — moles of calcium carbonate:* n = mass ÷ Mr = 5.00 ÷ 100 = 0.05 mol.
*Step 2 — mass of carbon dioxide lost:* the equation CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂ shows one mole of CaCO₃ produces one mole of CO₂, so mass of CO₂ = 0.05 × 44 = 2.2 g — this is the mass that escapes through the cotton wool plug.
*Step 3 — new balance reading:* the flask and contents started at 122.2 g, and the balance falls by the mass of gas lost: 122.2 − 2.2 = 120.0 g.
2025-06-1CR:7-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:7-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: plot each remaining point exactly at its coordinates — every plotted point must sit within half a small square of its true position.**
The points already drawn cover 0–3 minutes, so plot (4, 1.72), (5, 1.76), (6, 1.80), (7, 1.80) and (8, 1.80): read the time along the x-axis and the total mass of CO₂ produced up the y-axis, and mark each crossing with a small, neat cross.
2025-06-1CR:7-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:7-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: a single smooth curve of best fit, joining all the plotted points.**
The results follow a smoothly changing rate, so draw one continuous curve — free-hand, passing as close as possible to every point rather than dot-to-dot straight segments. The curve rises steeply at first and then flattens, levelling off towards 1.80 g at the top right of the graph.
2025-06-1CR:7-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:7-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: about 0.5 g/minute.**
*Step 1 — tangent:* rest a ruler on the curve at 2 minutes so the straight line just touches the curve at that point and matches its slope, then draw the tangent long enough to read coordinates from it.
*Step 2 — read two convenient points on the tangent:* for example (0, 0.4) and (2, 1.4) — any two clear points on your own tangent will do.
*Step 3 — gradient of the tangent:* gradient = change in mass ÷ change in time = 1.4 − 0.4 = 1.0 and then 1.0 ÷ 2 = 0.5, so the rate of reaction at 2 minutes is about 0.5 g/minute (grams per minute). The units are g/minute (g min⁻¹) because the gradient is a mass divided by a time.
2025-06-1CR:7-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:7-b-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: The curve starts steep, becomes less and less steep, and finally levels off flat — each stage reflects what is happening to the reaction.**
*Steep at the start:* the gradient is greatest in the first minutes because the reaction is fastest then — the acid concentration is at its highest and there is the greatest mass of calcium carbonate (the most chips) available for collisions.
*Less steep later:* as the reaction proceeds the gradient decreases because the reaction slows down — the acid becomes more dilute and less calcium carbonate remains, so collisions happen less often each second.
*Levels off:* the curve becomes horizontal (gradient zero) when all the calcium carbonate has reacted and been used up — no more CO₂ can form, so the total mass stays fixed at 1.80 g from about 6 minutes onwards.
2025-06-1CR:7-b-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:7-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: the rate of reaction increases.**
The powder and the chips have the same mass, but powdering splits the solid into many tiny particles, giving a much greater surface area for the acid to attack. With more exposed surface there are more collisions per unit time (more frequent collisions between acid particles and the solid surface), so the reaction is faster and the graph would rise more steeply at first. The total mass of carbon dioxide made does not change — the curve still levels off at 1.80 g, just sooner.
2025-06-1CR:7-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:8-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: a strong electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of the two atoms and the shared pair of electrons.**
In a covalent bond the outer shells overlap and a pair of electrons is shared. Both positively charged nuclei are attracted to that same shared pair — and it is this attraction between the nuclei and the shared electrons that holds the bonded atoms together. The attraction acts inside the molecule; it is not the intermolecular attraction between separate molecules.
2025-06-1CR:8-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:8-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: one shared pair of electrons between the H and the Cl, with three lone pairs left on the chlorine.**
Draw the hydrogen atom with its single outer electron (one cross) and the chlorine atom with its seven outer-shell electrons (dots). Overlap one cross with one dot between the two nuclei: that overlapping pair is the single covalent bond. The rest of the molecule must be correct too — chlorine keeps three lone pairs of its own (plus its inner-shell electrons if you draw them), so both atoms end with complete outer shells.
2025-06-1CR:8-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:8-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: because HCl is made of simple molecules with weak intermolecular forces of attraction.**
To boil hydrogen chloride you do not break the strong covalent bonds inside each HCl molecule — you only separate one molecule from the next. The intermolecular forces between the molecules are weak, so they require little energy to overcome: only a small amount of energy is needed to pull the molecules apart, and so the boiling point is low.
2025-06-1CR:8-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:8-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: because it is smaller than the silicon atoms — and because of how it is bonded.**
Oxygen atoms have only two shells of electrons while silicon atoms have three, so the smaller spheres in the network are the oxygen atoms. You can also check the bonding: each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms, and each oxygen atom (like particle A) is bonded to two silicon atoms — whichever way you count, the smaller particle A fits the oxygen pattern.
2025-06-1CR:8-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:8-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: silicon dioxide is acidic and calcium oxide is basic — the two react as an acid with a base.**
SiO₂ is the oxide of a non-metal, so it is an acidic oxide; CaO is the oxide of a metal, so it is a basic oxide (a base — not an alkali, since the oxide itself does not dissolve in water). An acidic oxide and a basic oxide neutralise each other in an acid–base reaction, forming the salt calcium silicate: SiO₂ + CaO → CaSiO₃.
2025-06-1CR:8-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:8-c-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent structure — a rigid 3D tetrahedral lattice like diamond — and that structure, with its strong covalent bonds, explains both properties.**
Every silicon atom is bonded covalently to four oxygen atoms (and each oxygen to two silicons), so the bonding network extends in all directions through the whole crystal: one giant molecule rather than separate small ones.
The covalent bonds holding the atoms together are very strong. To melt silicon dioxide you must break those strong covalent bonds throughout the giant lattice, and breaking them requires a lot of energy — hence the very high melting point.
It is also very hard because the atoms cannot slide over each other: there are no layers of atoms (as there are in graphite), and any attempted slide would mean breaking strong covalent bonds, so the structure resists scratching and denting.
2025-06-1CR:8-c-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:9-a.solutionMd: **Answer: alkanes.** Crude oil is largely a mixture of hydrocarbons from one homologous series — the alkanes, the saturated series with general formula CnH2n+2. Alkenes are not found to any great extent in crude oil; they are made from alkanes by cracking.
2025-06-1CR:9-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:9-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: the sulfur impurity burns to make sulfur dioxide, which dissolves in rain water to give acid rain.**
Many fuels from crude oil contain sulfur as an impurity. When the fuel combusts, the sulfur burns (reacts with oxygen) and sulfur dioxide, SO₂, forms. This acidic gas then dissolves in the rain clouds — it reacts with the rain water — and the acidic solution that falls is acid rain.
2025-06-1CR:9-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:9-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: a temperature of about 600 °C to 700 °C, with a catalyst of alumina (Al₂O₃).**
In catalytic cracking the vaporised long-chain alkane is passed over a hot catalyst at roughly 600–700 °C. Silica (SiO₂), aluminosilicates or zeolites are equally correct choices of catalyst.
2025-06-1CR:9-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:9-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: because cracking converts low-demand long-chain alkanes into short-chain products the industry needs.**
The long-chain alkanes from fractional distillation are less useful and have a lower demand than smaller hydrocarbons. Cracking produces shorter alkanes, which are more flammable and far more useful as fuels — the petrol/gasoline fraction — and it also produces alkenes, reactive molecules used to make polymers (plastics) and alcohols. Cracking therefore turns a surplus of big molecules into high-demand small ones.
2025-06-1CR:9-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:9-d-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural (displayed) formulae.**
They contain exactly the same atoms in exactly the same numbers — the molecular formula is identical — but those atoms are connected in a different arrangement, so the structures drawn out in full (the structural or displayed formulae) differ from one another.
2025-06-1CR:9-d-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:9-d-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: draw 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane.**
The structure given is straight-chain pentane. Isomer 1, 2-methylbutane: draw a chain of four carbons and attach the fifth carbon as a CH₃ branch on the second carbon from one end, completing every carbon's four bonds with hydrogens. Isomer 2, 2,2-dimethylpropane: draw three carbons in a row and attach two CH₃ groups to the middle carbon. In total each drawing still shows five carbons and twelve hydrogens — C₅H₁₂ — the same molecular formula as pentane but a different displayed formula, which is exactly what makes them isomers.
2025-06-1CR:9-d-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:10-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: replace the glass beaker with a polystyrene cup (better insulated, ideally with a lid) — and take the starting temperature once it has reached a steady value.**
Glass conducts heat out of the solution, so some of the energy released escapes to the surroundings and the measured rise is too small. Polystyrene is a much better insulator, so less heat is lost and the recorded temperature rise is closer to the true value. Recording the initial temperature only once the solution has reached a steady temperature also stops any drift from spoiling the rise.
2025-06-1CR:10-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:10-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: because the zinc is in excess.** The temperature rise depends on the copper(II) sulfate — the limiting reactant — being fully used up; adding anywhere between 5 g and 6 g of zinc powder simply guarantees that. The exact mass of the surplus zinc does not change the energy released, so it does not need to be known precisely.
2025-06-1CR:10-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:10-a-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: from blue to colourless.** The blue colour comes from the Cu²⁺ ions in the copper(II) sulfate solution. As the more reactive zinc displaces copper, blue Cu²⁺ ions are removed from the solution and replaced by colourless Zn²⁺ ions (zinc sulfate solution), so the colour fades from blue to colourless — and orange-brown copper metal collects on the zinc.
2025-06-1CR:10-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:10-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: Q = 3160.5 J.**
*Step 1 — temperature rise:* ΔT = 48.6 − 18.5 = 30.1 °C.
*Step 2 — mass of solution:* the volume is 25.0 cm³ and each 1.0 cm³ of solution has a mass of 1.0 g, so the mass of solution is 25.0 g.
*Step 3 — heat energy change:* Q = mass × c × ΔT = 25.0 × 4.2 × 30.1 = 3160.5 J.
2025-06-1CR:10-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:10-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: ΔH = −95 kJ/mol.**
*Step 1 — moles of copper(II) sulfate:* n = 6.38 ÷ 159.5 = 0.04 mol.
*Step 2 — energy change per mole:* 3800 ÷ 0.04 = 95 000 J per mole.
*Step 3 — convert to kilojoules:* division by 1000 gives 95 kJ per mole.
*Step 4 — the sign:* the temperature of the solution rose, so the reaction released energy — it is exothermic — and the molar enthalpy change is negative: ΔH = −95 kJ/mol.
2025-06-1CR:10-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:11-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: do a flame test for the sodium ions, then a precipitation test for the sulfate ions.**
*Sodium ions:* clean a nichrome wire loop with hydrochloric acid, dip it into a solution of the solid, and hold it in a blue Bunsen flame — a yellow (golden-orange) flame confirms sodium ions.
*Sulfate ions:* dissolve a fresh sample of the solid in water. Add a few drops of dilute hydrochloric acid to acidify it (HCl or nitric acid — never sulfuric acid, which would add sulfate ions of its own and give a false result), then add barium chloride solution, BaCl₂. A white precipitate (insoluble barium sulfate) proves sulfate ions are present.
A yellow flame together with a white precipitate after adding barium chloride shows the white solid is sodium sulfate, Na₂SO₄.
2025-06-1CR:11-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:11-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: the last two results are the same — the mass has become constant.**
The readings after 8 minutes and after 10 minutes both equal 24.99 g. When successive heatings give the same mass, no more water is being lost, so heating to constant mass shows that every trace of water has been removed from the crystals.
2025-06-1CR:11-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:11-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: 1.42 g.** The crucible plus the fully heated (anhydrous) contents weigh 24.99 g, and the empty crucible alone was 23.57 g, so the mass of anhydrous sodium sulfate remaining = 24.99 − 23.57 = 1.42 g.
2025-06-1CR:11-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:11-b-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: 1.80 g.** The crucible and hydrated crystals weighed 26.79 g at the start, and the contents weigh 24.99 g once all the water is gone, so the mass of water lost = 26.79 − 24.99 = 1.80 g.
2025-06-1CR:11-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-1CR:11-b-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: x = 10 — the crystals are Na₂SO₄·10H₂O.**
*Step 1 — moles of anhydrous sodium sulfate:* 1.42 ÷ 142 = 0.01 mol.
*Step 2 — moles of water driven off:* 1.80 ÷ 18 = 0.10 mol.
*Step 3 — mole ratio:* 0.10 ÷ 0.01 = 10, so there are ten moles of water for every one mole of Na₂SO₄ and the value of x is 10 — the crystals are hydrated sodium sulfate, Na₂SO₄·10H₂O.
