2025-06-2C:1-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: water.**
Water, H₂O, is a compound because two different elements — hydrogen and oxygen — are chemically joined together in a fixed proportion. Nothing else in the box qualifies: calcium, fluorine, helium, neon and silicon each contain only one kind of atom (they are elements), and petrol is a mixture of many hydrocarbons rather than one bonded substance.
2025-06-2C:1-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:1-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: petrol.**
Petrol is a mixture: it is a blend of many different hydrocarbon compounds that are not chemically bonded to one another, and its exact composition varies from batch to batch. Every other substance in the box is pure — calcium, fluorine, helium, neon and silicon are elements, and water is a single compound.
2025-06-2C:1-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:1-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: fluorine (F₂).**
Diatomic means built from exactly two atoms, and fluorine exists as F₂ molecules. Helium and neon are monatomic noble gases with single atoms; calcium and silicon are giant structures holding huge numbers of atoms; water is a molecule of three atoms (H₂O), not two; and petrol is a mixture, not one molecule.
2025-06-2C:1-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:1-a-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: calcium (Ca).**
Calcium is a metal element: all its atoms are the same kind, and it shows typical metallic behaviour of a Group 2 metal — shiny when freshly cut, a good conductor of electricity and malleable. Fluorine, helium and neon are non-metal elements, silicon is a metalloid (a semiconductor), and petrol and water are not elements at all.
2025-06-2C:1-a-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:1-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: fractional distillation.**
Crude oil is heated so its hydrocarbons evaporate, then the vapours rise up a fractionating column and condense at different heights: each fraction collects the compounds whose boiling points fall in a similar narrow range. It is the column plus the spread of boiling points that lets one continuous process split crude oil into its useful fractions.
2025-06-2C:1-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:1-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: fuel for aircraft — jet fuel (aeroplane fuel).**
Kerosene burns with a hot, steady flame, which is why this fraction is refined into aviation fuel for jet engines; it can equally be burned as fuel for lamps, heaters and stoves. Naming “aviation” or “aircraft” on its own would not state a use — the use must say the kerosene is burned as a fuel.
2025-06-2C:1-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:2-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: heat (thermal energy) is given out, released to the surroundings.**
In an exothermic reaction energy leaves the chemicals as heat, so the temperature of the surroundings — here the acid and the apparatus — rises. Saying just “energy is given out” is not enough: the energy transferred must be heat or thermal energy released to the surroundings, which is exactly why the gas syringe setup warms up as the magnesium reacts.
2025-06-2C:2-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:2-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.**
Magnesium chloride is MgCl₂ because each Mg²⁺ ion pairs with two Cl⁻ ions, and the hydrogen released is the diatomic molecule H₂. Balance check: the 2HCl supply two H atoms (which form one H₂) and the two Cl atoms (which form MgCl₂), while the single Mg atom on each side already balances. The subscripts and the case of the letters must all be correct — mgcl2 or MgCL2 would not do.
2025-06-2C:2-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:2-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: a smooth curve that starts at the origin (0, 0), rises steeply at first and then levels off horizontally at a constant volume.**
The curve begins at the origin because no hydrogen has been collected at the instant the reaction starts. It is steepest at the beginning, when the reaction is fastest, and its gradient falls as the acid is used up. Because the magnesium is in excess, the reaction only stops when all the acid has reacted — from then on the volume no longer changes, so the line runs flat to the right. A curve that keeps rising, or one that dips and humps, would both be wrong.
2025-06-2C:2-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:2-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: the rate increases because the particles collide more often and more of the collisions are successful.**
Heating the hydrochloric acid gives its particles (the H⁺ ions, and the magnesium atoms at the surface) more kinetic energy, so the molecules move faster.
Faster particles collide more often — there are more collisions per unit time (more frequent collisions).
Most importantly, a greater proportion of the colliding particles now have the necessary activation energy, Ea, so a bigger share of the collisions are successful collisions. The rate of reaction increases for both reasons together: more collisions in total, and more of them energetic enough to react.
2025-06-2C:2-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:2-e.solutionMd:
**Answer: an exothermic reaction profile — product line below the reactant line, one activation hump between them, Ea arrow up and ΔH arrow down.**
*Step 1 — labels:* put energy on the vertical axis and reaction progress on the horizontal axis, then label the reactants (magnesium and hydrochloric acid) on the left and the products (magnesium chloride and hydrogen) on the right — names or formulae are both fine.
*Step 2 — line positions:* because the reaction is exothermic, the product line sits below the reactant line, drawn to the right of it.
*Step 3 — the hump:* join the two levels with a single curve that rises from the reactants over an activation hump and falls to the products.
*Step 4 — Ea:* label the activation energy with a vertical arrow pointing upwards from the reactant line to the top of the hump — a downwards or double-headed arrow would be wrong.
*Step 5 — ΔH:* add a second arrow showing ΔH downwards, from the reactant level to the product level, because energy is released overall.
2025-06-2C:2-e.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:3-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: isotopes are atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.**
The three isotopes in the sample are all magnesium because each nucleus contains the same number of protons; what makes them isotopes of one another is that their nuclei hold different numbers of neutrons, which is why their mass numbers are 24, 25 and 26. Electron numbers do not come into the definition — atoms of the same element can gain, lose or share electrons and still be the same element, so referring to electrons cannot distinguish isotopes.
2025-06-2C:3-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:3-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: Ar = 24.4.**
*Step 1 — weighted sum:* multiply each mass number by its percentage abundance and add the three products: 76.5 × 24 + 10.5 × 25 + 13.0 × 26 = 2436.5.
*Step 2 — divide by 100:* 2436.5 ÷ 100 = 24.365, because the abundances were quoted as percentages.
*Step 3 — round:* to one decimal place, 24.365 → 24.4.
Stopping at 24.365, or writing just 24 with no working shown, would each lose marks — the whole chain must be visible.
2025-06-2C:3-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:3-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — calcium sulfate.**
Most sulfates dissolve in water, but the sulfate of calcium is one of the few insoluble exceptions (with barium and lead sulfates), so calcium sulfate is the compound that settles out as an insoluble solid. The other three choices are all soluble, which rules each of them out: calcium nitrate (A) dissolves because every nitrate is soluble; magnesium nitrate (C) is soluble by the same nitrate rule; and magnesium sulfate (D) is a soluble sulfate — magnesium is simply not one of the metals whose sulfate is insoluble.
2025-06-2C:3-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:3-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: Mg²⁺ drawn with shells 2,8 and O²⁻ drawn with shells 2,8, each ion labelled with its charge.**
*Step 1 — the magnesium ion:* a magnesium atom (2,8,2) loses its two outer electrons. Draw two concentric shells holding 2 electrons in the inner shell and 8 in the outer shell, and label the ion Mg²⁺ (charge 2+). Dots, crosses or a mixture of both all work.
*Step 2 — the oxide ion:* an oxygen atom gains the two electrons needed to fill its outer shell. Draw the oxide ion with 2 electrons in the first shell and 8 in the second, labelled O²⁻ (charge 2−). You may include the two inner shells for both ions; if the inner circles of electrons are missing from both drawings, only one of the two ion diagrams can be credited.
*Step 3 — the charges:* the charges are credited on their own, so even with perfect shells you must still write Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ — writing the number before the sign (Mg+2) is fine too.
2025-06-2C:3-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:3-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: water is a covalent molecular liquid with no charged particles free to move; solid magnesium chloride is an ionic solid with its ions locked in fixed positions; aqueous magnesium chloride conducts because its ions are free to move.**
Water is covalent — its molecules are held together by shared pairs of electrons. It contains no ions and no delocalised electrons, so there are not enough charged particles and none are free to move and carry a current: water cannot conduct electricity.
Magnesium chloride is an ionic compound: a giant lattice of alternating Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. In the solid the ions can only vibrate about their fixed positions in the lattice — they cannot move through it — so solid magnesium chloride does not conduct.
Dissolving the solid in water breaks the lattice apart: the ions separate and move freely through the solution, so aqueous magnesium chloride conducts well. It is the moving ions that carry the current in the solution, not electrons.
2025-06-2C:3-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:3-e-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.**
At the positive electrode (the anode) chloride ions are discharged: two Cl⁻ ions each give up one electron, forming one molecule of chlorine, Cl₂, and releasing two electrons into the circuit. The electrons sit on the right-hand side of the half-equation because they are products here, and the charges and atoms both balance.
2025-06-2C:3-e-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:3-e-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: because the chloride ions lose electrons.**
Oxidation is defined as the loss of electrons, and in 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ each Cl⁻ ion gives up an electron — the electrons appear as products on the right-hand side. Be precise about the species: it is the chloride ions that lose the electrons, not chlorine atoms or Cl₂ molecules, so phrasing it as “chlorine loses electrons” would name the wrong particle.
2025-06-2C:3-e-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:4-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄).**
Ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid by potassium dichromate(VI) only when the mixture is acidified, and the standard acidified oxidising agent uses dilute sulfuric acid. (Phosphoric acid, H₃PO₄, is credited as well.) The acid supplies the acidic conditions the dichromate needs, and it does not get consumed in the oxidation itself.
2025-06-2C:4-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:4-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: from orange to green.**
The orange dichromate(VI) ion, Cr₂O₇²⁻, oxidises the ethanol to ethanoic acid and is itself reduced to chromium(III), whose ions are green — so the reaction mixture changes from orange to green. The order matters: describing the change as green to orange would be the reverse of what actually happens in the flask.
2025-06-2C:4-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:4-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + CO₂ + H₂O.**
An acid reacting with a carbonate always gives the salt, carbon dioxide and water. Two acid molecules are needed per sodium carbonate because Na₂CO₃ carries two Na atoms, so two formula units of the salt sodium ethanoate, 2CH₃COONa, form (2NaCH₃COO is an equally correct way to write it), along with one CO₂ and one H₂O. Counting atoms across the arrow confirms the balance: 4 H, 4 C, 8 O and 2 Na on each side.
2025-06-2C:4-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:4-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: brisk bubbling (fizzing / effervescence) and the solid sodium carbonate disappearing as it gets used up.**
The carbon dioxide made in the reaction escapes as fizzing — that is the first observation. As it proceeds, the white solid is consumed: the sodium carbonate gets smaller and finally disappears into the solution — the second observation. A third thing you might notice is the sharp vinegar smell of the ethanoic acid fading as the acid is used up. Simply writing “gas produced” is too vague to count as an observation; name the bubbles you see.
2025-06-2C:4-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:4-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: it acts as the catalyst.**
The few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid speed up the reaction between the ethanol and the ethanoic acid without being consumed themselves, so a catalytic amount is all that is needed. Its job is to make the ester form faster — it changes the rate, not the amount of product the equilibrium can eventually reach.
2025-06-2C:4-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:4-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: because ethanol is highly flammable.**
A Bunsen flame could ignite the ethanol vapour (the ethyl ethanoate product is flammable too), so a naked flame nowhere near the boiling tube. A hot water bath warms the mixture gently to a controlled temperature, well away from any ignition risk.
2025-06-2C:4-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:4-c-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: by its distinctive fruity (sweet) smell.**
Esters carry a characteristic fruity odour, quite unlike the sharp smell of the ethanoic acid or the ethanol — a sweet, nail-varnish-like smell tells the student that ethyl ethanoate has formed. An oily liquid forming in the tube is credited as well. Waft the vapour towards your nose with your hand rather than sniffing the tube directly.
2025-06-2C:4-c-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:4-c-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: the displayed formula of ethyl ethanoate shows every bond in CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ — the ester functional group –C(=O)–O– with CH₃ on one side and C₂H₅ on the other.**
    H   O   H   H
    |   ‖   |   |
H — C — C — O — C — C — H
    |       |   |
    H       H   H
*Step 1 — the functional group:* the C=O double bond with a single C–O bond either side of it is the ester link, and that carries the first requirement.
*Step 2 — the rest of the molecule:* three H atoms on the first C (the CH₃ end), the double-bonded O on the second C, then two H on the next C and three H on the last C (the C₂H₅ end). Dropping one H, or drawing the C=O as C–O, would leave the structure wrong.
2025-06-2C:4-c-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:5-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: a pipette.**
A 25.0 cm³ pipette delivers one fixed volume, calibrated to a single etched mark, so it is more accurate and repeatable than measuring 25.0 cm³ in a measuring cylinder or running it out of a burette. In a titration the alkali volume is one of the numbers used to work out the acid concentration, so it must be measured as precisely as possible.
2025-06-2C:5-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:5-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: so that the colour change can be seen clearly.**
Against the white tile the end-point colour change of methyl orange stands out sharply; a coloured or cluttered background masks the faint change and makes the exact moment to stop adding acid hard to judge. The white background gives maximum contrast for spotting the first permanent tint in the flask.
2025-06-2C:5-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:5-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: final burette reading 32.25 cm³ and volume of sulfuric acid added 28.10 cm³.**
*Step 1 — the final reading:* the diagram places the meniscus between the 32 and 33 graduations, and burette readings are quoted to the nearest 0.05 cm³, which fixes the final reading at 32.25 cm³.
*Step 2 — the volume added:* subtract the initial reading from the final reading: 32.25 − 4.15 = 28.10 cm³.
Each value must be given to two decimal places — burette readings are always recorded to 0.05 cm³, so 28.1 or 28.100 would be recorded wrongly.
2025-06-2C:5-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:5-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: tick titrations 1, 3 and 4 — the volumes 27.40, 27.30 and 27.35 cm³ are the concordant set.**
Concordant means within 0.20 cm³ of one another. Titration 2 fails that test: 27.65 − 27.30 = 0.35 cm³, which is more than 0.20 cm³, so 27.65 is the outlier and gets no tick. The other three stay inside the limit — 27.40 − 27.30 = 0.10 cm³ and 27.35 − 27.30 = 0.05 cm³ — so they carry the three ticks.
2025-06-2C:5-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:5-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: mean volume of sulfuric acid = 27.35 cm³.**
*Step 1 — add the ticked (concordant) results:* 27.40 + 27.30 + 27.35 = 82.05 cm³.
*Step 2 — divide by three:* 82.05 ÷ 3 = 27.35 cm³.
Only the three ticked titrations go into the mean — including the 27.65 outlier would drag the average up — and the answer is quoted to two decimal places, matching how the burette readings were taken; a third decimal place would be false precision.
2025-06-2C:5-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:5-d-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: 0.236 mol/dm³.**
*Step 1 — moles of KOH:* n = c × V = 0.500 × 25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.0125 mol.
*Step 2 — moles of H₂SO₄:* the equation 2KOH + H₂SO₄ → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O shows the alkali : acid ratio is 2 : 1, so n(H₂SO₄) = 0.0125 ÷ 2 = 0.00625 mol.
*Step 3 — concentration of the acid:* c = n ÷ V = 0.00625 ÷ 0.0265 = 0.236 mol/dm³, using the mean titre of 26.50 cm³ converted to dm³.
The halving in Step 2 is where marks are lost: forgetting the 2 in front of KOH would give 0.472 mol/dm³, double the true concentration.
2025-06-2C:5-d-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:5-d-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: evaporate the solution until some crystals form, let it cool so crystals grow, filter them off, then dry them gently.**
*Step 1 — concentrate:* gently heat the potassium sulfate solution in an evaporating basin so that some of the water boils away; stop when the solution is saturated and crystals just begin to form. Do not heat it to complete dryness — the solid would spit and overheat, so only partial evaporation is wanted.
*Step 2 — crystallise:* leave the concentrated solution to cool; potassium sulfate crystals keep growing as it cools.
*Step 3 — separate:* filter the mixture, keeping the crystals on the filter paper (decanting the liquid away from the crystals works too).
*Step 4 — dry:* dab the crystals between filter papers and leave them to dry in a warm place or in a desiccator — not in a hot oven or over a fierce flame, which could spoil them. That leaves pure, dry potassium sulfate crystals from the 26.50 cm³ reaction mixture.
2025-06-2C:5-d-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:6-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: hold a lighted splint at the gas — it burns with a pop.**
The test for hydrogen is a lighted (burning) splint: the hydrogen ignites with a pop sound, often described as a squeaky pop. A glowing splint is the test for oxygen and would be the wrong tool here — hydrogen needs a flame, not a glowing splint, and the pop is what identifies the gas.
2025-06-2C:6-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:6-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the ⇌ symbol shows that the reaction is reversible.**
Both changes happen at once in the sealed container: the forward change (hydrogen and iodine vapour joining to make hydrogen iodide) and the backward change (hydrogen iodide breaking apart again). So ⇌ means the reaction goes both ways at the same time — naming “equilibrium” misses the point, because the symbol itself is telling you the change can run forwards and backwards.
2025-06-2C:6-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:6-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: the yield of hydrogen iodide increases, because the forward reaction is endothermic.**
The equation carries ΔH = +26 kJ/mol, so the forward reaction takes heat in. Raising the temperature from 500 °C to 600 °C shifts the equilibrium position towards the right-hand side — the endothermic direction — because the equilibrium responds by absorbing the extra heat. More HI is present at equilibrium, so the yield increases; the pressure is unchanged at 2 atm, so it plays no part here.
2025-06-2C:6-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:6-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: no effect on the yield, because there are the same number of gas molecules on both sides of the equation.**
H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g): one molecule of hydrogen plus one molecule of iodine makes two molecules of hydrogen iodide — 2 moles of gas on the left and 2 moles on the right. A pressure change only shifts an equilibrium when the mole totals differ, so dropping the pressure from 2 atm to 1 atm at 500 °C leaves the position of equilibrium, and the yield of HI, exactly as before.
2025-06-2C:6-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2C:6-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: 7.68 × 10³ cm³ (that is 7 680 cm³).**
*Step 1 — moles of iodine:* n(I₂) = 50.8 ÷ 254 = 0.2 mol.
*Step 2 — moles of HI:* H₂ + I₂ → 2HI makes 2 mol of HI for every 1 mol of I₂, and only 80% of that maximum is actually formed: 0.2 × 2 = 0.4 mol theoretical, then 0.4 × 80 ÷ 100 = 0.32 mol of HI at equilibrium.
*Step 3 — volume at rtp:* volume = 0.32 × 24 000 = 7 680 cm³.
*Step 4 — standard form:* 7 680 cm³ expressed in standard form is 7.68 × 10³ cm³.
The hydrogen is in excess, so the iodine is the limiting reactant, and the 80% yield is applied after the mole ratio — applying it in the wrong order would give 9 600 cm³ or 3 840 cm³ instead.
2025-06-2C:6-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:1-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: helium and neon.**
These two are the Group 0 gases in the box — the noble gases, whose atoms have full outer shells and exist as single, unreactive atoms. Both names are needed together for the answer to count; the other four gases in the box are compounds or Group 5 elements, not Group 0.
2025-06-2CR:1-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:1-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: oxygen (O₂).**
About 21% of the atmosphere is oxygen. Nitrogen is actually the most abundant gas in the air, but it supplies the larger share, not the 21% — so the gas matching this figure is oxygen.
2025-06-2CR:1-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:1-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: carbon dioxide (CO₂).**
CO₂ is the greenhouse gas in the box: its molecules absorb infrared radiation given out by the Earth and re-emit energy back towards the surface, warming the lower atmosphere. Helium, neon, nitrogen, oxygen and carbon monoxide are not greenhouse gases.
2025-06-2CR:1-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:1-a-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: carbon monoxide (CO).**
When a hydrocarbon burns in a limited supply of oxygen, incomplete combustion produces the toxic gas CO instead of (or alongside) CO₂. Carbon monoxide is poisonous because it binds to the haemoglobin in red blood cells, stopping the blood from carrying oxygen around the body.
2025-06-2CR:1-a-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:1-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: bubble the gas through limewater — it turns cloudy/milky.**
Bubble the gas through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution). If the gas is carbon dioxide, the colourless limewater turns cloudy or milky, because the CO₂ reacts with the dissolved calcium hydroxide to make insoluble calcium carbonate — a white precipitate that scatters light.
2025-06-2CR:1-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:2-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: fractional distillation.**
The crude oil is heated so that most of it evaporates, and the vapours rise up a fractionating column. Each fraction condenses at a different height, where the column temperature matches its boiling range, so the mixture separates into fractions.
2025-06-2CR:2-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:2-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: surfacing roads.**
The thick, sticky bitumen fraction — the residue left near the bottom of the column — is used for surfacing roads (as road tar or tarmac) and for waterproofing flat roofs.
2025-06-2CR:2-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:2-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: C₄H₁₀.**
Count the atoms in the displayed formula: there are 4 carbon atoms in the chain and 10 hydrogen atoms bonded to them, so the molecular formula is C₄H₁₀.
2025-06-2CR:2-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:2-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: butane.**
Four carbons give the stem but-, and every bond in the displayed formula is a single covalent bond, so the compound is an alkane: butane, the fourth member of the homologous series.
2025-06-2CR:2-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:2-c-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: CnH2n+2.**
Alkanes always carry twice as many hydrogens as carbons, plus two spare hydrogens. Check it against butane: 2 × 4 + 2 = 10 hydrogens, which matches its molecular formula C₄H₁₀ from the displayed structure.
2025-06-2CR:2-c-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:3-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: a solution that has dissolved as much solute as possible at that temperature.**
The potassium permanganate solution is saturated when no more solid will dissolve in it: as much solute as the water can hold at that particular temperature has already dissolved, so each extra spatula-full just sits on the bottom, undissolved.
2025-06-2CR:3-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:3-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the solubility of potassium permanganate decreases as the temperature falls.**
Cooling from 50 °C to room temperature lowers the solubility of the solid, so the solution is holding more dissolved solid than it can keep dissolved at the lower temperature — the surplus comes out of solution and builds up as crystals.
2025-06-2CR:3-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:3-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: 5 g per 100 g of water.**
*Step 1 — mass of crystals:* the potassium permanganate left behind weighs 65.35 − 64.10 = 1.25 g.
*Step 2 — mass of water:* the dish held 25 cm³ of water, and 1.00 cm³ of water has a mass of 1.00 g, so the water present has a mass of 25 g.
*Step 3 — scale up to 100 g of water:* 1.25 ÷ 25 = 0.05 g of potassium permanganate per gram of water and then 0.05 × 100 = 5, so the solubility of potassium permanganate (potassium manganate(VII)) is 5 g per 100 g of water.
2025-06-2CR:3-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:3-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: a glowing splint relights.**
Collect a tube of the gas and lower into it a splint that is glowing (glowing, not still burning): oxygen relights a glowing splint. O₂ is the gas released by the decomposition, so a relight confirms the gas is oxygen.
2025-06-2CR:3-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:3-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 197.**
Add up the relative atomic masses in the formula K₂MnO₄: 2 × Ar of potassium, plus 1 × Ar of manganese, plus 4 × Ar of oxygen give Mr = 197. Mr is a ratio of masses, so it carries no units.
2025-06-2CR:3-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:3-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: it is an oxygen donor — it loses oxygen, and is reduced itself.**
An oxidising agent oxidises another substance by taking electrons from it. Potassium permanganate does exactly this: it is an oxygen donor, and as it gives oxygen away (which is why O₂ is one of the decomposition products) it gains electrons and is reduced itself.
2025-06-2CR:3-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:4-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2Li(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2LiOH(aq) + H₂(g).**
Lithium is a solid metal, water is a liquid, the lithium hydroxide formed dissolves in the excess water (so it is aqueous), and the hydrogen produced escapes as a gas — s, l, aq and g in that order.
2025-06-2CR:4-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:4-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: effervescence (fizzing/bubbling), and the lithium gets smaller until it disappears.**
The reacting lithium gives off hydrogen gas, seen as fizzing/bubbling (effervescence), and the piece of metal gets smaller until it disappears. It also floats and moves about on the surface — quote any two of these observations. Do not write melting into a ball or a flame: with lithium neither happens.
2025-06-2CR:4-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:4-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 0.21875 g — about 0.22 g, which is between 0.20 g and 0.30 g.**
*Step 1 — moles of hydrogen:* n(H₂) = 375 ÷ 24000 = 0.015625 mol, using 1 mol of gas = 24 000 cm³ at rtp.
*Step 2 — moles of lithium:* from 2Li + 2H₂O → 2LiOH + H₂, twice as many moles of lithium react as molecules of hydrogen: 0.015625 × 2 = 0.03125 mol.
*Step 3 — mass of lithium:* mass = moles × Ar = 0.03125 × 7 = 0.21875 g, which rounds to 0.22 g — inside the 0.20 g to 0.30 g window the question points at.
2025-06-2CR:4-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:4-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: the potassium melts — it turns into a small ball.**
Potassium reacts so vigorously that the heat released melts the metal: the piece turns into a shining ball that darts around the surface. Faster movement and faster effervescence are also seen, and a lilac flame often appears — none of these happen with lithium.
2025-06-2CR:4-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:4-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: potassium's outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.**
Potassium has a bigger atom than lithium — four shells of electrons instead of two — so potassium's outer-shell electron sits further from the nucleus. That electron is more shielded from the nuclear attraction by the extra inner shells, so it feels less pull towards the nucleus. Because the outer electron in potassium is less strongly attracted to the nucleus, it is more easily lost — and losing the outer electron is what reacting means — so potassium is the more reactive metal.
2025-06-2CR:4-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:5-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: electrolysis — of molten sodium chloride.**
Sodium is more reactive than carbon: it sits above carbon in the reactivity series, so carbon cannot displace sodium from its compound and heating with carbon would produce no sodium. The sodium ions must instead be forced to change at the cathode using electricity — electrolysis of the molten chloride (passing electricity through the aqueous solution would give hydrogen at the cathode instead, so the melt is used).
2025-06-2CR:5-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:5-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: the layers of atoms in a pure metal can slide over one another.**
The atoms in a pure metal (positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons) sit in neat layers/rows. When a force is applied, whole layers can slide over one another without breaking the metallic structure, so the metal bends and reshapes instead of shattering — that is why pure metals are soft.
2025-06-2CR:5-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:5-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: sodium atoms lose electrons and the oxygen atom gains them.**
Each sodium atom gives away its single outer electron and becomes a Na⁺ ion. Two sodium atoms lose one electron each, and one oxygen atom gains those two electrons to complete its outer shell, becoming an O²⁻ ion. The oppositely charged ions then attract each other, and the ionic compound sodium oxide, Na₂O, is formed.
2025-06-2CR:5-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:5-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: sodium is a giant metallic structure but sodium oxide is a giant ionic lattice, and the ionic bonds take far more energy to overcome.**
Sodium is a giant metallic structure/lattice: positive ions sit in a sea of delocalised electrons, held by electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons. Sodium oxide is a giant ionic structure — an ionic lattice of Na⁺ and O²⁻ ions with strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions acting in all directions through the crystal. Because those ionic bonds are much stronger than the metallic bonding, more energy is required to overcome the bonds in sodium oxide than in sodium, so sodium oxide melts at 1132 °C while sodium melts at only 98 °C.
2025-06-2CR:5-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:6-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: two improvements, each given as a pair of points — the change you make and the reason it gives more accurate results.**
1 Use a pipette instead of a measuring cylinder to transfer the 25 cm³ of alkali: a pipette delivers a much more precise volume of alkali, so the titration starts from an accurately known amount.
2 Add the acid dropwise as the endpoint approaches, swirling the flask between drops: one drop at a time means the exact endpoint is seen instead of being overshot, and swirling keeps the acid and alkali fully mixed so the colour change happens evenly through the whole mixture.
Also worth knowing: repeat the titration and average concordant results (that flags anomalous runs); stand the flask on a white tile so the indicator colour change is easy to see; and rinse the burette with the acid before filling, so water left inside does not dilute the acid and change its concentration.
2025-06-2CR:6-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:6-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: 31.3 cm³ of phosphoric acid solution.**
*Step 1 — moles of potassium hydroxide:* n(KOH) = 25.0 × 0.150 ÷ 1000 = 0.00375 mol.
*Step 2 — moles of acid:* the equation H₃PO₄ + 3KOH → K₃PO₄ + 3H₂O shows that 3 mol of KOH react with 1 mol of H₃PO₄, so n(H₃PO₄) = 0.00375 ÷ 3 = 0.00125 mol.
*Step 3 — volume of acid:* V = n ÷ c = 0.00125 ÷ 0.0400 = 0.03125 dm³ and then 0.03125 × 1000 = 31.25 cm³, which is 31.3 cm³ to three significant figures.
2025-06-2CR:6-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:6-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2K₃PO₄(aq) + 3CaCl₂(aq) → Ca₃(PO₄)₂(s) + 6KCl(aq).**
Balance element by element: the Ca₃ needs 3CaCl₂; that brings 6 chlorine atoms, so put 6KCl on the right; those 6 potassium atoms come from 2K₃PO₄ (2 × 3 = 6), and the 2 phosphate groups then match the (PO₄)₂.
2025-06-2CR:6-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:6-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 91.9 % — about 90 %.**
*Step 1 — theoretical amount:* from 2K₃PO₄ + 3CaCl₂ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 6KCl, every 2 mol of potassium phosphate make 1 mol of calcium phosphate, so 0.0400 mol of K₃PO₄ gives 0.0400 ÷ 2 = 0.0200 mol of Ca₃(PO₄)₂.
*Step 2 — theoretical mass:* 0.0200 × 310 = 6.2 g.
*Step 3 — percentage yield:* 5.70 ÷ 6.2 × 100 = 91.9 %, which is indeed about 90 % as the question asks you to show.
2025-06-2CR:6-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:6-c-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: filter the solid off, wash it, then leave it to dry.**
Calcium phosphate is the insoluble solid, so first filter the mixture: the residue left on the filter paper is the calcium phosphate (evaporation to dryness would only suit a soluble salt, which this is not). Next wash the residue with distilled water to rinse off the soluble potassium chloride that would otherwise dry onto the crystals. Finally leave the solid to dry — pressed between filter papers, in a warm oven (not a hot one) or in a desiccator.
2025-06-2CR:6-c-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:7-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: yeast.**
Yeast is the added substance: the enzymes inside the yeast cells (zymase) catalyse the fermentation of glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide.
2025-06-2CR:7-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:7-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: C — 30 °C.**
Fermentation needs the yeast's enzymes working fast but undamaged, and about 30 °C is ideal. A (0 °C) is far too cold: the enzymes are almost inactive, so fermentation barely proceeds. B (10 °C) is still too low for a practical reaction rate. D (100 °C) is far too hot: the heat denatures the enzymes and the yeast dies, stopping fermentation completely.
2025-06-2CR:7-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:7-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: because oxygen in the air would oxidise the ethanol to ethanoic acid.**
If air is present, the oxygen reacts with the ethanol (the alcohol) that fermentation makes — the ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid, the acid in vinegar, so the product is spoiled. With air available the yeast can also respire the glucose aerobically instead of fermenting it, and then no ethanol forms at all. Keeping air out protects the ethanol.
2025-06-2CR:7-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:7-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: ΔH = −1263 kJ/mol, i.e. about −1300 kJ/mol.**
*Step 1 — bonds broken (energy taken in):* C₂H₅OH holds 5 C–H, 1 C–C, 1 C–O and 1 O–H, and the 3O₂ adds 3 O=O, so from the table 346 + 5 × 414 + 358 + 463 + 3 × 498 = 4731 kJ/mol.
*Step 2 — bonds made (energy given out):* the products hold 4 C=O bonds in the 2CO₂ and 6 O–H bonds in the 3H₂O: 4 × 804 + 6 × 463 = 5994 kJ/mol.
*Step 3 — the enthalpy change:* 5994 − 4731 = 1263 kJ/mol more energy is given out than taken in.
ΔH is therefore negative: ΔH = −1263 kJ/mol — about −1300 kJ/mol, exactly the value the question asks you to show.
2025-06-2CR:7-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:7-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the products sit on a lower line than the reactants.**
Draw two horizontal energy lines. Label the left-hand line with the reactants, writing both balanced formulae: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ (ethanol and oxygen). Label the right-hand line with the products: 2CO₂ + 3H₂O (carbon dioxide and water). The right-hand line must be drawn below the left-hand line, because the combustion is exothermic — ΔH = −1263 kJ/mol from (b)(i) means the products end up with less energy than the reactants started with.
2025-06-2CR:7-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:7-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: more energy is given out when the new bonds are made than is taken in when the original bonds are broken.**
Breaking bonds is endothermic — it takes in energy: 4731 kJ/mol to break the C–H, C–C, C–O, O–H and O=O bonds in the reactants. Making bonds is exothermic — it releases energy: 5994 kJ/mol as the new C=O and O–H bonds form in the CO₂ and H₂O. Since the energy released (5994 kJ/mol) is bigger than the energy taken in (4731 kJ/mol), there is a net output of 1263 kJ/mol of energy to the surroundings — the reaction is exothermic.
2025-06-2CR:7-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:7-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: compound A is ethanoic acid and compound C is water.**
An ester forms when an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid, so compound A is ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, and compound C is water, H₂O. Draw every bond in the displayed formulae: in ethanoic acid the first carbon carries three H atoms on C–H bonds, and the second carbon is double-bonded to one O and single-bonded to an O–H. In water the O sits in the middle with two single O–H bonds (H–O–H). The ethanol's C₂H₅ group plus the acid's COOH group make up the ester link in B.
2025-06-2CR:7-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-06-2CR:7-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: ethyl ethanoate.**
Read ester B's chain as C–C–O–C–C with a C=O on the carbon beside the single-bonded O: the C₂H₅ (ethyl) group came from the ethanol and the CH₃COO (ethanoate) part came from the ethanoic acid — so the ester is ethyl ethanoate.
2025-06-2CR:7-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:1-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: X is melting, Y is boiling and Z is sublimation.**

Arrow X joins the solid to the liquid state, and that change of state is melting. Arrow Y joins the liquid to the gas state, which is boiling — evaporation names the same liquid-to-gas change. Arrow Z goes straight from solid to gas without the particles becoming a liquid in between, and that solid-to-gas change is sublimation.
2025-11-1C:1-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:1-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: H₂O (g) → H₂O (l).**

Water vapour is water in the gas state, so start with the formula H₂O carrying the state symbol (g). Condensation turns that gas into liquid water: the formula stays H₂O and the state symbol becomes (l) for liquid. Both formulae and both state symbols are needed before the change of state is described completely.
2025-11-1C:1-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:1-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: in a solid the particles are packed closely together in a regular arrangement, whereas in a gas the particles are widely spaced and arranged randomly.**

In the solid drawing every particle sits in a neat, repeating pattern touching its neighbours, which is why a solid keeps its own shape and volume. In the gas drawing the particles are scattered in no regular order with large gaps between them. The contrast the question wants is about arrangement and spacing, not about how fast the particles move.
2025-11-1C:1-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:2-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: nitrogen.**

A nitrogen molecule, N₂, holds its two atoms together with three shared pairs of electrons — a triple bond — which is also why it is so unreactive. None of the other gases in the box has one: oxygen, O₂, has a double bond, carbon dioxide has C=O double bonds, water vapour has only single bonds, and argon exists as separate atoms with no bonds at all.
2025-11-1C:2-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:2-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: argon.**

Argon is a noble gas with a complete outer electron shell, so its atoms are stable on their own and it exists as individual atoms rather than molecules. Every other gas in the box exists as molecules — two or more atoms bonded together (O₂, N₂, CO₂, H₂O) — so argon is the only one made of single, unbonded atoms.
2025-11-1C:2-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:2-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: oxygen.**

Combustion is burning, and burning is a reaction with oxygen: the oxygen is a reactant in every combustion reaction, so nothing can burn without it. Nitrogen and argon are too unreactive to support burning, carbon dioxide is often used to put fires out because it smothers them, and water vapour is what forms when hydrogen-containing fuels burn rather than something needed for burning.
2025-11-1C:2-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:2-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: heat the copper(II) carbonate strongly — it thermally decomposes, breaking down into copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide, so carbon dioxide gas is given off.**

The equation for the decomposition is CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂. Copper(II) carbonate is not stable to heat, so heating it splits it into the black oxide and the gas. There is a second way to form the gas: add an acid to the carbonate, because a carbonate reacting with a dilute acid forms a salt, water and carbon dioxide.
2025-11-1C:2-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:2-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: 17.2% (approximately 17%).**

*Step 1 — height of air used up (the oxygen):* 93 − 77 = 16 mm. The iron wool rusted, which used up the oxygen from the column of air.

*Step 2 — percentage of the original column:* 16 ÷ 93 × 100 = 17.2%.

So the sample of air was about 17% oxygen, judged from the 93 mm initial and 77 mm final heights.
2025-11-1C:2-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:2-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: leave the apparatus until the water level stops changing instead of measuring after a fixed week.**

Only about 21% of air is oxygen, so the iron reacts slowly, and finishing too early leaves oxygen unreacted and the final height too high. Waiting until the height is constant means every trace of oxygen has reacted before the final reading is taken. Useful refinements alongside this: use a graduated tube so the heights are read more precisely, pack in more iron wool (or use iron filings) to give a bigger surface area, and keep the apparatus somewhere warmer to speed up the rusting. Simply repeating and averaging runs would not help, because the shortfall comes from the method rather than random error.
2025-11-1C:2-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:3-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — X is the proton.**

X is drawn inside the nucleus carrying a single positive charge, and a proton is exactly that: the positive particle found in the nucleus. A (W) is the neutron — it also sits in the nucleus but carries no charge, so it cannot be the proton. C (Y) is an electron — a tiny negatively charged particle moving in shells around the nucleus. D (Z) is the nucleus as a whole — the central cluster of protons and neutrons, not one single particle.
2025-11-1C:3-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:3-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — W, the neutron, has a relative charge of 0.**

Neutrons are the neutral particles in the nucleus: they add mass but no charge at all. B (X) cannot be right because X is a proton with a relative charge of +1. C (Y) cannot be right because Y is an electron with a relative charge of −1. D (Z) cannot be right because Z is the nucleus, which contains protons and therefore has an overall positive charge rather than zero.
2025-11-1C:3-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:3-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the nucleus.**

Z points to the compact cluster in the centre of the atom where all the protons and neutrons are gathered; the electrons (labelled Y in the diagram) move around it in shells. Almost the entire mass of the atom is concentrated in this tiny, positively charged nucleus.
2025-11-1C:3-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:3-a-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — the group number is 3.**

The group number counts the electrons in the outer shell. Counting the electrons drawn in the diagram, this atom has shells holding 2 + 3 = 5 electrons altogether, so three of them sit in the outer shell and the element belongs in group 3. A (2) is wrong because two is the number of occupied shells, which gives the period rather than the group. C (5) is wrong because five is the total number of electrons (the atomic number), not the outer-shell count. D (11) is wrong because an atom with eleven electrons would be a much bigger atom with more shells than the one drawn.
2025-11-1C:3-a-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:3-a-v.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — the period number is 2.**

The period number equals the number of occupied shells in the atom, and the diagram shows electrons filling exactly two shells, so this element sits in period 2. B (3) is wrong: three counts the outer-shell electrons, which gives the group. C (5) is wrong: five is the total electron count (the atomic number), not the number of shells. D (11) is wrong: eleven electrons would fill three shells, so it cannot describe this atom.
2025-11-1C:3-a-v.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:3-a-vi.solutionMd:
**Answer: B.**

Three outer-shell electrons put the element in group 3 and two occupied shells put it in period 2; the atom carries 2 + 3 = 5 electrons, so its atomic number is 5. The element with atomic number 5 is boron — in the table of period 2 elements it falls between Be (atomic number 4) and C (atomic number 6) — and its chemical symbol is B.
2025-11-1C:3-a-vi.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:3-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: a positive ion (a cation).**

Electrons are negatively charged, so when an atom loses its outer-shell electrons it is left with more protons than electrons. The particle that remains has an overall positive charge and is called a positive ion, or cation. It is not an anion — that name is kept for the negatively charged ions formed when atoms gain electrons.
2025-11-1C:3-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:3-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: label the y-axis in even steps of 2, starting at 6.0.**

Write 6.0 at the origin and one value per large square, adding 2 each time: 6.0 + 2 = 8.0, then 8.0 + 2 = 10.0, and so on up the axis. This even scale uses the whole grid and comfortably covers the largest value to be plotted, 20.2. Keep every large square worth the same amount — an uneven scale would make the plotted pattern misleading.
2025-11-1C:3-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:3-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: plot the eight points (3, 6.9), (4, 9.0), (5, 10.8), (6, 12.0), (7, 14.0), (8, 16.0), (9, 19.0) and (10, 20.2) as neat crosses, and leave them unjoined.**

Read across for the atomic number and up for the relative atomic mass, placing each cross exactly on the nearest grid line so every point is as accurate as the grid allows. Do not join the points with a line or draw a line of best fit: these are eight separate measurements of eight different elements, not one continuous experiment, so joining them would invent values between the elements.
2025-11-1C:3-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:3-c-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: there is a positive correlation between relative atomic mass and atomic number — as the atomic number increases across the period, the relative atomic mass increases too.**

Reading the plotted points from left to right, they climb steadily from 6.9 at atomic number 3 up to 20.2 at atomic number 10. Describe this as a positive correlation: the two quantities rise together, but not in a straight-line, fixed-ratio way, so avoid claiming the points are proportional.
2025-11-1C:3-c-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:4-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: draw the chloride ion with three shells holding 2, 8 and 8 electrons.**

A chlorine atom becomes a chloride ion by gaining one extra electron into its outer shell, so the ion has the complete outer-shell configuration 2, 8, 8: draw two electrons in the inner shell, eight in the middle shell and eight in the outer shell. That is 2 + 8 + 8 = 18 electrons in total, all in shells around the nucleus. The charge on the ion does not have to be shown, though adding square brackets with a minus sign outside is good practice.
2025-11-1C:4-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:4-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: distinguish the two solutions by testing for the anion, since both contain the same ammonium cation. For the chloride: add a few drops of dilute nitric acid, then add silver nitrate solution — a white precipitate confirms chloride ions. For the sulfate: add a few drops of dilute nitric acid (or hydrochloric acid), then add barium chloride solution (barium nitrate works equally well) — a white precipitate confirms sulfate ions.**

The beaker giving the white precipitate with silver nitrate contains the ammonium chloride: the nitric acid is added first to remove carbonate impurities that would otherwise give a false result, and then the silver ions react with chloride ions to form insoluble silver chloride. Do not acidify with hydrochloric acid in this test, because that would add chloride ions of its own and turn white in both beakers.

The beaker giving the white precipitate with barium chloride contains the ammonium sulfate: barium ions react with sulfate ions to form insoluble barium sulfate. Here the acid must not be sulfuric acid, which would add sulfate ions and spoil the test.

So one beaker turns white with silver nitrate (ammonium chloride) and the other turns white with barium chloride after acidifying with nitric or hydrochloric acid (ammonium sulfate).
2025-11-1C:4-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:4-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: the solid ammonium chloride has been drawn in the wrong place — the white ring should form closer to the hydrochloric acid end, further from the ammonia solution.**

Ammonia, NH₃, has a lower relative molecular mass (Mr) than hydrogen chloride, HCl. Lighter molecules diffuse faster, so the ammonia vapour travels further along the tube before meeting the hydrogen chloride. The heavier hydrogen chloride molecules diffuse more slowly and cover the shorter distance, so the two gases meet, react and deposit the white solid nearer the hydrochloric acid cotton wool. The student has drawn the ring roughly in the middle, which gets the argument the wrong way round.
2025-11-1C:4-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:4-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: NH₃ (g) + HCl (g) ⇌ NH₄Cl (s).**

Both reactants are gases inside the tube — ammonia evaporates from the concentrated ammonia solution and hydrogen chloride evaporates from the concentrated hydrochloric acid — so each carries the state symbol (g). They combine to form the white solid ring of ammonium chloride, so the product carries (s).
2025-11-1C:4-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:5-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: copper(II) carbonate is insoluble — it does not dissolve in water.**

The method depends on pouring a solution of the copper compound into the polystyrene cup and measuring the temperature change as the metal is added. Copper(II) carbonate will not dissolve, so it cannot form the solution the method needs; that is exactly why the soluble salt copper(II) sulfate is used instead.

2025-11-1C:5-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: a polystyrene cup is used because it is a better thermal insulator than a glass beaker, so less heat is lost from the reaction mixture.**

Polystyrene conducts heat far more poorly than glass, so more of the energy released by the displacement reaction stays in the solution instead of escaping through the walls. The measured temperature increase is therefore closer to the true value and the results are more accurate. Remember the claim is that less heat is lost — an insulator reduces heat loss, it cannot prevent it completely.

2025-11-1C:5-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: two key variables to control are the concentration of the copper(II) sulfate solution and the volume of copper(II) sulfate solution used with each metal.**

A more concentrated solution (or a larger volume) contains more copper(II) ions and would release a different quantity of heat, making the temperature increases for W, X, Y and Z impossible to compare fairly. Other sensible controls: stir at the same rate each time, use the same surface area of metal, start each run at the same initial temperature and use the same polystyrene cup throughout. Using the same mass of metal is not the deciding factor here, because the method already adds each metal in excess.

*Step 2 — divide by the number of results:* 18.4 ÷ 3 = 6.13 °C.

*Step 3 — round to two significant figures:* the mean temperature increase for metal Y is 6.1 °C.

Stirring more quickly mixes the reactants better and would increase the rate of reaction, so a fast-stirred run should reach a higher temperature increase, not a lower one — it certainly would not drop to 2.0 °C while the other two runs stayed above 4.0 °C. **Answer: the order of reactivity is Z > Y > W > X.**

The displacement of copper from copper(II) sulfate is exothermic, so the more reactive the metal, the more heat it releases and the bigger the temperature increase. The mean temperature increases are 8.5 °C for Z, 6.1 °C for Y, 4.1 °C for W and 0.0 °C for X. Z releases the most heat and is the most reactive, Y comes next, then W, while X produces no temperature rise at all because it does not displace the copper, making it the least reactive.

A metal below copper in the reactivity series cannot displace copper from copper(II) sulfate, so no displacement reaction happens. With no reaction there is no heat released and no displacement of copper, which matches the mean temperature increase of 0.0 °C recorded for X. So X behaved exactly as an unreactive metal like silver would.

Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons with different boiling points, so heating it and letting the vapours rise up a fractionating column separates it into fractions, one of which is kerosene. Each fraction condenses at the height where the column temperature matches its boiling range. Running the oil through a fractionating column — fractionation — is the same process under another name.

**Answer: the two conditions are a temperature of 600–700 °C and a catalyst of silica/alumina (zeolite).**

Process 2 is cracking: the kerosene fraction is passed over a hot catalyst made from silicon dioxide (SiO₂, silica) mixed with aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃, alumina) — often called a zeolite or aluminosilicate — at 600–700 °C. The heat and the catalyst together split the large alkane molecules into smaller alkanes and alkenes such as ethene.

Check the balance: the right-hand side has 8 + (3 × 2) = 14 carbon atoms and 18 + (3 × 4) = 30 hydrogen atoms, matching the 14 carbons and 30 hydrogens in C₁₄H₃₀. The large alkane has cracked into octane plus three molecules of ethene.

It is the released heat that makes octane useful as a fuel, so all three links — the use, the reaction with oxygen and the heat released — belong in the answer.

**Answer: 'After the crossing point the temperature change falls again.'**

Once neutralisation is complete (from about 21.6 cm³ onwards) there is no further exothermic reaction to warm the mixture, so each added portion of cool sodium hydroxide solution simply mixes with, and dilutes, the warmer contents of the beaker — that is why the second line on the graph slopes downwards as more alkali is added.

2025-11-1C:7-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: 37 °C.**

*Step 1 — total mass of solution:* the 25 cm³ of acid plus the 25 cm³ of alkali gives 25 + 25 = 50 g, because each 1.0 cm³ of solution has a mass of 1.0 g.

*Step 2 — energy equation:* use Q = mcΔT, so 3780 = 50 × 4.2 × ΔT.

*Step 3 — temperature rise:* 50 × 4.2 = 210 and then ΔT = 3780 ÷ 210 = 18 °C.

*Step 4 — add the starting temperature:* the acid began at 19 °C, so the maximum temperature reached is 19 + 18 = 37 °C.

2025-11-1C:7-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: ΔH = −47.8 kJ/mol (the sign is negative because neutralisation is exothermic).**

*Step 1 — energy per mole:* 0.079 mol of nitric acid was neutralised, releasing 3780 J, so 3780 ÷ 0.079 = 47848 J/mol.

*Step 2 — convert to kJ:* 47848 ÷ 1000 = 47.8 kJ/mol.

*Step 3 — fix the sign:* the temperature of the solution rose, so the reaction released heat to the surroundings. Reactions that release heat have a negative ΔH, giving ΔH = −47.8 kJ/mol. Forgetting the minus sign turns a correct magnitude into a wrong answer here.

2025-11-1C:8-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: the missing formulae are Mg(NO₃)₂, Li₂SO₄ and AlPO₄.**

Ionic formulae are fixed by balancing the charges. Magnesium is Mg²⁺ and nitrate is NO₃⁻, so two nitrate ions are needed to balance one magnesium ion, giving Mg(NO₃)₂. Lithium is Li⁺ and sulfate is SO₄²⁻, so two lithium ions balance one sulfate ion, giving Li₂SO₄. Aluminium is Al³⁺ and phosphate is PO₄³⁻, so the 3+ and 3− charges cancel in a 1 : 1 ratio, giving AlPO₄.

The completed set of compounds is therefore: with Li⁺ — LiNO₃, Li₂SO₄ and Li₃PO₄; with Mg²⁺ — Mg(NO₃)₂, MgSO₄ and Mg₃(PO₄)₂; with Al³⁺ — Al(NO₃)₃, Al₂(SO₄)₃ and AlPO₄.
2025-11-1C:8-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:8-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: both sodium chloride and magnesium oxide are giant ionic lattices held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions, but the attractions in MgO are stronger because its ions carry higher charges, so more energy is needed to overcome them — and that is why MgO melts at a higher temperature.**

Both substances are ionic: a giant lattice of positive and negative ions packed in a regular pattern, with every ion pulled from all sides by electrostatic attraction towards the oppositely charged ions around it. These ionic bonds act in every direction and must be overcome for the crystal to melt.

The difference lies in the size of the charges. In MgO the ions are Mg²⁺ and O²⁻, each carrying a double charge, while in NaCl the ions are Na⁺ and Cl⁻ with only single charges. The ions in MgO therefore have a much higher charge density, so the electrostatic attraction between them is stronger than the attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻.

Stronger attraction means more energy must be supplied to overcome the forces holding the lattice together, so magnesium oxide has the higher melting point.
2025-11-1C:8-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:9-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: displayed formula — three carbons in a chain with the C=C drawn between the first two and every bond shown; molecular formula C₃H₆; empirical formula CH₂; relative formula mass 42.**

For the displayed formula draw two carbon atoms joined by a double bond with two hydrogens on each, and the third carbon as a CH₃ group holding three hydrogens — every single bond and the double bond must appear (H₂C=CH–CH₃). The empirical formula comes from simplifying the ratio of atoms: 3 : 6 simplifies to 1 : 2, giving CH₂. The relative formula mass uses C = 12 and H = 1: 3 × 12 = 36 and 6 × 1 = 6, then 36 + 6 = 42.
2025-11-1C:9-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:9-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: draw three carbon atoms in a row, each adjacent pair sharing an outer-shell electron pair (one dot and one cross), and give each carbon enough hydrogens to complete four single bonds — propane is C₃H₈.**

Only outer-shell electrons are drawn: each carbon uses its four outer electrons to form four shared pairs (one with each neighbouring carbon and the rest with hydrogen atoms), and each of the eight hydrogen atoms shares its single electron with a carbon, so every atom reaches a full outer shell. Use dots for the electrons of one atom and crosses for another's — any consistent combination of dots and crosses works, provided every shared pair contains one dot and one cross.
2025-11-1C:9-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:9-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — one product for propene with bromine and two products for propane with bromine.**

Propene is an alkene: its C=C double bond opens up and both bromine atoms add across it in a single addition reaction, so only one product (a dibromopropane) can form. Propane is an alkane, so it reacts with bromine by substitution, and the bromine can replace a hydrogen on an end carbon or on the middle carbon, giving two different isomeric bromopropanes. A (1 and 1) is wrong because propane's substitution has two possible positions, not one. C (2 and 1) is wrong because propene's addition has only one possible outcome — there is no choice of position, so two products cannot form. D (2 and 2) is wrong on the propene side for exactly that reason.
2025-11-1C:9-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:9-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: ultra violet light (UV radiation).**

Alkanes such as propane react with bromine only by substitution, and that needs ultra violet radiation: the UV supplies the energy to break the Br–Br bond and start the free-radical substitution chain. Without the UV the two can be mixed with no reaction — the opposite of an alkene like propene, which needs no such condition to react with bromine water.
2025-11-1C:9-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:9-c-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the empirical formula is C₃H₇OBr.**

*Step 1 — divide each percentage by the relative atomic mass (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16, Br = 80):* 25.9 ÷ 12 = 2.16 and 5.0 ÷ 1 = 5.0 and 11.5 ÷ 16 = 0.72 and 57.6 ÷ 80 = 0.72. (Divide — never multiply — and use atomic masses, not atomic numbers.)

*Step 2 — divide every result by the smallest (0.72):* 2.16 ÷ 0.72 = 3 and 5.0 ÷ 0.72 = 6.94, approximately 7, and 0.72 ÷ 0.72 = 1 for both the oxygen and the bromine.

*Step 3 — read off the whole-number ratio:* 3 : 7 : 1 : 1, so the empirical formula is C₃H₇OBr — consistent with bromine water adding across an alkene's double bond to give a bromo-alcohol.
2025-11-1C:9-c-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:9-d-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: the functional group is the atom or group of atoms in a molecule that determines its chemical properties — the part of the molecule responsible for its characteristic reactions.**

For example, the C=C double bond is the functional group of the alkenes: it is the reactive site where addition reactions happen, which is why ethene and propene behave in the same characteristic way, while alkanes like propane, with only C–C and C–H single bonds, react quite differently.
2025-11-1C:9-d-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:9-d-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: draw cyclopropane.**

Cyclopropane has the same molecular formula as propene, C₃H₆, but its three carbon atoms are joined in a ring — a triangle — by single C–C bonds only, with two hydrogen atoms on each carbon, so all three corners are CH₂ groups. With no C=C double bond it has no alkene functional group, making it an isomer of propene with a different functional group.
2025-11-1C:9-d-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:6-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: incomplete combustion of ethane can produce carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas that reduces the capacity of the blood to transport oxygen.**

When oxygen is limited, ethane burns without enough air to form CO rather than CO₂. Once breathed in, carbon monoxide attaches to the haemoglobin in red blood cells in place of oxygen, so the blood carries less oxygen round the body — which is why the gas is toxic. A second incomplete-combustion product, soot (carbon), is also a problem: released into the air it causes breathing difficulties such as asthma and other respiratory problems.
2026-06-1C:6-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:6-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: ethane's dot-and-cross diagram shows every bond as one shared pair of electrons, with a shared pair (2 electrons) between the two carbon atoms.**

Use dots for carbon's outer-shell electrons and crosses for hydrogen's. Draw the two carbon atoms side by side with exactly 2 electrons (one dot and one cross, or one dot and one dot) in the overlap between them — that is the C–C single bond. Then draw the rest of the molecule correct as well: give each carbon three hydrogen neighbours, where every C–H bond is another shared pair drawn in the overlap between a carbon and a hydrogen. Each hydrogen ends up with 2 electrons in its outer shell and each carbon with eight — a full outer shell — counting shared electrons as belonging to both atoms.
2026-06-1C:6-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:6-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: at 25 °C ethane is a gas, so its particles are randomly arranged, widely spaced, and moving quickly in random directions.**

Ethane boils at −89 °C, and 25 °C is 114 degrees hotter than that (25 − (−89) = 114), so at room temperature the molecules are well beyond their boiling point and no liquid can remain. In the gas the molecules have an irregular, random arrangement with large gaps between them, and they fly about at high speed with high kinetic energy, moving randomly in all directions, colliding with each other and the container walls.
2026-06-1C:6-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:6-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: ethane has weaker intermolecular forces between its molecules than octane does, so less energy is needed to overcome them.**

Ethane is a small molecule with only two carbon atoms, while octane's long chain of eight carbons gives far more contact between neighbouring molecules and hence stronger intermolecular forces. Boiling means separating the molecules from one another — the covalent bonds inside the molecules are never broken — so the weaker the forces between the molecules, the less energy (and the lower the temperature) needed to pull them apart into a gas. That is why ethane boils far below octane.
2026-06-1C:6-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:6-e-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: ultraviolet radiation (UV light).**

Ethane and bromine do not react in the dark; in sunlight the ultraviolet component supplies the energy that splits Br₂ molecules into reactive bromine atoms, which is what starts the substitution reaction.
2026-06-1C:6-e-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:6-e-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: product 1 is bromoethane, drawn as a displayed formula with every bond shown; product 2 is hydrogen bromide, drawn as H–Br.**

A substitution swaps one H of ethane for a Br, so product 1's displayed formula shows two carbon atoms joined by a single bond, one carbon carrying three hydrogen atoms and the other carrying two hydrogen atoms plus one bromine atom, with each single bond drawn as a line — writing just C₂H₅Br would not be a displayed formula. Product 2 is the hydrogen displaced in that substitution, combined with bromine: draw the bond between them as H–Br (a line joining H and Br), not the molecular formula written as plain letters.
2026-06-1C:6-e-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:6-f.solutionMd:
**Answer: because ethane has only one possible structure — isomers are molecules with the same molecular formula but different structural (displayed) formulae, and no alternative arrangement of C₂H₆ exists.**

Isomers arise when the same atoms can be connected in more than one way, for example as a straight chain or a branched chain. With just two carbon atoms and six hydrogens, ethane cannot be branched or rearranged into any other structure, so there is no second displayed formula to match its molecular formula — only one arrangement, therefore no isomers.
2026-06-1C:6-f.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:10-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — 3 elements.**

The formula Al₂(SO₄)₃ contains just three different elements: aluminium, sulfur and oxygen. Option B (5) is wrong because no five types of element are present — the brackets only group sulfur and oxygen together. Option C (14) is wrong because 14 is nothing like the count of element types in the formula. Option D (17) is wrong because it counts atoms, not elements: 2 aluminium atoms and 3 sulfur atoms and 12 oxygen atoms gives 2 + 3 + 12 = 17 atoms in one formula unit, but these are only three kinds of atom.
