2025-11-1C:10-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: the residue on the filter paper is the excess aluminium powder; the solution collected in the beaker (the filtrate) contains the aluminium sulfate dissolved in water.**

Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. The aluminium was added until it was in excess, so some solid aluminium cannot react and is trapped by the filter paper. Everything that dissolved passes through: the aluminium sulfate formed in the reaction and the water from the dilute acid, so the beaker holds aluminium sulfate solution.
2025-11-1C:10-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:10-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: to make sure that all of the sulfuric acid reacts.**

By adding more aluminium than the equation requires, the acid becomes the limiting reactant, so every bit of the dilute sulfuric acid is used up (the acid is completely neutralised). This guarantees the maximum possible amount of aluminium sulfate is formed, and the leftover solid aluminium is easy to remove later by filtration.
2025-11-1C:10-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:10-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: a powder has a greater surface area (to volume ratio) than large pieces, so the reaction with the acid is faster.**

Because powdered aluminium presents more of its particles to the dilute sulfuric acid, there are more frequent successful collisions between acid particles and aluminium surfaces each second. More frequent successful collisions increase the rate of reaction, so the aluminium sulfate forms more quickly than it would with lumps of metal.
2025-11-1C:10-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:10-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: the aluminium is the reactant in excess, so the sulfuric acid cannot be in excess.**

*Step 1 — moles of aluminium used:* n(Al) = 3.20 ÷ 27 = 0.119 mol.

*Step 2 — acid needed to use up this much aluminium:* from 2Al + 3H₂SO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3H₂, each mole of Al needs 1.5 moles of H₂SO₄, so acid required = (0.119 × 3) ÷ 2 = 0.179 mol. Only 0.120 mol of acid was added, so the acid runs out first.

*Check the other way round:* 0.120 mol of H₂SO₄ could only react with (0.120 × 2) ÷ 3 = 0.080 mol of Al, and 0.119 mol is available, so there is leftover aluminium. The acid is therefore the limiting reactant and is not in excess.
2025-11-1C:10-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:10-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 15.46 g of aluminium sulfate.**

*Step 1 — moles of aluminium sulfate from the acid:* from 2Al + 3H₂SO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3H₂, 3 moles of acid give 1 mole of aluminium sulfate, so n(Al₂(SO₄)₃) = 0.120 ÷ 3 = 0.04 mol.

*Step 2 — theoretical mass:* mass = moles × Mr = 0.04 × 342 = 13.68 g.

*Step 3 — the recorded (actual) mass at 113% yield:* a percentage yield of 113% is a multiplier of 1.13, since 113 ÷ 100 = 1.13, so actual = theoretical × 1.13 = 13.68 × 1.13 = 15.46 g.

A yield above 100% is impossible for a pure dry product, which is why the recorded mass here is bigger than the theoretical mass.
2025-11-1C:10-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-1C:10-c-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the crystals were not left to dry fully, so they still contained water when weighed.**

Weighing a damp product adds the mass of the water to the mass of aluminium sulfate, so the recorded actual mass comes out too high and the calculated yield can exceed 100%. The same effect would follow from other weighing mistakes in the method, such as using sulfuric acid more concentrated than stated, or a larger volume of acid than the method gave — both would produce more aluminium sulfate than the calculation assumed. Simply adding more aluminium would not do it, because the acid was already the limiting reactant.
2025-11-1C:10-c-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-2C:1-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: P and R tick titration, Q ticks titration and measures different volumes, S and T tick evaporates solvent to produce crystals, and U gets no tick at all.**

The burette Q already carries the given tick for titration, and it earns a second tick for measuring different volumes, because its graduated scale lets you deliver any chosen volume. P (the conical flask) and R (the pipette) are also titration apparatus — the pipette may only measure its one fixed 25 cm³ volume, so it does not tick the different-volumes column. S and T (the evaporating basin and the watch-glass dish) both serve to evaporate solvent to produce crystals, since heating the solution drives off water until the solid crystallises out. U (the dropping pipette) can do none of the three processes: it dispenses drops without measuring a volume, it takes no part in a titration, and it cannot be heated to evaporate solvent. Keep exactly one tick in each of these rows — an extra tick in any row loses the mark for that row, and any tick put in row U loses a mark too.

2025-11-2C:3-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: pure iron is more malleable than high-carbon steel, so pure iron is used where a material must be bent or beaten into shape, while high-carbon steel is used where hardness matters.**

High-carbon steel is an alloy. Its carbon atoms are different-sized atoms sitting among the iron atoms, and this disrupts the regular arrangement of the structure, so the layers of atoms (metal ions) can no longer slide over each other easily. That makes high-carbon steel much harder but far less malleable. In pure iron every particle is the same size, so the neat rows of atoms stay in regular layers that can slide over one another — this is why pure iron is the more malleable of the two.

This comparison of malleability between pure iron and high-carbon steel decides their uses. Malleable pure iron can be hammered into shape or drawn out, so it is used for gates, railings, nails, wires, chains and car bodies. Very hard high-carbon steel keeps a sharp edge and withstands heavy loads without denting, so it is used for cutting tools, knives, blades, springs, hammers and rail tracks.

Keep the whole explanation in terms of atoms and sliding layers: bringing ionic bonds, covalent bonds or intermolecular forces into a metallic structure would break the model the explanation needs.
2025-11-2C:3-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-2C:3-d-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: because the Zn²⁺ ions gain electrons.**

Reduction is gain of electrons. In Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn each of the zinc ions (the Zn²⁺ cations) takes up two electrons and becomes a neutral zinc atom — an ion turning into an atom by electron gain is reduction. Take care to say the ions gain the electrons: neutral zinc atoms cannot gain electrons and turn into zinc.
2025-11-2C:3-d-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2025-11-2C:3-d-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻.**

Balance it step by step. The four hydroxide ions supply oxygen atoms in pairs, so they produce one molecule of O₂. Their four hydrogen atoms end up in 2H₂O. Finally balance the charge: the left-hand side carries a total charge of 4−, so four electrons must be released on the right as 4e⁻. Now everything checks: 4 oxygen atoms and 4 hydrogen atoms on each side, and a charge of 4− on both sides.
2025-11-2C:3-d-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

Ethanol is manufactured by reacting steam with ethene, the hydration reaction: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH. The ethene supplies the two-carbon skeleton and the steam provides the −OH group and the extra hydrogen that turn it into ethanol.

White anhydrous copper(II) sulfate (CuSO₄) absorbs water and becomes blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate, so a white-to-blue colour change is the positive test for water. The same job can be done with cobalt(II) chloride paper, which changes from blue to pink when it meets water. Make sure the starting copper sulfate is described as anhydrous (or white) — already-blue copper sulfate tells you nothing.

A compound is made from two or more different elements whose atoms are chemically joined to one another. Ammonia is NH₃, so add the mass of the nitrogen atom to the combined mass of the three hydrogen atoms: 14 + 3 = 17. The relative molecular mass of ammonia is therefore 17.

The same ammonia molecule is also a base in the proton sense: it can take up a proton (an H⁺ ion) from an acid, and by gaining H⁺ ions it neutralises acids.

Two solid observations to quote: first, effervescence — the vigorous fizzing as hydrogen bubbles stream off the metal; second, the piece of sodium floats on the water surface and moves around, because it is less dense than water and the escaping hydrogen pushes it along. Other correct observations include the sodium melting into a shiny sphere/ball, leaving a white trail behind it, and gradually disappearing (getting smaller) until it is all used up.

The reactants are sodium and water; the products are sodium hydroxide (the alkali that dissolves in the trough) and hydrogen gas (the bubbles seen fizzing off the metal). In symbols the same reaction is 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.

*Step 1 — formula:* amount = mass ÷ Mr, and sodium's relative atomic mass is 23.

*Step 2 — substitute:* n(Na) = 0.25 ÷ 23 = 0.0108696 mol.

Potassium has a greater relative atomic mass than sodium (39 against 23), so a 0.25 g piece contains fewer moles of metal: 0.25 ÷ 39 = 0.0064 mol, compared with 0.25 ÷ 23 = 0.011 mol for the sodium. Potassium and sodium react in exactly the same pattern with water — each mole of metal releases the same number of moles of hydrogen — so with fewer moles of potassium reacting, the volume of hydrogen collected is smaller than in the sodium experiment.

State symbols: sodium is a solid, Na(s); oxygen is a gas, O₂(g); sodium oxide is the white solid product, Na₂O(s). Balancing: sodium oxide needs two Na per formula unit, so put 4 in front of Na and 2 in front of Na₂O — then 4 Na atoms and 2 O atoms appear on each side and the equation balances.

2026-06-1C:2-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: minimum, exothermic, ionic, basic.**

Activation energy is the *minimum* energy needed to start the reaction — not the maximum, which is why that box word is wrong here. A negative enthalpy change means energy leaves the reaction to the surroundings, so the reaction is *exothermic* (endothermic reactions take energy in and have positive enthalpy changes). Sodium is a metal and oxygen a non-metal, so electrons transfer and sodium oxide contains *ionic* bonding rather than covalent or molecular bonding. Metal oxides like sodium oxide are *basic* — they react with acids and give alkaline solutions; it is the oxides of non-metals that are acidic.

The displayed formula in Diagram 1 contains just two kinds of atom: carbon (C) and hydrogen (H), joined by covalent bonds. A hydrocarbon is a compound whose molecules are built from hydrogen and carbon only, and isoprene fits that definition exactly. When you explain this, always mention that only those two elements are present — no oxygen, chlorine or any other element appears in the diagram.

2026-06-1C:4-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: the calculation gives the simplest ratio 5 : 8, so the empirical formula is C₅H₈.**

*Step 1 — moles of each element in 100 g of isoprene:* amount of C = 88.2 ÷ 12 = 7.35 mol; amount of H = 11.8 ÷ 1 = 11.8 mol.

*Step 2 — simplest ratio:* divide both by the smaller, 7.35: 7.35 ÷ 7.35 = 1 and 11.8 ÷ 7.35 = 1.6, so C : H = 1 : 1.6.

*Step 3 — whole numbers:* ratio 1 : 1.6 is not all whole atoms, so multiply both parts by 5: (1 × 5) : (1.6 × 5) = 5 : 8. The empirical formula is therefore C₅H₈, as stated.

2026-06-1C:4-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: because propene is an alkene with the general formula CnH₂n (one double bond), while isoprene has more than one double bond, so it cannot fit that general formula.**

Every alkene contains exactly one C=C double bond, which is why its members follow CnH₂n — substituting n = 5 (2 × 5 = 10) would give C₅H₁₀ for a five-carbon alkene. Isoprene is C₅H₈: it has two C=C double bonds, so it has four fewer hydrogens than the alkene general formula allows and belongs to a different series (a diene), not the same one as propene.

2026-06-1C:4-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: 3.7 mol of carbon dioxide (3.675 mol before rounding).**

*Step 1 — Mr of isoprene:* C₅H₈ has Mr = (5 × 12) + (8 × 1) = 60 + 8 = 68.

*Step 2 — moles of isoprene burned:* n = mass ÷ Mr = 50 ÷ 68 = 0.735 mol.

*Step 3 — moles of carbon dioxide:* the equation C₅H₈ + 7O₂ → 5CO₂ + 4H₂O shows 1 mol of isoprene makes 5 mol of CO₂, so n(CO₂) = 0.735 × 5 = 3.675 mol ≈ 3.7 mol.

Isoprene's C=C double bonds open up and each chlorine atom from Cl₂ joins onto a carbon of the former double bond, so the two reactants add together to form the single product X with no other substance made.

*Step 2 — percentage yield:* % yield = actual mass ÷ theoretical mass × 100: 0.212 ÷ 6.95 = 0.0305, and then 0.0305 × 100 = 3.05%.

2026-06-1C:5-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: crude oil is separated by fractional distillation into fractions, and some of the long-chain fractions are then cracked to make the smaller hydrocarbons that are in high demand.**

*Fractional distillation:* crude oil is heated so most of it evaporates, and the vaporised mixture enters a tall fractionating column with a temperature gradient — it is hottest at the bottom and coolest at the top. The hydrocarbons in crude oil have different boiling points, so as the vapours rise, each fraction condenses at the temperature where its boiling point is reached: long-chain hydrocarbons with high boiling points condense low down where it is hot, and shorter-chain alkanes with low boiling points keep rising and condense higher up where it is cooler. In this way the mixture is separated into useful fractions.

*Why cracking is needed:* fractional distillation produces far more long-chain hydrocarbons than can be sold, while short-chain alkanes are in much greater demand than the fractions supply — so the excess long-chain fraction is cracked. Cracking is done by heating the hydrocarbon vapours to about 600–700 °C over a catalyst such as silica, alumina or zeolite. It splits large alkane molecules into shorter-chain alkanes, which are more flammable and make better fuels, and into alkenes, which are valuable reactive starting materials used to make polymers (plastics).
2026-06-1C:5-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:5-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: a fuel is a substance that, when it burns, releases heat (thermal) energy.**

The burning — combustion — is deliberately useful: fuels such as methane, petrol or coal are burned to release the energy stored in their bonds, and that released heat is then put to work in boilers, engines and power stations.
2026-06-1C:5-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:5-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: sulfur impurities in fuels burn to make sulfur dioxide, which dissolves in rain to form acid rain.**

Many hydrocarbon fuels contain sulfur as an impurity. When the fuel burns, the sulfur burns too — it reacts with oxygen in the air to form sulfur dioxide, SO₂: S + O₂ → SO₂. This acidic gas escapes up the chimney with the rest of the exhaust. In the atmosphere the sulfur dioxide dissolves in rain clouds (it reacts with water in the air), so the rain that falls is acidic — acid rain — which damages buildings, plants, lakes and wildlife far from where the fuel was actually burned.
2026-06-1C:5-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:7-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: x = 3.**

*Step 1 — mole ratio:* the student found 1.75 mol of CuSO₄ reacting with 5.25 mol of H₂O. In CuSO₄·xH₂O the value of x is the ratio of water to salt, so x = 5.25 ÷ 1.75 = 3.

*Step 2 — meaning:* every mole of copper(II) sulfate is joined by 3 moles of water of crystallisation, giving the formula CuSO₄·3H₂O. The ratio comes out as a simple whole number because water of crystallisation is incorporated in fixed whole-number amounts.

2026-06-1C:7-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the ⇌ symbol shows that the reaction is reversible.**

A reversible reaction goes both ways: anhydrous copper(II) sulfate can take water in to form the hydrated blue crystals, and the hydrated crystals can lose that water again to give back the white anhydrous powder. Both the forward and the backward change keep happening, so neither direction runs to completion on its own.
2026-06-1C:7-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:7-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: run the reaction forwards and backwards — add water to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, then heat hydrated copper(II) sulfate — and use the colour changes as the observations.**

Experiment 1 (forwards): put a little anhydrous copper(II) sulfate in a dry boiling tube and add a few drops of water. The white powder turns blue as hydrated copper(II) sulfate forms, and the tube feels warm because the change is exothermic.

Experiment 2 (backwards): put some blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals in an evaporating basin (a suitable vessel — a boiling tube works too) and heat them to dryness with a gentle flame. The crystals turn from blue back to white as the water is driven off, and a colourless liquid appears near the cool mouth of the tube — water vapour escaping as steam and condensing to drops.

White to blue on adding water, blue to white on heating: the reaction clearly runs in both directions, so the ⇌ symbol is justified.

2026-06-1C:7-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — black.**

Copper(II) oxide is a black solid. B (blue) is wrong because blue is the colour of hydrated copper(II) sulfate and of copper(II) sulfate solution, not of the oxide; C (green) is wrong because nothing in this reaction is green — the oxide itself is black; D (white) is wrong because white is the colour of the anhydrous sulfate, while the oxide stays black.

2026-06-1C:7-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O.**

Copper(II) oxide is a metal oxide (a base), so it neutralises dilute sulfuric acid: the products are the salt copper(II) sulfate and water. Write the correct reactant formulae — CuO and H₂SO₄ — then the products CuSO₄ and H₂O, and check the atom balance: one Cu, one S, two H and five O on each side, so the chemical equation is balanced with one of everything.
2026-06-1C:7-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:7-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: excess copper(II) oxide is chosen because the leftover solid is easy to remove and it guarantees all the acid is used up.**

CuO is insoluble in water, so once the acid has all reacted, the unreacted black solid can simply be filtered off at the end — and because it is a visible solid you can see when some is left over and the reaction has stopped. That leaves a clean copper(II) sulfate solution with no solid contaminant. The excess also makes sure every trace of acid is used up (neutralised), so no acid can contaminate the crystals when the solution is evaporated to give the product.
2026-06-1C:7-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:7-b-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it will not react with the dilute acid.**

A metal only displaces hydrogen from a dilute acid if it is more reactive than hydrogen. Copper is unreactive — it sits at the bottom of the reactivity series — so copper metal plus dilute sulfuric acid gives no reaction at all: no hydrogen is released and no copper(II) sulfate forms.
2026-06-1C:7-b-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:8-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2,7.**

Fluorine is in Group 7, so a fluorine atom has seven electrons in its outermost shell, with one complete inner shell of two electrons before that. Written in order the shells hold 2 then 7 — the atom is a single electron short of a full outer shell, which is what makes fluorine so reactive.
2026-06-1C:8-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:8-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — Period 2.**

Periods are the horizontal rows of the Periodic Table, numbered by how many shells the atoms fill. Fluorine fills two shells (2,7), so it belongs to Period 2. A (Period 1) is wrong because Period 1 elements use only a single shell; C (Period 3) is wrong because Period 3 atoms occupy three shells; D (Period 7) is wrong because it confuses the period with the group number — fluorine is in Group 7 but sits in Period 2.
2026-06-1C:8-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:8-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: the two fluorine atoms share a pair of electrons — a single covalent bond.**

Each fluorine atom has seven outer electrons, one short of a full outer shell. As the atoms combine, each contributes one electron to a shared pair that sits between the two nuclei; the electrostatic attraction between that shared pair of electrons and both nuclei is the covalent bond itself. Because the shared pair counts towards both atoms, each fluorine now has a full outer shell, giving the F₂ molecule.
2026-06-1C:8-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:8-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 1.6 × 10²⁴ molecules.**

*Step 1 — amount of F₂:* the Mr of F₂ is 38, so amount = mass ÷ Mr = 100 g ÷ 38 g per mol = 2.63 mol.

*Step 2 — molecules:* one mole of fluorine contains 6.0 × 10²³ molecules, so the number of molecules = 2.63 × 6.0 × 10²³, which is approximately 1.6 × 10²⁴ molecules.

*Step 3 — standard form check:* 1.6 × 10²⁴ has a single digit before the decimal point, exactly as standard form requires — keep it in this shape rather than writing it out in full.
2026-06-1C:8-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:8-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: fluorine changes from 2.7 to 2.8 — it gains one electron; lithium changes from 2.1 to 2 — it loses one electron.**

Lithium (configuration 2.1) hands its single outer electron over to a fluorine atom. Losing that electron leaves lithium with just the complete first shell, so its arrangement drops from 2.1 to 2 and the atom becomes a Li⁺ ion. Fluorine takes that electron into its outer shell, so its arrangement rises from 2.7 to 2.8, forming a fluoride ion. Both ions finish with full outer shells, which is what drives the transfer.
2026-06-1C:8-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:8-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions takes a lot of heat energy to break, so lithium fluoride has a high melting point.**

LiF is a giant ionic lattice built from Li⁺ and F⁻ ions. Every ion is pulled on by all of its oppositely charged neighbours through strong electrostatic forces of attraction, and those forces act throughout the whole giant structure. To melt the solid you have to overcome that attraction everywhere at once, which requires a very large amount of energy — hence the high melting point. Keep the explanation about ions: it is nothing to do with weak forces between molecules, and there are no covalent bonds in the lattice.
2026-06-1C:8-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:9-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: C — displacement.**

Beaker 1 has zinc metal standing in iron(II) sulfate solution. Zinc is above iron in the reactivity series, so zinc pushes the iron out of the solution and takes its place — that is a displacement reaction. A (addition) is wrong because two substances are not combining into a single product; B (combustion) is wrong because nothing is burning in oxygen; D (neutralisation) is wrong because there is no acid and base here — both solutions are salts.
2026-06-1C:9-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:9-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: FeSO₄ + Zn → ZnSO₄ + Fe.**

Reactants first: iron(II) sulfate, FeSO₄, and zinc, Zn. In the displacement the zinc takes the place of the iron, so write the correct formulae of the products: zinc sulfate, ZnSO₄, and iron metal, Fe. One zinc atom swaps with one iron ion, so counting atoms gives the same numbers of Fe, S, O and Zn on both sides — the chemical equation is balanced as written.
2026-06-1C:9-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:9-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the oxidising agent is the iron(II) ion, Fe²⁺, in the FeSO₄ solution.**

An oxidising agent is the species that takes electrons in a reaction. In beaker 1 the zinc atoms lose electrons (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻) and those electrons are accepted by the Fe²⁺ ions, which turn into iron atoms. Because the Fe²⁺ ion gains electrons, it causes the zinc to be oxidised — and the species that oxidises another substance by accepting its electrons is the oxidising agent. Name Fe²⁺ rather than iron metal: the metal appearing is the product of the reduction, not the agent doing the oxidising.
2026-06-1C:9-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:9-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: nothing happens in beaker 2 because iron is less reactive than zinc, so it cannot displace zinc from zinc sulfate.**

A displacement reaction needs the added metal to be the more reactive one. Iron sits below zinc in the reactivity series, so no displacement reaction takes place: the iron rod cannot push zinc out of its sulfate solution. With no reaction, the iron stays unchanged and the solution keeps its colour — exactly what the student observes.
2026-06-1C:9-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:9-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: add barium chloride solution (or barium nitrate solution) — a white precipitate confirms sulfate ions.**

Acidify a sample from each beaker first, then add a few drops of barium chloride solution. Sulfate ions combine with the barium ions to make barium sulfate, which is insoluble and shows up as a white precipitate. A white precipitate with both samples proves that both solutions contain sulfate ions. Use a non-sulfate acid such as dilute hydrochloric acid for the acidifying — sulfuric acid would introduce sulfate ions of its own and ruin the test.
2026-06-1C:9-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1C:9-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: acidifying removes other ions that would otherwise react with the barium ions and spoil the result.**

Some negative ions — carbonate ions, for example — also form a white precipitate with barium ions, because barium carbonate is white and insoluble. The acid destroys those interfering ions first: carbonates are reacted away, fizzing carbon dioxide off. With them gone, the only white precipitate that can form is barium sulfate, so the test gives no false white precipitates and the sulfate result can be trusted.
2026-06-1C:9-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:1-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: neutron.**

In the diagram the nucleus holds two kinds of particle: particle Y (the proton, positively charged) and particle Z, which has mass but no charge at all. The uncharged nuclear particle is the neutron; the electrons orbit in shells outside the nucleus.
2026-06-1CR:1-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:1-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: 15.**

The mass number counts the particles in the nucleus. The atom has 7 protons and its nucleus also holds 8 neutrons (15 − 7 = 8), so mass number = 7 + 8 = 15. The 7 electrons outside the nucleus carry almost no mass and are not counted.
2026-06-1CR:1-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:1-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: Group 5, Period 2.**

Count from the electron arrangement. The atom's 7 electrons fill the first shell with 2 and leave 5 in the second shell (2 + 5 = 7). Two occupied shells put the element in Period 2, and the 5 electrons in the outer shell put it in Group 5.
2026-06-1CR:1-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:1-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: the numbers of protons and electrons are equal — 7 of each.**

Every proton carries one positive charge and every electron one negative charge. Because the atom has the same number of protons and electrons — 7 protons balancing 7 electrons — the positive and negative charges cancel exactly and the atom is left with no overall charge.
2026-06-1CR:1-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:1-e-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: nitrogen.**

Seven protons means atomic number 7, and the element with 7 protons is nitrogen (symbol N). That also matches the Group 5, Period 2 position worked out from the shells — exactly where nitrogen sits in the Periodic Table.
2026-06-1CR:1-e-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:1-e-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 3−.**

A nitrogen atom has 5 electrons in its outer shell, so it gains 3 electrons to complete that shell (5 + 3 = 8). Adding three negatively charged electrons leaves the ion with three more electrons than protons, so the ion carries a charge of 3−.
2026-06-1CR:1-e-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:2-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: oxygen (from the air) and water.**

Iron rusts only when both are present together: oxygen from the air and water (moisture) must both reach the metal surface. Keep either one away and the iron does not rust — which is why rusting needs air and moisture at the same time.
2026-06-1CR:2-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:2-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: magnesium.**

Magnesium sits above iron in the reactivity series, so it reacts with dilute sulfuric acid more vigorously and delivers the same volume of hydrogen in a shorter time. Zinc or aluminium would work as well — both are more reactive than iron yet still safe to react with dilute acid in a school laboratory.
2026-06-1CR:2-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:2-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: hold a lighted (burning) splint at the mouth of the tube — the hydrogen ignites with a squeaky pop.**

Collect a tube of the gas and put a lighted splint at its mouth: the hydrogen mixes with air, ignites and the tube pops as the small flame burns the gas. A glowing splint would not do here — the splint must be burning, not just glowing, so the hydrogen can catch light and give the pop.
2026-06-1CR:2-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:2-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: D — basic, giant ionic.**

Iron(III) oxide is a metal oxide, and metal oxides are basic (they neutralise acids); its structure is a giant lattice of Fe³⁺ and O²⁻ ions held by ionic bonding, so it is giant ionic. A (acidic, giant ionic) is wrong because metals do not form acidic oxides; B (basic, simple molecular) is wrong because iron(III) oxide is not made of small molecules — it is a giant ionic lattice; C (acidic, simple molecular) is wrong on both counts.
2026-06-1CR:2-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:3-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: pour solvent into a beaker, stand the paper in it with the spots above the liquid, leave the solvent to rise almost to the top, then dry the paper.**

*Step 1* — pour the solvent into a beaker (or chromatography tank) to a shallow depth. *Step 2* — place the paper in the beaker so its lower edge dips into the solvent while the spots of food colourings A, B, C and D on the pencil start line stay above the solvent level; submerged spots would simply wash off into the solvent instead of travelling up the paper. *Step 3* — leave the paper undisturbed until the solvent has almost reached the top, then mark the level the solvent front reaches. *Step 4* — take the paper out and leave it to dry before examining the separated spots.
2026-06-1CR:3-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:3-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the description of colouring A is a mixture containing two dyes — one that is also present in food colouring B, and a second dye that appears in none of the other colourings.**

The finished chromatogram shows the following for column A: two separated spots. One has travelled exactly as far as the single spot in column B, so that dye is the same substance in both colourings. The other spot in A sits at a height matched by no spot in B, C or D, so A also contains an extra dye of its own.
2026-06-1CR:3-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:3-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: repeat the chromatography using a different solvent (or use thin-layer chromatography).**

Dyes only separate if they dissolve to different extents in the moving solvent, so running the experiment again with a different solvent (for example ethanol or pure water — any named solvent) changes how far each dye travels and can pull the dyes in food colouring D apart.
2026-06-1CR:3-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:3-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: Rf = 0.78 (Rf values have no units).**

The most soluble dye is the one that travels furthest up the paper. Reading the chromatogram: distance moved by the dye = 4.9 cm and distance moved by the solvent = 6.3 cm. Then Rf = 4.9 ÷ 6.3 = 0.78. Careful consistent readings give values anywhere between 0.75 and 0.80, and any value in that window obtained by dye distance ÷ solvent distance is sound.
2026-06-1CR:3-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:4-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: freezing, sublimation, dissolving (in that order).**

Water changing into ice is freezing — a liquid turning to a solid as it cools. Solid iodine changing directly into a vapour skips the liquid state entirely: that is sublimation. Sodium chloride crystals stirred in hot water break up and spread through the liquid: that is dissolving.
2026-06-1CR:4-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:4-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: hot water evaporates faster because its particles have more kinetic energy, so more of them can escape.**

Heating gives the water molecules extra kinetic energy, so they move faster. Moving faster, more molecules can overcome the intermolecular forces holding neighbours together and break away from the liquid surface into the air. In cold water fewer molecules have enough energy to escape, so evaporation is slower.
2026-06-1CR:4-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:4-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: measure the melting point of each solid — the pure solid melts sharply at a single fixed temperature while the impure solid melts over a range of temperatures.**

*Step 1* — warm a small sample of each solid slowly and record the temperature at which it melts. *Step 2* — compare the behaviour: a pure solid has a sharp, definite, fixed melting point, melting completely within a very narrow interval, whereas an impure solid (a mixture) melts gradually over a range of temperatures because the impurities disturb the regular lattice. The solid with the sharp melting point is the pure one; the one that softens and melts bit by bit is the impure one.
2026-06-1CR:4-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:5-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: argon, carbon dioxide, ethene, nitrogen.**

The gas that makes up about 1% by volume of air is argon. Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon burns it in oxygen and produces carbon dioxide (along with water). The gas used to make a polymer is ethene — small ethene molecules add on to each other to build poly(ethene) chains. The gas occurring as diatomic molecules is nitrogen: each N₂ molecule is two nitrogen atoms joined by a covalent bond.
2026-06-1CR:5-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:5-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: both atoms already have full outer shells of electrons, so they neither need to gain nor lose any.**

Helium's single shell is complete with 2 electrons, and neon's outer shell is complete with 8. With a full outer shell already achieved there is no electron transfer or sharing to be done, so these noble-gas atoms stay unreactive.
2026-06-1CR:5-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:5-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: so the final volume is measured at room temperature — a gas expands when hot and the steam made in the reaction must be given time to condense.**

The volume of a gas changes with temperature: heated gas expands and cooled gas shrinks. During the experiment the hydrogen reacts to form water vapour, so recording the volume straight away would catch the remaining gases still hot and expanded, with the steam not yet condensed. Cooling to room temperature first lets the gas contract and the steam condense to liquid, so the recorded volume is the true remaining volume.
2026-06-1CR:5-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:5-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: hydrogen is flammable (explosive), so a naked Bunsen flame could ignite it.**

The gas stream contains hydrogen, which burns in air; a spark or open flame from a Bunsen burner could set the mixture alight. An electric heater supplies the heat needed to reduce the copper(II) oxide with no flame anywhere near the hydrogen.
2026-06-1CR:5-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:5-b-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: 32.0%.**

*Step 1 — volume of hydrogen:* hydrogen is the only gas in the mixture that reacts with the copper(II) oxide, so the fall in volume is the hydrogen: 157.0 − 106.7 = 50.3 cm³.

*Step 2 — percentage:* percentage = 50.3 ÷ 157.0 × 100 = 32.0%.

*Step 3 — rounding:* the question asks for one decimal place, so quote the answer as 32.0%.
2026-06-1CR:5-b-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:5-b-v.solutionMd:
**Answer: it is redox because both changes happen together: copper(II) oxide is reduced and hydrogen is oxidised.**

Copper(II) oxide loses oxygen — the oxygen is taken by the hydrogen — so the copper(II) oxide (more precisely the Cu²⁺ ion) is reduced; in ionic terms the copper ion gains electrons. Hydrogen gains that oxygen and becomes water, so the hydrogen is oxidised; in ionic terms H₂ loses electrons. One reactant losing oxygen while the other gains it is the classic redox pairing, and the equation CuO(s) + H₂(g) → Cu(s) + H₂O(g) shows both halves at once.
2026-06-1CR:5-b-v.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:6-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: NH₄Cl, AlCl₃ and MgO.**

Balance the charges to build each formula. Ammonium is NH₄⁺ and chloride is Cl⁻, so one of each balances: NH₄Cl. Aluminium is Al³⁺ and chloride is Cl⁻, so three chloride ions are needed to cancel one Al³⁺: AlCl₃. Magnesium is Mg²⁺ and oxide is O²⁻ — a 2+ charge against a 2− charge cancels with one of each ion: MgO. The NH₄⁺/O²⁻ cell is the one the table marks as no compound formed, so it stays blank.
2026-06-1CR:6-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:6-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: ammonium nitrate.**

NH₄NO₃ is built from the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, and the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻. Name the positive ion first and the negative ion second: ammonium nitrate — the nitrogen-rich fertiliser salt.
2026-06-1CR:6-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:6-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: 35 g.**

*Step 1 — nitrogen in one mole:* each formula unit of NH₄NO₃ contains 2 nitrogen atoms and Ar(N) = 14, so the nitrogen in one mole weighs 2 × 14 = 28 g.

*Step 2 — fraction that is nitrogen:* the Mr of NH₄NO₃ is 80, so the nitrogen fraction is 28 ÷ 80.

*Step 3 — mass in 100 g:* 28 ÷ 80 × 100 = 35 g.
2026-06-1CR:6-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:6-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.**

In magnesium chloride the positively charged Mg²⁺ ions and negatively charged Cl⁻ ions pull on each other through strong electrostatic attraction — positive attracts negative — and that attraction holds the ions throughout the giant lattice.
2026-06-1CR:6-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:6-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the magnesium atom loses its two outer electrons and the two chlorine atoms each gain one electron.**

One magnesium atom transfers both of its outer-shell electrons away, becoming a Mg²⁺ ion. Each of the two chlorine atoms takes one of those electrons into its outer shell, becoming a Cl⁻ ion. The electrons are transferred, not shared — metal to non-metal electron transfer — and the resulting Mg²⁺ and 2Cl⁻ ions then attract each other to build MgCl₂.
2026-06-1CR:6-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:6-b-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: acidify with dilute nitric acid and add silver nitrate solution — a white precipitate (silver chloride) proves chloride ions.**

Dissolve a little of the magnesium chloride in water, add a few drops of dilute nitric acid, then add silver nitrate solution. Chloride ions react with silver ions to give silver chloride, an insoluble white precipitate. The nitric acid clears away other ions that could form confusing precipitates; use nitric acid specifically, because hydrochloric acid would add chloride ions of its own and spoil the test.
2026-06-1CR:6-b-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:7-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: plot all 9 points from the table with neat crosses.**

Take each pair of values — (0, 0), (1, 16), (2, 18), (3, 30), (4, 36), (5, 40), (6, 40), (7, 40) and (8, 40) — and mark each one with a small ×, reading time in minutes along the horizontal axis and volume of gas up the vertical axis. Each point must sit within half a square of its true position, so count the grid lines carefully rather than estimating.
2026-06-1CR:7-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:7-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: join the points with one smooth curve of best fit, ignoring the anomalous point at 2 minutes.**

The 2-minute reading (18 cm³) sits well below the pattern of the other points — roughly between 16 cm³ at 1 minute and 30 cm³ at 3 minutes — so it is the anomaly and the curve should skip it. Draw a single smooth curved line through the remaining points: the reaction starts fast and gradually slows, so the line rises steeply at first and then flattens. Never rule short straight segments between neighbouring points.
2026-06-1CR:7-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:7-a-iii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the student recorded the volume too early — reading the syringe before the minute was complete.**

If the volume is written down while the plunger is still moving, the gas has not finished collecting and the reading comes out too small for that time. Taking each reading only when the timed minute is complete (and reading the syringe scale level with the eye) removes that mistake.
2026-06-1CR:7-a-iii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:7-a-iv.solutionMd:
**Answer: rest a ruler against the curve at the 4-minute point and draw the straight line that just touches the curve there.**

Set the ruler so it follows the slope of the curve exactly at 4 minutes — touching the curve at that single point without cutting across it — then draw along it. Extend the tangent far enough on both sides of the point to give two well-separated coordinates to read from.
2026-06-1CR:7-a-iv.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:7-a-v.solutionMd:
**Answer: rate = 4.5 cm³/minute.**

*Step 1 — coordinates from the tangent:* my tangent drawn on the graph passes through the plotted point 36 cm³ at 4 minutes and cuts the volume axis at about 18 cm³ at 0 minutes — two well-separated coordinate values.

*Step 2 — gradient:* gradient = 36 − 18 = 18 and then 18 ÷ 4 = 4.5, so the rate of reaction at 4 minutes is 4.5 cm³/minute. The unit is volume ÷ time, i.e. cm³ per minute.
2026-06-1CR:7-a-v.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:7-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: the reaction has finished — all the dilute hydrochloric acid has reacted, so no more hydrogen can be made.**

From 4 minutes onward the volume stays fixed at 40 cm³. The zinc powder is in excess, so zinc cannot be the limiting material; instead the acid has been completely used up. With no acid left there is nothing for the zinc to react with, the reaction has stopped, and the collected gas volume no longer changes.
2026-06-1CR:7-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:8-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: F.** A hydrocarbon contains hydrogen and carbon atoms only. The displayed formula of F shows bromine atoms (Br) joined onto the carbon chain, so F is not a hydrocarbon. Every other compound in the table (A, B, C, D and E) is built from carbon and hydrogen atoms alone, which is exactly what makes them hydrocarbons.
2026-06-1CR:8-a-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

B is the only compound in the table with a C=C double bond; all the others have only single bonds between their carbon atoms (the extra atoms in F are bromine, not a double bond), so they leave bromine water orange.

**Answer: a temperature in the range 600–700 °C, with aluminium oxide (alumina, Al₂O₃) as the catalyst — silicon dioxide (silica, SiO₂) or zeolites/aluminosilicates also work.**

The strong covalent bonds in a long-chain alkane need plenty of heat to break, and the hot catalyst surface speeds the reaction up so cracking happens quickly at this temperature. The temperature has to sit inside the 600–700 °C window: below it the reaction is far too slow, and going above it just wastes energy without improving the products.

2026-06-1CR:8-b-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: cracking converts a long-chain alkane into shorter, more flammable alkanes that are in greater demand as fuels, and into alkenes used to make polymers.**

In C₁₂H₂₆ → C₈H₁₈ + 2C₂H₄ the long hydrocarbon molecule is split into a shorter alkane, C₈H₁₈. Shorter hydrocarbons are more flammable than long-chain ones — they vaporise and ignite more easily — so they are more useful as fuels, and there is a greater demand for short-chain alkanes because they are needed for specific uses such as petrol. The reaction also produces alkenes, such as C₂H₄ (ethene), which are used to make polymers and plastics; alkenes can also be used to make ethanol. Cracking therefore turns surplus, less useful long chains into exactly the products that are needed.
2026-06-1CR:8-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:8-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: the repeat unit is –CH(CH₃)–CH(CH₃)–, drawn inside square brackets with a trailing bond sticking out on each side and the letter n at the bottom right.**

Compound B is but-2-ene, CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃. In addition polymerisation the C=C double bond opens up: the bond between carbon 2 and carbon 3 becomes a single bond, and each of those two carbons keeps its own hydrogen and its CH₃ group as a side branch. The rest of the repeat unit is exactly the atoms of B — two backbone carbons joined by that single bond, each carrying one H and one CH₃. Draw the unit inside square brackets, leave a short trailing bond sticking out from the carbon at each end, and write n at the bottom right outside the bracket to show the huge number of repeats. Do not draw a straight four-carbon chain with two hydrogens on every carbon — that would be butane; the two CH₃ groups must hang off the backbone as branches.

*Step 2 — moles of M:* in M + CuSO₄ → MSO₄ + Cu the mole ratio of M to Cu is 1 : 1, so 2.5 mol of M must have reacted.

In Cu²⁺ + M → Cu + M²⁺ each M atom donates (loses) two electrons, and those electrons are taken up by the Cu²⁺ ion. The species that gives away electrons is called the reducing agent, because by handing electrons over it makes the other species gain them. So M donates electrons to Cu²⁺, the copper ions are reduced to copper atoms, and M is itself oxidised to M²⁺ in the process.

2026-06-1CR:10-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: neutralisation.** A metal oxide reacting with an acid to give a salt plus water is an acid-base reaction: the oxide neutralises the acid. Here zinc oxide is the base, sulfuric acid is the acid, and the products are the salt zinc sulfate and water — the classic acid-plus-base outcome.

2026-06-1CR:10-a-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the sulfuric acid gives protons (H⁺ ions) to the zinc oxide.**

In terms of protons, an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor. Each sulfuric acid molecule donates H⁺ ions (protons) to the zinc oxide, and the zinc oxide takes up those protons — that proton transfer is what turns the oxide into water and leaves the zinc behind in the salt, zinc sulfate.

2026-06-1CR:10-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: add excess zinc carbonate to the acid, filter, then heat, cool and crystallise, filter again and dry the crystals.**

*Step 1 — react:* add the zinc carbonate powder to the 50 cm³ of dilute sulfuric acid a little at a time with stirring, until no more zinc carbonate reacts — the effervescence (fizzing) stops and a little excess powder just sits there without dissolving. Using excess powder guarantees all of the acid is used up.

*Step 2 — filter:* filter the mixture to remove the excess zinc carbonate, leaving a clear solution of zinc sulfate.

*Step 3 — concentrate:* heat the solution gently so that some of the water evaporates and the solution becomes saturated. Stop while it is still only partly evaporated — never heat it to dryness, because the crystals would spit and the water of crystallisation would be driven off.

*Step 4 — crystallise:* leave the warm solution somewhere to cool slowly. As it cools, hydrated zinc sulfate crystals grow.

*Step 5 — separate and dry:* filter off the crystals, then dry them by patting with filter paper or a paper towel, or by leaving them in a warm place (a warm oven is fine — a hot oven or a direct Bunsen flame is not, as it would cook the crystals). That leaves dry crystals of hydrated zinc sulfate.

2026-06-1CR:11-a.solutionMd: **Answer: they contain only one type of atom.** Diamond, C₆₀ fullerene and graphite are three different structures, but every atom inside each of them is a carbon atom. An element is a substance whose atoms are all the same kind, so all three are different forms (allotropes) of the element carbon — the atoms are just arranged differently in each structure.
2026-06-1CR:11-a.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:11-b.solutionMd:
**Answer: graphite has weak forces between its layers, so the layers can slide over one another.**

Within a layer each carbon atom is held to its neighbours by strong covalent bonds, but the forces holding one whole layer to the next are weak. When a force is applied — a pencil pressed onto paper, for example — the layers slip over each other and stay behind as graphite smears. That easy sliding of the layers is exactly what makes graphite a useful lubricant.
2026-06-1CR:11-b.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-1CR:11-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: diamond is a giant covalent lattice held together by strong covalent bonds running in every direction, while C₆₀ fullerene is a simple molecular substance whose molecules are held to each other only by weak intermolecular forces — so boiling diamond needs far more energy.**

*Diamond:* every carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others, producing a giant lattice that continues throughout the whole crystal. To boil diamond you have to break strong covalent bonds everywhere in that structure, which takes a very large amount of energy, so diamond's boiling point is extremely high.

*C₆₀ fullerene:* the bonds inside each C₆₀ molecule are covalent and strong, but the substance is simple molecular — the C₆₀ molecules are only attracted to their neighbours by weak intermolecular forces. Boiling does not break the covalent bonds inside the molecules; it only has to overcome the weak forces between the molecules to separate them, and that needs very little energy.

*The comparison:* breaking covalent bonds throughout the giant diamond lattice demands much more thermal energy than overcoming the weak intermolecular forces between C₆₀ fullerene molecules, which is why diamond has a much higher boiling point.
2026-06-1CR:11-c.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-2C:1-a.solutionMd:
**Answer: alkene — a monomer used to make an addition polymer; dicarboxylic acid — a monomer used to make a condensation polymer; condensation — the type of polymer that biodegrades; water — the product of condensation polymerisation.**

Alkenes carry a C=C double bond, so many alkene molecules can open their double bonds and add together end-to-end into long addition-polymer chains. Condensation polymerisation instead joins two different monomers, and a dicarboxylic acid (a molecule with two -COOH groups) is one of the monomers used, usually linked with a diol. Condensation polymers such as polyesters can be broken down by micro-organisms, so this type of polymer biodegrades, unlike addition polymers. Every time two monomers join in condensation polymerisation a small molecule is lost, and that product is water.

The two names left over do not fit anywhere: an alkane has no double bond, so it cannot open up as an addition monomer, and poly(chloroethene) is itself a polymer — not a monomer and not a small-molecule product.

B is not the correct answer because its drawing still shows a double bond that has not been opened up — a repeat unit must contain only single bonds, so it fails. In an open beaker the reactants and products keep escaping into the air — ethanol and ethyl ethanoate are both volatile and evaporate easily — so the amounts of substances present never stop changing and the equilibrium position cannot settle. (There is no sulfuric acid catalyst added either, so even in a closed vessel the reaction would be far too slow to get anywhere near equilibrium.)

2026-06-2C:5-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: a catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.**

Rather than forcing particles over the original high energy barrier, the catalyst offers a different route whose activation energy is lower. With the lower activation energy, many more collisions have energy equal to or greater than the minimum needed, so more collisions lead to reaction and both directions go faster. The catalyst is not consumed — it comes out unchanged at the end.
2026-06-2C:5-c-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-2C:5-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: the yield of ethyl ethanoate at equilibrium would not change.**

A catalyst increases the rate of the forward reaction and the backward reaction equally — it provides a lower-energy route for both directions — so equilibrium is simply reached sooner while the position of equilibrium stays put. Since the equilibrium position is unchanged, the amount of ethyl ethanoate at equilibrium is unchanged too; the yield is exactly what it would have been without the catalyst, only arriving earlier.
2026-06-2C:5-c-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-2C:5-d.solutionMd:
**Answer: raising the temperature lowers the equilibrium yield of ethyl ethanoate, but makes equilibrium arrive faster.**

*Effect on yield:* the forwards reaction (ester formation) is exothermic, so the backwards reaction is endothermic. When the temperature is increased, the system opposes that change by favouring the direction that takes heat in — the endothermic, backwards direction — so the equilibrium position shifts to the left, towards the reactants, and the yield of ethyl ethanoate at equilibrium decreases.

*Effect on rate:* at the higher temperature every particle has more kinetic energy and moves faster, so collisions become more frequent, and a bigger fraction of them involve energy equal to or greater than the activation energy — more frequent successful collisions. The rate therefore increases, and equilibrium is reached sooner even though there is less ester waiting at the end.
2026-06-2C:5-d.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-2C:3-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: a covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positive nuclei of the two bonded atoms.**

Two atoms each put one electron (or more) into a shared pair, and that negatively charged pair sits between the two nuclei, attracting both of them at once. This mutual electrostatic attraction between the shared pair of electrons and the positive nuclei is the force that holds the atoms together in the molecule.

2026-06-2C:3-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: because there are no charged particles free to move through the structure.** Covalent compounds contain no delocalised electrons — every electron is locked into a shared pair or an inner shell — and no ions either. With nothing charged and free to move, no current can flow through them however large a voltage is applied, which is why covalent substances do not conduct electricity.

The electrodes dip into molten lead(II) bromide at 400 °C, so the electrode material must carry the current and survive the heat without melting or reacting. Graphite does all of this: it conducts electricity, it has a very high melting point, and it is unreactive so it does not react with the products formed at the electrodes. (Platinum or another unreactive, high-melting metal would also be a suitable choice.)

2026-06-2C:3-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: cations.** Positive ions are called cations — the name literally points at the electrode they move towards, because during electrolysis cations are attracted to the negative electrode (the cathode). The lead ions in this electrolysis are cations, and they collect lead metal at the cathode.

**Answer: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.**

At the positive electrode each bromide ion loses its extra electron — that loss is oxidation — and the two bromine atoms produced pair up into one bromine molecule. The half-equation shows exactly that: two Br⁻ ions on the left, one Br₂ molecule plus two electrons released on the right, keeping the atoms and the charge balanced.

2026-06-2C:3-c-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: molten sodium chloride gives sodium at the negative electrode; aqueous sodium chloride gives hydrogen at the negative electrode.**

In the molten compound the only positive ion present is Na⁺, so sodium metal forms at the negative electrode. In the aqueous solution there is a second positive ion — the H⁺ ions from water — and because hydrogen is less reactive than sodium, the H⁺ ions are discharged instead and hydrogen gas bubbles off. (The table already shows chlorine at the positive electrode in both cases.)

2026-06-2C:3-c-ii.solutionMd:
**Answer: chloride ions migrate to the positive electrode, lose their extra electrons, and the chlorine atoms pair up into chlorine molecules.**

*Step 1 — attraction:* the negative Cl⁻ ions move through the solution towards the positive electrode (the anode), which attracts them.

*Step 2 — electron loss:* each chloride ion gives up its extra electron to the electrode, so a neutral chlorine atom forms — Cl⁻ → Cl + e⁻.

*Step 3 — pairing:* two chlorine atoms then combine in pairs to form chlorine molecules, Cl₂, which bubble off as gas. The overall half-equation is 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.

2026-06-2CR:2-a-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — electrons are free to move in the solid.**

Solid aluminium is a metal: its outer electrons are delocalised, meaning they are not attached to any one aluminium atom, so they drift through the whole lattice and carry charge from place to place. That moving charge is the electric current.

Why the other options fail: B adds neutrons to the claim, but neutrons sit inside the nucleus and are never free to move, so they cannot carry charge. C adds protons, but protons are also locked inside the nucleus and cannot flow through the solid. D claims the ions move, but in solid aluminium the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice — only the electrons flow (ions only become mobile in a molten metal or in solution).

2026-06-2CR:2-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: aluminium is malleable because its layers of atoms can slide over one another.** In the metallic lattice the aluminium atoms (positive ions surrounded by delocalised electrons) are arranged in neat layers. When a force is applied, those layers can slide over one another and settle into new positions without the metallic bonding breaking, so the metal bends and reshapes instead of shattering. It is the layers that slide — not the electrons, and not any negative ions, since there are none in a metal lattice.
2026-06-2CR:2-a-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-2CR:2-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — aluminium is more reactive than carbon.**

Carbon removes oxygen from the oxides of metals that are less reactive than itself. Aluminium sits above carbon in the reactivity series, so carbon cannot pull the oxygen away from aluminium oxide — heating the two together simply gives no reaction, and electrolysis is needed instead.

Why the other options fail: B says carbon is an oxidising agent, but in these reactions carbon gains oxygen, so it is acting as the reducing agent, not an oxidising agent. C says the reaction has a low activation energy, but the opposite is true — the barrier is a very high activation energy, which ordinary heating cannot supply. D says the reaction is explosive, but nothing that dramatic happens: carbon and aluminium oxide simply do not react with each other.
2026-06-2CR:2-b-i.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-2CR:2-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: oxygen.** In the molten aluminium oxide the negative oxide ions (O²⁻) migrate to the positive electrode, where each loses electrons and the atoms pair up as oxygen gas: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻. The aluminium ions do the opposite and gain electrons at the negative electrode to form the molten aluminium.
2026-06-2CR:2-b-ii.source: authored from the printed QP + MS of record (topic.json solution_md + mark_points)

2026-06-2CR:2-b-iii.solutionMd: **Answer: aluminium oxide has a high melting point, so the process needs a lot of energy.** The oxide has to be kept molten for the electrolysis to work at all, and holding a large industrial cell at that high temperature while pushing big currents through it consumes a huge amount of energy and electricity — that running cost is what makes the extraction of aluminium expensive.

2026-06-2CR:2-c.solutionMd: **Answer: aluminium has a low density, so the can is light to carry.** It brings other useful properties to a drinks can too: it is unreactive with the drink inside, it is strong, non-toxic and corrosion resistant, and it can be recycled. 2026-06-2CR:5-c-i.solutionMd: **Answer: combustion is exothermic because more energy is given out when the new bonds are made than is taken in when the original bonds are broken.** Breaking bonds always takes in energy, and making bonds always releases energy. There is a net release of energy to the surroundings, so the mixture warms up: that surplus is what makes the reaction exothermic.

*The arrow:* draw a single-headed arrow pointing downwards from the reactant level to the product level and label it ΔH, since the negative enthalpy change is the fall in energy between the two levels.

*Step 2 — amount of sugar burned:* the equation B + y O2 → 12CO2 + zH2O shows that each mole of sugar B makes 12 mol of CO2, so the amount of sugar B is 0.3 ÷ 12 = 0.025 mol.

*Step 3 — relative formula mass:* 8.55 g of sugar B was burned, so Mr = 8.55 ÷ 0.025 = 342.

The mass divided by the amount in moles gives the Mr of sugar B as 342.

2026-06-2CR:7-a-i.solutionMd: **Answer: the reaction is reversible.** The ⇌ symbol means the reaction goes in both directions at the same time: ammonia and oxygen react to form nitrogen monoxide and steam, while at the same time nitrogen monoxide and steam react to re-form the ammonia and oxygen. Both the forward and the backward reaction are always happening.

2026-06-2CR:7-a-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: dynamic equilibrium means the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.** Both reactions never stop — molecules keep forming products in one direction and breaking back down in the other, at an equal rate — so in the closed system there is no overall change in the amounts of reactants and products. Constant does not mean equal: the two concentrations stay steady, but they do not have to be the same as each other.

2026-06-2CR:7-b-i.solutionMd:
**Answer: the rate of reaction increases, but the yield of products decreases.**

Rate of reaction: raising the temperature from 800 °C to 1000 °C gives every particle more kinetic energy, so many more collisions have energy greater than the activation energy, and the faster-moving particles also collide more often. More frequent successful collisions per unit time means the rate of reaction increases.

Yield of products: the forward reaction 4NH3 + 5O2 → 4NO + 6H2O is exothermic — ΔH is −900 kJ/mol, and a negative ΔH means energy is released going forwards. When the temperature is raised, the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction, which is the backwards reaction here, to absorb the extra energy. So the position of equilibrium moves to the left and the yield of products decreases, even though equilibrium is reached sooner. The pressure stays at 10 atm throughout, so pressure causes no extra change in the yield.

2026-06-2CR:7-b-ii.solutionMd: **Answer: because the rate of reaction would be too slow.** At a lower pressure the gas particles are spread further apart, so collisions between the molecules happen less often and less frequently per second. The plant would then make nitrogen monoxide — and downstream, nitric acid — far too slowly to be economic, even though a lower pressure would raise the yield.

2026-06-2CR:7-c.solutionMd:
**Answer: rinse the burette with the sodium hydroxide solution before filling, measure the acid with a volumetric pipette, rinse the conical flask with distilled water, add the sodium hydroxide dropwise near the end point while swirling, and repeat the titration until the results are concordant.**

Rinsing the burette with sodium hydroxide before filling removes any water or air bubbles left inside, so the solution that runs out is at its true concentration. Measuring the 25.0 cm3 of nitric acid with a volumetric pipette fixes that volume much more precisely than pouring. Rinsing the conical flask with distilled or deionised water clears out residues without touching the amount of acid, because the water adds no extra acid to neutralise. A white tile under the flask makes the methyl orange colour change easy to see against a pale background. Swirling the flask as the alkali runs in keeps every drop mixed through the solution, and near the end point the sodium hydroxide should be added dropwise so the first permanent colour change is caught exactly. Finally, record the burette reading at that end point and repeat the whole titration until two results agree within 0.1–0.2 cm3 — those concordant titres give an accurate value for the volume of sodium hydroxide that neutralises the acid.
